items.name: 90/90 hip lift
items.equipment: A wall, plus a rolled hand towel or a small inflatable ball — the 5–6 inch kind, like a child's playground ball — to hold between the knees
items.dose: 5 breaths. Once or twice a day.
items.why: Breathing is upstream of most of it. Everything else on this list is downstream effect.

fields.tool: A wall, plus a rolled hand towel or a small inflatable ball — the 5–6 inch kind, like a child's playground ball — to hold between the knees
fields.release: Lie on your back with your feet flat on a wall, hips about a foot out from it. Knees bent 90° and hips bent 90°, so your shins are parallel to the floor. Put the towel or ball between your knees. Squeeze it lightly and keep squeezing the whole time. Exhale through pursed lips, slowly, and keep going about 3 seconds past the point where you would normally stop. This is the part that matters — the last of the air is what drops the ribs out of flare. As you exhale, push your heels into the wall until your tailbone lifts about an inch off the floor. An inch. Your low back should flatten against the floor. Hold empty for 3 seconds. Let air fall back in through your nose without releasing the position or the knee squeeze.
fields.notice: Low back rests flat on the floor without you holding it there. Ribs feel dropped rather than flared. This is the drill that most directly targets the anterior tilt and rib flare you identified yourself. Hamstrings and low abdominals working. If you feel your quads, low back, or hip flexors, you have lifted too high — come down.
fields.careful: This is not a glute bridge. An inch of lift, no more. If you get lightheaded, stop and breathe normally for a minute — that is the CO2 shift, and it settles as tolerance builds.

photos.caption: Not the drill, but it shows the tilt underneath it. Yours is an inch of lift with the feet on a wall, on a long exhale.

items.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
items.why: Both knees at 90 degrees, switch sides by rotating hips

fields.release: Sit on the floor with both knees bent at 90 degrees, one leg in front and one behind, creating a "90/90" position. Rotate your hips to switch both legs to the other side so the front leg becomes the back leg and vice versa. Keep your chest tall throughout. This exercise mobilizes the hips through internal and external rotation.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hips, hip internal rotation, hip external rotation.

items.name: A lift, and a full let-go
items.why: The load partner for every pelvic floor item here. And note what it is called — the release is half of the exercise, not an afterthought. A muscle that can only contract is not strong; it is stuck.

fields.tool: Nothing.
fields.release:
Lying or sitting comfortably. Breathe out, and as you do, gently draw the base of your pelvis up and in — a lift, not a clench, and much smaller than most people produce on the first attempt. Then breathe in and let it go completely, all the way back down to where it started. The letting go should take at least as long as the lift and should feel like a real release, not just stopping.

Gentle effort. If your buttocks squeeze, your inner thighs grip, your belly hardens, or you hold your breath, the effort is too big — halve it.
fields.notice: Whether the release is as clear as the lift. Many people can lift and cannot fully let go, and finding that out is worth more than any number of repetitions. Whether anything else joins in.
fields.careful: No bearing down, ever. Gentle. If you have symptoms — leaking, pain, heaviness, difficulty emptying — get an assessment before building a programme around this, because the right instruction for you depends on which problem you have, and an app cannot tell.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: pelvic floor symptoms are more common with hypermobility and both over- and under-activity occur. The case for a pelvic floor physiotherapist's assessment is stronger for you rather than weaker. Orthostatic: lying or supported sitting.
items.dose: [undetermined] — this is precisely the parameter that should come from an assessment rather than from an app, because the right number depends on which problem you have.

levels.name: Find the release
levels.note: One small lift, one long full let-go. The let-go is the rung.

levels.name: Coordinate with the breath
levels.note: Lift on the out-breath, release on the in-breath, several times.

levels.name: In upright positions
levels.note: The same, sitting and then standing, where the floor actually has to work.

evidence.grade: Pelvic floor muscle training is established first-line care for several pelvic floor conditions; the relaxation half is supported by expert consensus and small series rather than large trials.
evidence.basis: Pelvic floor muscle training is recommended as first-line management for pelvic floor dysfunction by international bodies. Down-training for the high-tone presentation rests on expert consensus and treatment algorithms plus pilot studies and clinical series. Also relevant and often not said: breathing-based approaches alone are not effective for strengthening the pelvic floor — which is why this item exists alongside the breath items rather than being replaced by them.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: A-Skip
items.why: Drive knee up, skip with purpose, stay tall

fields.release: Move forward in a skipping motion, driving one knee up toward your chest with each skip while staying tall and pumping your arms. Focus on getting height with each skip rather than distance. This drill improves running mechanics, hip flexor power, and coordination. Land on the ball of your foot and maintain an upright posture.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors, calves.

items.name: Ab Wheel / Rollout
items.why: Brace hard, roll out controlled, pull back with abs not hips

fields.release: Kneel on the floor and place your hands on an ab wheel or a towel on a smooth surface. Brace your core hard and slowly roll forward, extending your body as far as you can without letting your lower back sag. Pull yourself back to the starting position using your abs, not your hips. Start with a small range of motion and gradually extend further as you build strength.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, lats.

levels.name: Knee Rollout (Towel)
levels.note: Towel on smooth floor, from knees

levels.name: Standing Rollout to Wall
levels.note: Stand, roll to wall for stop

items.name: Acupressure / acupuncture
items.why: Stimulates meridian points — relieves pain, supports organ function, reduces stress

items.name: Acupressure mat
items.dose: 15–20 minutes, 3–4× a week. Evening works best.
items.why: Direct downregulation. Cheap, and most of it needs no equipment at all.

fields.tool: The mat you already have
fields.release: Lie on it, bare back if you can tolerate it, for 15–20 minutes. Run extended-exhale breathing the entire time. This is what turns it from a sensation into a nervous system drill. The first 2–3 minutes are unpleasant, then it flips to warmth. Wait for the flip.
fields.notice: You said yourself that it helps and that you underuse it. Attach it to a fixed cue — after dinner, or while reading — rather than relying on remembering.
fields.careful: Your skin bruises and marks easily. A thin t-shirt for the first few sessions is a sensible place to start.

items.name: All-fours belly lift
items.why: Breathing is upstream of most of it. Everything else on this list is downstream effect.

fields.tool: None
fields.release: Hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Round your low back slightly and tuck your tailbone under — the opposite of the arch you default into. Exhale fully through pursed lips. At the bottom, without inhaling, draw your belly up toward your spine and hold 3 seconds. Inhale through your nose and aim the air into the BACK of your rib cage — imagine widening the space between your shoulder blades. Keep the tuck the whole time.
fields.notice: You can feel your back widen on the inhale rather than your chest rising. Strange at first. Most people have never breathed into the back of the ribs and it takes a few sessions to find.
fields.careful: This one makes people lightheaded faster than the 90/90. Sit back on your heels if it does.

photos.caption: The belly-lift mechanic, standing: exhale everything out, then draw the navel up toward the spine and hold. Yours is the same draw on all fours with the tailbone tucked, then breathing into the BACK of the ribs.

items.name: Ankle CARs
items.why: Slow controlled circles through full ankle range of motion

fields.release: Sit or stand on one leg and slowly draw large circles with your foot by moving your ankle through its full range of motion. Move clockwise for several reps, then counterclockwise. CARs (Controlled Articular Rotations) help maintain and improve joint health. Keep the movement slow and deliberate, exploring every part of the range.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: ankles, calves, tibialis.

items.name: Ankle Hops
items.why: Stiff ankles, quick bounce, minimal ground contact time

fields.release: Stand tall and bounce up and down using only your ankles and calves, keeping your knees nearly straight. The goal is to spend as little time on the ground as possible with each bounce. Think of your ankles as stiff springs. This builds ankle stiffness and reactive strength, which is important for running and jumping performance.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, ankles.

items.name: Arm Circles
items.why: Arms straight out, controlled circles, both directions

fields.release: Stand tall and extend both arms straight out to your sides at shoulder height. Make small controlled circles with your arms, gradually increasing the size. Perform circles in both forward and backward directions. You should feel a burn in your shoulders; keep your core engaged and avoid shrugging.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders.

items.name: Around the sitting bones — external only
items.why: The pelvic floor attaches to bone you can actually find and sit on. This is as close as external work gets, and for many people it is the first time anything in the area has responded to direct contact.
items.equipment: A soft ball and a firm chair

fields.tool: A soft or air-filled ball on a firm chair. Not a hard ball — this area does not want one.
fields.release: Sit on a firm chair and find your sitting bones by rocking side to side; they are the two bony points taking your weight. Place a soft ball just to the inside of one of them and sit onto it gently, taking weight through your feet and hands so you control the pressure. Hold. Then let the breath work run underneath — breathe wide, and let the area soften into the ball on each in-breath.
fields.notice: Whether one side is tenderer. Whether the area softens under the contact or stays braced. Whether you are holding your breath, which is almost universal the first few times.
fields.careful: Just inside the sitting bone and no further forward — this item stays on the muscle beside the bone and does not go near anything else. Soft ball, light weight, short. Numbness, pins and needles, or shooting sensation into the leg means come off immediately: a large nerve passes through this region. If you have haemorrhoids, tailbone pain, recent pelvic surgery, or any pelvic pain condition, skip this and take it to a pelvic floor physiotherapist instead.
fields.load: Hip work — glutes and deep rotators — plus the lift-and-release item.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: bruising risk, soft ball only, and less weight than feels productive. Orthostatic: sitting item, no floor transfer required, which makes it one of the easier ones in this file for you.

levels.name: Find the sitting bones
levels.note: Rocking to locate them, no ball. Knowing where they are is genuinely useful on its own.

loadAfter.name: A lift, and a full let-go

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Around the tailbone
items.why: The back edge of the pelvic floor attaches near the tailbone, and so do muscles running up into the low back. It is a place that gets sore from sitting and that almost nobody addresses.
items.equipment: A soft ball or a folded towel

fields.tool: A soft ball, or a folded towel if a ball is too much.
fields.release: Lying on your back with knees bent, place a soft ball just to one side of the tailbone — beside it, on the muscle, never on the bone itself. Let your weight settle gently. Breathe. Then the other side. Alternatively, seated on a firm chair, place a folded towel just to one side of the tailbone and lean slightly into it.
fields.notice: Whether the two sides feel different. Whether this area is tender in a way you had not realised — very common in people who sit a lot or who tuck the pelvis under habitually.
fields.careful: Beside the tailbone, never on it. If you have had a tailbone injury, tailbone pain, or pain sitting, this item is not for you and belongs with a clinician. Soft ball, light pressure, short.
fields.load: Pelvic tilting through a full comfortable range, and glute work — a tucked-under pelvis is usually the reason this area is loaded in the first place.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: bruising over bony areas happens readily; soft ball and light pressure only. Orthostatic: the seated version avoids floor transfers entirely.

levels.name: Seated, folded towel
levels.note: The gentlest version, and enough for most people.

levels.name: Lying, soft ball
levels.note: Slightly more pressure, one side at a time.

loadAfter.name: Pelvic tilts through full range
loadAfter.note: The existing rise-block hip rocks may cover this. Match at S5.

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Assisted hang
items.why: Re-test: Every 2 weeks. Higher is better.

fields.release: Feet partly on the ground, shoulder blades pulled DOWN. Time until the blades give up and the shoulders ride toward the ears. Stop there — the seconds after that are not the thing being measured.
fields.notice: Recorded in sec.

items.name: Balance Board Plank
items.why: Plank with hands or feet on board, keep it stable

fields.release: Set up in a plank position with either your hands or feet on a balance board. Hold the plank while keeping the board as stable as possible. The unstable surface increases the demand on your shoulders and core. Start with the board under your hands (easier) and progress to having it under your feet for a greater challenge.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: core, shoulders.

levels.name: Plank + Tap
levels.note: Tap shoulder or hip while balancing

items.name: Balance Board Push-Up
items.why: Push-up with hands or feet on board, stay balanced

fields.release: Perform push-ups with either your hands or feet on a balance board. Keep the board as level and stable as possible throughout each rep. The instability forces your stabilizer muscles to work overtime, making this a more challenging version of the standard push-up. Use a slow, controlled tempo to maintain balance.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, core.

levels.name: Alternating
levels.note: Switch hand/feet on board each set

items.name: Balance Board Single-Leg Stand
items.why: One foot on board, keep it level, stay tall and stable

fields.release: Stand on a balance board with one foot in the center. Keep the board as level as possible while standing tall. Focus on keeping your ankle, knee, and hip stable. This is excellent for developing ankle proprioception and balance, which helps prevent sprains and improves athletic performance. Use a wall for support when starting out.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: ankles, core.

items.name: Balance Board Squat
items.why: Stand on board, keep it level, squat with control

fields.release: Stand on a balance board with feet roughly shoulder-width apart. Once you have your balance, perform controlled squats while keeping the board as level as possible. The unstable surface forces your ankles and core to work much harder than a normal squat. Start by just balancing on the board before adding the squat movement.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, ankles, core.

items.name: Band Pull-Apart
items.why: Arms straight in front, pull band apart to chest level

fields.release: Hold a resistance band in front of you at shoulder height with arms straight and hands about shoulder-width apart. Pull the band apart by squeezing your shoulder blades together until the band touches your chest, then slowly return. Keep your arms straight throughout. This exercise strengthens the rear delts and rhomboids for better posture.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: rear delts, rhomboids.

items.name: Banded Ankle Dorsiflexion
items.why: Band pulls ankle back, drive knee forward over toes

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band low and loop it around the front of your ankle. Face away from the anchor point in a half-kneeling position. The band pulls your ankle backward, creating a distraction force. Drive your knee forward over your toes against the band resistance. This improves ankle dorsiflexion, which is crucial for squatting depth and athletic performance.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: tibialis anterior, ankles.

items.name: Banded Chest Fly
items.why: Band behind back, press hands together in front, squeeze chest

fields.release: Loop a resistance band around your upper back and hold each end in your hands. Stand with arms out to the sides. Press your hands together in front of your chest against the band resistance, squeezing your chest muscles hard. Slowly open back to the starting position. This replicates a cable fly and is great for building chest definition without heavy weights.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest.

items.name: Banded Crab Walk
items.why: Band above knees, quarter squat, step laterally with tension

fields.release: Place a resistance band just above your knees and stand in a quarter-squat position with feet hip-width apart. Step sideways with one foot, maintaining tension in the band, then follow with the other foot. Keep your hips low and your knees pushed outward against the band. You should feel this in your outer glutes and hip abductors.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hip abductors.

items.name: Banded Curl
items.why: Stand on band, curl with elbows pinned

fields.release: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with both feet and hold the ends in each hand. Curl your hands up toward your shoulders, keeping your elbows pinned at your sides throughout the movement. Lower with control. The band provides increasing resistance at the top, which matches where your biceps are strongest.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: biceps.

items.name: Banded Deadlift
items.why: Stand on band, hinge and grip, drive hips forward to stand

fields.release: Stand on the center of a resistance band with both feet, hip-width apart. Grab the ends of the band and hinge at the hips with a flat back, lowering the band toward the floor. Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return to standing. Keep the band close to your body and your back flat throughout. This mimics a barbell deadlift pattern.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings, glutes.

items.name: Banded Face Pull
items.why: Pull band to face, elbows high, squeeze rear delts

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band at about face height. Hold both ends and step back to create tension. Pull the band toward your face with elbows high and wide, squeezing your rear deltoids and upper back at the end position. Return slowly. This exercise is excellent for posture and shoulder health.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: rear delts, upper back.

items.name: Banded Good Morning
items.why: Band over neck, hinge at hips, flat back, squeeze glutes to stand

fields.release: Loop a resistance band around the back of your neck and step on both ends with your feet. Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at the hips with a flat back, pushing your butt back until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings. Squeeze your glutes to drive your hips forward and return to standing. Keep the band taut throughout.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings, lower back.

items.name: Banded Hip Abduction
items.why: Band above knees, push knees apart against resistance

fields.release: Place a resistance band just above your knees. From a standing, seated, or side-lying position, push your knees apart against the band resistance. Hold briefly at the widest point, then slowly return. You should feel this in the outer portion of your glutes. This is an excellent activation exercise for the hip abductors and glute medius.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hip abductors.

levels.name: Side-Lying
levels.note: Lying on side, open top leg

items.name: Banded Hip Flexor Stretch
items.why: Band pulls hip forward into extension, squeeze glute, breathe

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band at a low point behind you and loop it around the front of your hip crease. Step forward into a half-kneeling lunge position. The band pulls your hip forward, creating a distraction that deepens the hip flexor stretch. Squeeze the glute on the kneeling side and breathe deeply to increase the stretch.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors.

items.name: Banded Hip Thrust
items.why: Band over hips, drive up, squeeze glutes hard at top

fields.release: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Loop a resistance band across your hips and anchor it to the floor with your hands. Drive your hips up toward the ceiling against the band resistance, squeezing your glutes as hard as possible at the top. Lower with control. The band adds resistance at the top where your glutes are strongest.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes.

items.name: Banded Lat Pulldown
items.why: Anchor band high, pull elbows to ribs, squeeze lats

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band at a high point above you. Kneel or stand facing the anchor and grab both ends of the band with arms extended overhead. Pull your elbows down to your ribs, squeezing your lats hard at the bottom, then slowly extend your arms back up. Think about driving your elbows into your back pockets.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lats, biceps.

items.name: Banded Leg Press
items.why: Lie on back, band around feet, press out against resistance

fields.release: Lie on your back and loop a resistance band around both feet. Bend your knees toward your chest and press your feet out against the band resistance, extending your legs at roughly a 45-degree angle. Slowly return to the bent position. Keep your lower back pressed into the floor throughout. This mimics a leg press without any equipment beyond a band.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

levels.name: Heavy
levels.note: Heavy band, lying with feet pressing band

items.name: Banded Monster Walk
items.why: Band above knees or at ankles, walk in wide steps, stay low

fields.release: Place a resistance band around your ankles or just above your knees. Get into a quarter-squat position and walk forward in exaggerated wide steps, maintaining tension in the band at all times. Keep your hips low and your toes pointing forward. You should feel this in your glutes and outer hips. This is an excellent glute activation exercise for warmups.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hip abductors.

items.name: Banded Overhead Press
items.why: Stand on band, press overhead, brace core, full lockout

fields.release: Stand on the center of a resistance band with both feet and hold the ends at shoulder height. Brace your core and press both hands straight overhead until your arms are fully locked out, then lower back to shoulder height. Avoid arching your lower back. The band provides increasing resistance as you press higher, which builds strong shoulders.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders.

items.name: Banded Push-Up
items.why: Band across upper back, loop around hands, push through

fields.release: Loop a resistance band across your upper back and hold each end under your palms as you set up in a push-up position. Perform push-ups as normal; the band adds resistance at the top of the movement where you are strongest. Keep your body in a straight line and fully lock out each rep.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, triceps.

items.name: Banded Row
items.why: Wrap band around feet or anchor low, pull elbows back

fields.release: Sit on the floor with legs extended and loop a resistance band around your feet, or anchor it to a low point in front of you. Sit tall, grab both ends of the band, and pull your elbows straight back, squeezing your shoulder blades together. Return to the start with control. Keep your chest lifted and avoid rounding your back.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: back, biceps.

items.name: Banded Shoulder Dislocate
items.why: Wide grip on band, pass it over head and behind back, arms straight

fields.release: Hold a resistance band in front of you with a wide grip and straight arms. Slowly raise the band overhead and continue the arc behind you until it touches your lower back, keeping your arms straight the entire time. Reverse the motion back to the front. Use a wider grip if you cannot complete the full range. This opens the shoulders and chest.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, chest.

items.name: Banded Shoulder External Rotation
items.why: Elbow at side, rotate forearm outward against band

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band at elbow height. Stand sideways to the anchor and hold the band with the far hand, elbow bent at 90 degrees and pinned to your side. Rotate your forearm outward away from your body against the band resistance, then return slowly. This strengthens the rotator cuff and is essential for shoulder health and injury prevention.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: rotator cuff.

items.name: Banded Sprint
items.why: Band around waist, partner or anchor holds, sprint against resistance

fields.release: Loop a resistance band around your waist and have a partner hold the other end or anchor it behind you. Sprint forward against the resistance of the band, focusing on driving your knees and leaning into the resistance. This overloads the sprinting muscles and improves acceleration mechanics. Start with a march and progress to full sprints.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, quads.

items.name: Banded Squat
items.why: Band above knees, push knees out, squat deep, drive up

fields.release: Place a resistance band just above your knees and stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Push your knees out against the band to activate your glutes, then squat as deep as you can while maintaining outward pressure on the band. Drive through your heels to stand. The band reinforces proper knee tracking and fires up the glute medius.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

items.name: Banded Tricep Pushdown
items.why: Anchor band high, elbows pinned to sides, full extension

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band at a high point such as the top of a door. Face the anchor, grab the band with both hands, and pin your elbows tightly to your sides. Push your hands downward by straightening your arms, squeezing your triceps at the bottom, then slowly return to the start. Do not let your elbows drift forward.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: triceps.

items.name: Base of skull
items.equipment: Two balls in a sock, or the foam peanut
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Two balls in a sock, or the foam peanut
fields.release: Lie on your back and place them either side of the spine right at the base of the skull. Let the head rest into them, 3–5 min. Run slow extended-exhale breathing the whole time.
fields.load: Chin nods — lying on your back, gently nod the chin toward the throat without lifting the head. Hold 5 sec ×10. These are the deep neck flexors, the stabilizers whose absence makes the neck feel like it needs cracking.
fields.notice: The urge to crack drops. Forward-head posture is easier to correct and holds longer.
fields.careful: This replaces neck cracking. Self-manipulating the cervical spine with lax connective tissue is the one item here with a serious downside — the vertebral arteries run through the joints you would be torquing.

photos.caption: The load, seated: gentle resistance with no actual movement of the head. Yours is done lying on your back — nod the chin toward the throat without lifting the head, hold 5 seconds. Resistance, never rotation.

items.name: Base of the skull — pressure while the head nods
items.why: A different approach to a region the library already touches. The small deep muscles at the base of the skull do fine head-nodding adjustments; holding pressure while they do their own job is often more productive than pressing harder while they sit still.
items.equipment: Two balls in a sock, or fingertips

fields.tool: Two balls in a sock, or your fingertips hooked up under the bony ridge.
fields.release: Lie down and place the balls just under the bony ridge at the back of your skull, either side of the middle. Let your head rest on them. Then make a very small nod — as if saying a tiny yes, moving the head on the neck rather than the neck on the shoulders. A centimetre of movement is plenty. Slowly, several times, keeping the contact.
fields.notice: How small the movement can be while still being felt. Whether it is easier to nod one direction than the other. Headache-like sensation spreading up the back of the head or toward the eye is the pattern traditionally described here — recorded as a claim, and your own experience is the better evidence.
fields.careful: Small nod, gentle pressure. This area sits close to the top of the neck joint, and the pressure should never feel like it is pushing the head forward on the neck. Dizziness, visual change, or nausea is a stop.
fields.load: Chin nods, unsupported, are the direct pair — the same movement, held, without anything under your head.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is the highest-caution spot in the neck for you. Upper cervical instability presents right here, and the symptoms — headache at the base of the skull, visual disturbance, a heavy or unsupported feeling in the head, symptoms on looking up — are worth knowing before you work here rather than after. Light pressure, small movement, and if any of those appear, stop and take it to a clinician.

levels.name: Fingertips, seated, no movement
levels.note: Just contact and holding, so you learn where the ridge is.

levels.name: Lying, small nods
levels.note: Head weight as pressure, tiny nod added.

loadAfter.name: Chin nods — the front of the neck

evidence.grade: Undetermined for the self-administered form; clinician-delivered versions have small trials against comparators.
evidence.basis: Clinician-applied pin-and-stretch approaches have been compared against other manual techniques in small trials with mixed results. Nothing I found tests the self-administered version specifically. The rationale — that tissue moving under a fixed contact restores glide between layers — is a mechanism story, not a demonstrated finding, and is written here as such.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Deliberately a different technique family from the imported 'Base of skull' card, which is static pressure — this is the pin-and-move version.

items.name: Base of the skull — the position of ease version
items.why: For a neck too irritable to be pressed at all — after a headache day, a flare, or anything that makes contact unwelcome. Instead of pressing, you shorten and support until the spot stops complaining.
items.equipment: A folded towel or small cushion

fields.tool: A folded towel to prop the head, and one finger to monitor.
fields.release: Lying on your back, rest one fingertip lightly on the tender point under the ridge — light enough to feel it, not enough to press it. Then make very small changes to your head position: a slight tip, a slight turn, a slight nod one way or the other. You are looking for the position where the tenderness under the finger drops most. When you find it, prop the head there with the towel so you can hold it without any muscular effort, and wait. Come out of the position slowly, moving your head with your hand rather than with your neck muscles.
fields.notice: That the position of ease is often the opposite of the direction you expected — usually toward the tender side, not away from it. That it takes small adjustments, not big ones.
fields.careful: Nothing here should hurt at any point. If a position increases the tenderness, it is simply not the one — keep looking rather than pushing. Never a position you cannot come out of comfortably.
fields.load: Gentle and later. Something irritable enough to need this is not ready for loading in the same session — do chin nods the next day.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: because there is no stretch sensation to warn you, it is possible to settle into a position that is at the end of your neck's range without noticing. Prop generously and keep the position obviously small. PEM/pacing: near-zero exertion; one of the few neck items genuinely available on a bad day.
items.dose: [undetermined] — see the fold-and-hold guide for the conventional hold time and why it carries no evidence weight.

levels.name: Find one position of ease
levels.note: One spot. Finding it is the whole rung.

levels.name: Refine it
levels.note: Small adjustments in several directions to find where tenderness drops furthest.

loadAfter.name: Chin nods — the front of the neck
loadAfter.note: Later session, not the same one.

evidence.grade: Very low certainty. Some effect on tender-point pain, mainly as an addition to other treatment; not supported as a standalone.
evidence.basis: A meta-analysis of the technique's effect on tender-point palpation pain found a pooled benefit from low-quality studies. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in low back pain graded the certainty as very low and found benefit when combined with other treatment but not as a standalone. It is in this library because it is gentle, it opens a door for irritable tissue that tolerates nothing else, and its risk profile is close to zero — not because the evidence is strong. Tier: exploratory.

items.name: Basic Jump
items.why: Light bounce on toes, wrists turn the rope, elbows in

fields.release: Stand with your feet together and the rope behind your heels. Swing the rope overhead with your wrists (not your whole arms) and jump just high enough to clear it. Stay on the balls of your feet with a slight knee bend and keep your elbows tucked close to your sides. Focus on a consistent rhythm and relaxed breathing.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, shoulders.

items.name: Bear Crawl
items.why: Knees hover off floor, opposite hand and foot move together

fields.release: Start on all fours and lift your knees just one to two inches off the floor. Crawl forward by moving the opposite hand and foot together (right hand with left foot, then left hand with right foot). Keep your back flat and your knees hovering low. Avoid letting your hips rock side to side. This builds core stability, shoulder endurance, and coordination.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core, quads.

items.name: Bent Over DB Row
items.why: Hinge at hips, flat back, pull both DBs to ribs

fields.release: Stand with feet hip-width apart, hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor, and hold a dumbbell in each hand with arms hanging down. Pull both dumbbells up to your ribcage by driving your elbows back, squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top, then lower. Keep your back flat and core braced throughout.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: back, biceps.

items.name: Between the ribs
items.equipment: A TENNIS BALL, or your FOAM lacrosse ball. Soft. Not the firm rubber one, and not a big inflatable exercise ball
items.dose: 2–3 spots per side, 5 breaths each. Two or three times a week.
items.why: This works what pulls on the rib cage, not the cage itself.

fields.tool: A TENNIS BALL, or your FOAM lacrosse ball. Soft. Not the firm rubber one, and not a big inflatable exercise ball
fields.release: Stand side-on to a wall. Put the ball between the side of your rib cage and the wall, starting just below the armpit. Raise that arm overhead and rest it on the wall. This opens the spaces between the ribs and is what makes the drill work. Lean in gently. Feel for a tender spot BETWEEN two ribs — in the soft strip, not on the hard bone. Stay on that spot and breathe. Big slow inhale, feel the rib push out against the ball. Long exhale. 5 breaths, then move down a few inches and find the next spot.
fields.notice: Side ribs expand more on the inhale. The breath feels wider rather than just deeper. Odd and very specific. You will feel the breath reaching somewhere it has not been.
fields.careful: Light pressure only. This is bone with thin muscle strips between — a firm ball lands on the rib instead of in the gap, and you bruise easily. If it feels like pressing on bone, move the ball.

items.name: Between the shoulder blade and the spine
items.why: The muscles running at an upward angle from the spine to the inner edge of the shoulder blade are the classic 'burning between the shoulder blades' spot for anyone at a keyboard. They are usually long and overworked rather than short — which changes what you do afterward.

fields.tool: A ball against a wall.
fields.release: The trick is getting the shoulder blade out of the way first. Reach the arm on the working side across your body and hold the opposite shoulder — that slides the blade outward and exposes the strip between its inner edge and the spine. Now place the ball in that strip, lean into the wall, and hunt. Once you find a spot, hold it, then slowly let the arm come back across and reach forward again while keeping the contact.
fields.notice: That the burning ache is usually not where the tenderness is. That it is often worse on your mouse side. Whether reaching across to expose the blade is itself difficult.
fields.careful: In the strip beside the spine, not on the bony bumps and not on the edge of the blade itself.
fields.load: This is the important part for this muscle. It is usually already long and tired from holding a rounded posture — stretching it further is the wrong direction. Load it: set the shoulder blade, and work on getting the chest to open at the front so the blade has somewhere to sit.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: reaching across pulls your own shoulder toward its end range; keep the reach moderate and supported. Also relevant — if this area burns constantly, the answer is usually more support at the front and more strength behind, not more release.

levels.name: Static, blade slid out of the way
Move the blade under the ball
levels.note: Reach across and back while keeping contact.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back
loadAfter.note: Lives in release-neck-jaw.json — cross-file reference.

evidence.grade: Undetermined for the self-administered form; clinician-delivered versions have small trials against comparators.
evidence.basis: Clinician-applied pin-and-stretch approaches have been compared against other manual techniques in small trials with mixed results. Nothing I found tests the self-administered version specifically. The rationale — that tissue moving under a fixed contact restores glide between layers — is a mechanism story, not a demonstrated finding, and is written here as such.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Deliberately distinct from the imported broad 'Mid & upper back' card: this one targets the strip beside the spine specifically and instructs a different setup.

items.name: Bicycle Crunch
items.why: Opposite elbow to knee, fully extend other leg, no neck pulling

fields.release: Lie on your back with hands lightly behind your head and legs off the floor. Bring one knee toward your chest while rotating your opposite elbow to meet it, simultaneously extending the other leg straight. Alternate sides in a pedaling motion. Avoid pulling on your neck; your hands should just lightly support your head.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, obliques.

items.name: Big toe lift
items.why: Re-test: Every 2 weeks. Higher is better.

fields.release: Four toes pressed down, lift only the big toe. 0 = nothing. 1 = a flicker. 2 = it lifts partway, other toes cheat. 3 = clean and easy. Score it honestly; the whole value is watching a 0 become a 3.
fields.notice: Recorded in 0–3.

items.name: Bird Dog
items.why: On all fours, extend opposite arm and leg, hips level

fields.release: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Simultaneously extend your right arm forward and left leg backward until both are parallel to the floor. Hold briefly, return to start, and switch to the opposite arm and leg. Keep your hips perfectly level and avoid rotating your torso. This builds core stability and lower back strength.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lower back, glutes, core.

items.name: Blue light glasses (evening)
items.why: Protects melatonin production after sunset

items.name: Box Jump
items.why: Swing arms, explode up, land soft with knees bent

fields.release: Stand in front of a sturdy box or platform. Swing your arms back, then explosively jump onto the box, landing softly with both feet and knees slightly bent. Stand fully upright on the box, then step (do not jump) back down. Focus on a soft, quiet landing to absorb force through your muscles rather than your joints.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes, calves.

items.name: Boxer Shuffle
items.why: Shift weight side to side, like a boxer bouncing

fields.release: While jumping rope, shift your weight from one foot to the other with each jump, like a boxer bouncing in the ring. One foot takes the majority of the weight while the other lightly taps the ground. Keep your jumps low and your rhythm smooth. This is easier on your calves than basic two-footed jumping and builds coordination.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, quads.

items.name: Boxing Stance + Footwork
items.why: Hands up, chin down, light on feet, move in all directions

fields.release: Stand with your dominant foot back, feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent. Keep your hands up near your chin with elbows tucked. Stay light on the balls of your feet and practice moving forward, backward, and side to side while maintaining your stance. Keep your chin down and your eyes forward at all times.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, quads, core.

items.name: Breath-coupled release — letting go on the exhale
items.why: The family for muscles you cannot reach and cannot press — the pelvic floor, the diaphragm, the deep abdominal wall, the jaw at rest. It is also the family that most directly connects release work to the nervous system, which is the app's whole thesis.

fields.tool: Your breath, and your attention.
fields.release: Set the position so the target is in a lengthened or unloaded shape. Breathe in through the nose, letting the belly and the lower ribs widen. Then breathe out slowly and completely, and on the way out, deliberately stop holding the target — let it drop, widen, or go soft. The exhale is the release; the inhale is the reset. Several breaths, unhurried. You are not doing the muscle a favour by trying harder — trying harder is the opposite of the instruction.
fields.notice: Whether you can find the muscle at all, and whether it responds to being asked to let go. Many people discover they have been holding something continuously and had no idea. That discovery is the item's real output.
fields.careful: If deliberate breathing makes you lightheaded, slow it down and shorten it — this is meant to be quieter than your normal breathing, not bigger. Nothing here should be forced or held.
fields.load: Down-training only opens the door. The paired work is learning to produce the muscle on purpose and time it with movement, which lives in the activation items.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: do these lying or sitting to begin with. Slow deep breathing can make lightheadedness worse in some people; if it does, shorten the breath rather than abandoning the item.
items.dose: [undetermined] — breath counts and session lengths in the down-training literature vary by clinic and are not standardised.

levels.name: Find it
levels.note: Just locate the sensation of holding, and the sensation of letting go. That is the whole rung.

levels.name: Let go on every exhale
levels.note: Several consecutive breaths with a deliberate release each time.

levels.name: Carry it into a position
levels.note: The same release inside a stretch or a supported position that lengthens the target.

evidence.grade: Expert consensus and small clinical series for down-training overactive muscle; not established as a strengthening method.
evidence.basis: For the high-tone pelvic floor specifically, expert consensus and treatment algorithms place relaxation-focused work — diaphragmatic breathing, paced exhale, graded desensitisation — as a first-line element, supported by pilot studies and clinical series rather than large trials. A separate and important finding: breathing-based approaches used alone are not effective for pelvic floor strengthening. Down-training and strengthening are different jobs and this family does the first one.

items.name: Bretzel Stretch
items.why: Lying twist hitting hips, upper back, and quads simultaneously

fields.release: Lie on your side with your top knee bent at 90 degrees and pinned to the floor in front of you. Reach back and grab the foot of your bottom leg to stretch the quad. Then rotate your upper body open toward the ceiling. This stretch simultaneously targets the hips, thoracic spine, and quads. Breathe deeply and hold each side for 30-60 seconds.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hips, thoracic spine, quads.

levels.name: Add Quad Pull
levels.note: Grab rear foot for quad stretch

items.name: Broad Jump
items.why: Swing arms forward, jump for max distance, stick landing

fields.release: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Swing your arms back and load your legs, then explosively swing your arms forward and jump as far forward as possible. Land softly on both feet with knees bent and hold the landing. Focus on generating horizontal distance rather than height. Stick each landing before taking the next jump.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes, calves.

levels.name: Depth to Broad
levels.note: Step off box into broad jump

items.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
items.why: Rear foot elevated, front knee over toes, upright torso

fields.release: Stand a couple of feet in front of a bench or step and place the top of one foot on the surface behind you. With your torso upright, bend your front knee to lower yourself until your rear knee nearly touches the floor. Drive through your front foot to stand back up. Keep your front knee tracking over your toes and avoid letting your torso lean forward.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

levels.name: Deficit
levels.note: Front foot on riser for more depth

items.name: Butterfly Stretch
items.why: Soles of feet together, knees fall outward

fields.release: Sit with soles of feet together, knees falling outward. Hold feet and sit tall. Gently press knees toward floor with elbows or let gravity work. For deeper stretch, fold forward from the hips while maintaining a long spine.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: adductors, groin, hips.

items.name: Calf Raise
items.why: Full stretch at bottom, high on toes at top, slow tempo

fields.release: Stand with feet hip-width apart, ideally with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step so your heels can drop below for a full stretch. Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, squeezing your calves at the top, then lower slowly below the step level. Use a slow, controlled tempo and avoid bouncing.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves.

levels.name: Elevated Edge
levels.note: Heels hang off step for stretch

items.name: Calf Roll
items.why: Sit with roller under calves, roll from ankle to knee

fields.release: Sit on the floor with the foam roller under your calves and your hands on the floor behind you for support. Lift your hips off the ground and slowly roll from just above your ankles to just below your knees. Pause on any tender areas. For more pressure, cross one leg over the other to roll one calf at a time. Rotate your leg inward and outward to hit different fibers.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves.

items.name: Calves
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: RolFlex, or a firm ball
fields.release: On the mid-belly of the calf — not the Achilles, not the shin bone. While compressed, slowly point and flex the foot 8–10×. Work the tighter side first.
fields.load: Bilateral heel raises ×15 slow, then lower on the weaker side alone ×8. Add seated bent-knee raises for the soleus.
fields.notice: Knee-to-wall distance improves on the side you worked. The ankle feels like it has more to give.
fields.careful: If either calf has been operated on or injured, release that side lightly or skip it. A weak calf needs strength, not length.

photos.caption: On the mid-belly of the calf. Not the Achilles, not the shin bone. Right side primary; the left is the weak one.

items.name: Castor oil pack
items.why: Liver area, 30–60 min with heat — supports detox and inflammation

items.name: Cat-Cow
items.why: Alternate arching and rounding spine, sync with breath

fields.release: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. On an inhale, arch your back and lift your chest and tailbone toward the ceiling (cow). On an exhale, round your spine upward and tuck your chin and pelvis (cat). Move slowly and coordinate each position with your breath. This gently mobilizes the entire spine.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: spine, core.

items.name: Chest & front of shoulder
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Soft ball against a wall
fields.release: Ball between your chest and a wall, just below and inside the front of the shoulder — the meaty part near the armpit, not on bone. Lean in, then slowly raise and lower that arm.
fields.load: Wall angels ×8 with the low back flat. Then banded external rotation ×12, elbow tucked at your side.
fields.notice: Shoulders sit back without effort. The chest stops caving in on the lungs. Breath gets deeper on its own.
fields.careful: Do not force shoulders-back-chest-out. That retraction is the move that reproduces thoracic-outlet symptoms in people who have them — let the position come from underneath.

photos.caption: The load, standing. Yours is the same with the elbow tucked at your side. Do not force the shoulders back — that retraction is what reproduces the thoracic outlet symptoms.

items.name: Chest expansion
items.why: Re-test: Weekly. Higher is better.

fields.release: Tape measure around the chest at nipple line. Full exhale, read it. Full inhale, read it. Record the difference. Under 5 cm is restricted, and it is the number most likely to move from the rib and diaphragm work.
fields.notice: Recorded in cm.

items.name: Child's Pose
items.why: Sit hips back to heels, arms extended, forehead to floor

fields.release: Kneel on the floor and sit your hips back toward your heels. Extend your arms forward along the floor and lower your forehead to the ground. Breathe deeply and let your body relax into the stretch. This gently stretches the back, hips, and shoulders and is an excellent resting position between exercises or as part of a cooldown.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: back, hips, lats.

levels.name: Wide Knee
levels.note: Knees apart for deeper hip stretch

levels.name: Lat Stretch
levels.note: Walk hands left/right for lat stretch

items.name: Chin nod hold
items.why: Re-test: Every 2 weeks. Higher is better.

fields.release: On your back, gently nod the chin toward the throat without lifting the head. Time until the front of the neck starts to shake or the jaw takes over.
fields.notice: Recorded in sec.

items.name: Chin nods — the front of the neck
items.why: The load partner for almost every neck release item in the library. The deep muscles at the front of your neck hold your head over your shoulders. When they are offline, the muscles at the back hold the head up by pulling — which is why the back of the neck is always tight and pressing it never fixes it.

fields.tool: Nothing. A folded towel under the head if lying makes it easier to feel.
fields.release: Lying on your back, make a small nodding movement — as if starting to say yes, lengthening the back of your neck slightly. The head barely moves. Then hold. What you are looking for is the small deep effort at the front of the throat, not the rope-like muscles at the sides standing out. If those ropes pop up, you are using the wrong muscles — make the nod smaller until they stay quiet.
fields.notice: Whether you can find it at all. Whether the ropes at the sides of the neck take over. How quickly the effort fades — for most people the honest answer at the start is 'almost immediately', and that is the information, not a failure.
fields.careful: Small. This is not a neck crunch and the head does not lift off the surface at the early rungs. Stop for any dizziness or visual change.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is one of the most valuable items in the neck module for you, because active support is what a lax neck needs and passive stretching is not. Keep it small, build the hold time slowly, and do not progress to lifting the head until the small version is genuinely easy and the side ropes stay quiet.
items.dose: [undetermined] — hold time and repetitions are the natural place for a clinician's number. Ask for one.

levels.name: Lying, nod and hold
levels.note: Head stays down. Finding the movement is the rung.

levels.name: Lying, longer hold
levels.note: Same movement, held longer, side ropes staying quiet.

levels.name: Nod, then lift the head slightly
levels.note: Hold the nod and lift the head a small amount. Only once the nod itself is easy — losing the nod as the head lifts means back a rung.

levels.name: Sitting and standing
levels.note: The same small nod upright, against gravity in a different direction. This is the one that transfers to your day.

evidence.grade: Established as a standard rehabilitation approach for neck pain; specific protocols vary.
evidence.basis: Deep cervical flexor training is standard content in neck-pain rehabilitation with a substantial trial literature behind the general approach. This card teaches the movement and deliberately leaves reps and hold times blank, because that is exactly the parameter a clinician should set for an individual neck.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner because the library has no neck activation content — arguably belongs in the strength and activation file instead. Kevin's call.

items.name: Chin-Up
items.why: Supinated grip, chin over bar, full extension at bottom

fields.release: Grab a pull-up bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands about shoulder-width apart. Start from a full dead hang, then pull yourself up until your chin is over the bar. Lower back down to a full extension. The underhand grip places more emphasis on the biceps compared to a standard pull-up, making it a good option if you are building toward your first pull-up.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: biceps, lats.

items.name: CO2 tolerance
items.why: Breathing is upstream of most of it. Everything else on this list is downstream effect.

fields.release: Sit quietly for 5 minutes first. Morning, before getting up, gives the most consistent reading. Breathe normally in through the nose, and normally out. Not a big breath, not a forced exhale. Pinch your nose. Time until the FIRST definite urge to breathe. Not how long you can hold on — the first real signal: a swallow, a contraction in the throat, a jerk in the belly. Release and breathe normally. If you are gasping afterwards you held too long and the number is invalid.
fields.notice: Under 10 seconds is a very reactive set-point. 10–20 is reactive and common with a breathing pattern disorder. 20–30 is moderate. 40+ is well regulated. The number rising over weeks IS the thing you are trying to fix, and it is the only hard metric in this document. Uncomfortable, not distressing. You should be able to breathe normally straight after.
fields.tool: Phone timer
fields.careful: Do it sitting or lying, never standing — more so if you are prone to lightheadedness when upright.

items.dose: Once a week, same time of day. Write it down.

items.name: Cobra / Upward Dog
items.why: Press chest forward and up, open shoulders, hips toward floor

fields.release: Lie face down with your palms on the floor beside your chest. Press your chest forward and up by straightening your arms, opening your shoulders and lifting your upper body while keeping your hips on or near the floor. In upward dog, your thighs lift off the floor as well. Avoid crunching your lower back; think about lengthening through the spine.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hip flexors, abs, spine extensors.

items.name: Coffee enema
items.why: Liver/gallbladder support — follow practitioner guidance

items.name: Cold exposure
items.why: Cold shower or plunge — reduces inflammation, boosts dopamine, builds resilience

items.name: Cold on the face
items.equipment: A bowl of cold water, or a cold pack
items.dose: When you need a reset. Not a daily requirement.
items.why: Direct downregulation. Cheap, and most of it needs no equipment at all.

fields.tool: A bowl of cold water, or a cold pack
fields.release: Bowl of cold water — face in, hold 20–30 seconds. Or hold a cold pack over your forehead and eyes. Face and forehead only. Not a cold shower and not full immersion. The trigger is the nerve endings around the eyes and forehead. That is what fires the dive reflex and slows the heart.
fields.notice: One of the very few things that shifts autonomic state within seconds rather than minutes.
fields.careful: Cold is a mast cell trigger for some people — test small and stop if you get flushing, itching, or hives. Not while alone if you are prone to feeling faint.

items.name: Compression flossing — wrapping a limb, then moving it
items.why: New to this library. A thick rubber band is wrapped firmly around a limb segment, you move the joint through range while it is on, then take it off. Widely used in sport, and the evidence has a specific and useful twist that the card below tells you about.
items.equipment: A wide latex compression band (not a resistance band)

fields.tool: A flat rubber floss band, several inches wide. A resistance band is not the same thing and should not be used for this.
fields.release: Wrap the limb segment with a firm overlapping spiral, working from the far end toward the body, tight enough to be clearly compressive but not so tight that the limb goes white or numb. Then move the joint actively and repeatedly through its range for a short time — the movement is the point. Unwrap. Move the joint again immediately afterward.
fields.notice: The range immediately after unwrapping versus before wrapping. And be honest with yourself about the comparison, because this technique produces a strong sensation that is easy to mistake for a result.
fields.careful: Short applications only. Take it off immediately for numbness, pins and needles, colour change, or pain that is not the compression itself. Never over a wound, a rash, a varicose vein, or an area with reduced sensation. Not over the front of the throat or the abdomen — this is a limb technique.
fields.load: The movement under the wrap already is loading, and it should continue after the wrap comes off.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: skin fragility and bruising make firm circumferential compression a poor first choice, and the range you gain is not the range you need. If you try it, wrap lighter and shorter than the sport instructions describe. Orthostatic: compression and rapid changes in limb blood flow are a bad combination with blood-pressure instability. Treat this as a family to raise with a clinician before using, not to experiment with.
items.dose: Applications in trials are short — around two minutes is typical [derived — flossing trial protocols and a perfusion study using a 2-minute application]. This library does not recommend longer.

levels.name: Ankle or wrist, light wrap, short
levels.note: Smallest segment, least compression, brief. Learn the sensation before anything else.

levels.name: Larger segment
levels.note: Calf or thigh, same short duration.

evidence.grade: Grade B, and the finding cuts against the technique: range improves before-to-after, but not compared with doing the same movements without the band.
evidence.basis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of compression flossing for ankle dorsiflexion found moderate improvement from before to after, and no effect compared with a control of the same range-of-motion activities alone — the authors' reading was that the gains came from the exercises, not the band. A separate perfusion study measured a marked drop in tissue oxygen during a two-minute application and did not confirm the rebound-blood-flow story the technique is usually sold with. It is in the library for breadth and because people ask about it; it is exploratory tier and the card says plainly what the trials found.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Worth raising with a clinician before use if you have orthostatic symptoms.

items.name: Concentration Curl
items.why: Elbow braced on inner thigh, full ROM, squeeze at peak

fields.release: Sit on a bench or chair with legs spread. Hold a dumbbell in one hand and brace the back of that elbow against your inner thigh. Curl the weight up toward your shoulder, squeezing hard at the top, then lower all the way down for a full stretch. This isolates the bicep and prevents cheating with body swing.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: biceps.

items.name: Contract–relax
items.equipment: A belt, strap, towel, wall, or doorframe. Something immovable to push against
items.dose: 2–3 times a week per muscle, not daily. This is a training stimulus, not a warm-up.
items.why: Loaded lengthening — the real answer to a nervous system guarding a range.

fields.tool: A belt, strap, towel, wall, or doorframe. Something immovable to push against
fields.release: Move into the stretch until you feel the FIRST real tension. Not the end of your range, not pain. That is your starting point. Push the stretched muscle against something immovable at about 25–50% effort. Not maximum. Keep breathing. Hold that push for 6–10 seconds. Let go completely. Long exhale. Ease into the new range that opens up — and there will be one. Repeat 3 times total, then stop and move on.
fields.notice: Range gained this way tends to still be there tomorrow. Range gained from passive holding usually is not. This is the tool for the question you actually asked. The gain right after the contraction is often immediate and surprising. That is the nervous system granting permission, which is exactly the mechanism you described.
fields.careful: 25–50% effort, not maximum. Only on restricted muscle — never used to push a joint that subluxes further into range.

photos.caption: The method itself. A partner braces the shoulders while you push your torso BACK at 25–50% for 10–20 seconds, then relax into the new range. A belt, wall or doorframe does the same job solo — the partner is just what the library had.
The starting position, not the whole method: move only to the FIRST real tension, then push against something immovable for 6–10 seconds before easing in.

items.name: Contract–relax — using the muscle to release itself
items.why: No equipment, works almost anywhere, and it is the release family that most naturally satisfies the pairing law — you have already asked the muscle to work by the time you finish.

fields.tool: Your own muscle, and something to push against — your hand, the floor, a doorframe.
fields.release: Take the muscle to the first point where you feel a stretch. Not the end of your range — the first honest sensation. Contract that same muscle gently against resistance without letting the position change, hold the contraction, then let go completely and breathe out. Usually you can then move a little further into the position. Repeat a few times. The contraction is submaximal — a gentle push, not a maximum effort.
fields.notice: Whether the new range appears after the release or whether nothing changes. Whether the contraction itself is easy to produce — a muscle you cannot voluntarily contract in a stretched position is telling you something useful, and it belongs to the strength side of the library, not this side.
fields.careful: Gentle contraction. Hard maximal contractions in a stretched position are where this technique causes strains. Never bounce out of the contraction into more range.
fields.load: Already halfway there. Finish by holding the end of the new range actively — no external support, the muscles doing the holding.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is one of the safer release families for you, because the contraction builds control in the range you are opening rather than just opening it. Do not use it to chase more range — most hypermobile people need less range and more control of what they have. Use the gained range as somewhere to get strong, not somewhere to go further.
items.dose: Contractions in the 20–25% of maximum range are as effective as near-maximal ones [derived — post-isometric relaxation literature; a study comparing 20% and 60% contractions found no advantage to the harder effort]. Hold times and number of rounds: [undetermined].

levels.name: Gentle contract, then let go
levels.note: One round. Learn the feel of the release before adding rounds.

levels.name: Several rounds
levels.note: Repeat, taking up whatever slack appears each time.

levels.name: Contract the opposite side too
levels.note: After releasing, actively contract the muscle on the other side of the joint to hold the new position. Harder, and it makes the range yours.

evidence.grade: Established for acute range of motion; no better than other stretching methods; mechanism is largely increased tolerance to stretch.
evidence.basis: Meta-analysis across stretching types finds contract-relax, static and dynamic stretching all improve range of motion acutely and over training periods, with no significant difference between them. A 2025 meta-analysis of static stretching mechanisms across 65 studies found range gains track increased tolerance to the stretch far more than any change in muscle length or stiffness. So: it works, and it works by changing what you will allow, not by lengthening tissue.

items.name: Contract–relax: calf
items.dose: 3 rounds per side, 3× a week. Right side is the tight one.
items.why: Loaded lengthening — the real answer to a nervous system guarding a range.

fields.tool: A wall
fields.release: Put the ball of one foot up against a wall with the toes pointing up the wall and the heel on the floor. Lean your shin toward the wall until you feel the first real tension in the calf. Press the ball of your foot INTO the wall at 25–50% effort for 8 seconds. Relax and lean the shin closer to the wall. 3 rounds each side.
fields.notice: Knee-to-wall distance increases. The deep squat gets easier, because the ankle stops being the limiter.
fields.careful: If either calf has been operated on or injured, go lighter on that side.

photos.caption: Ball of the foot up the wall, heel down. Press in at 25–50%, hold 8 seconds, then lean the shin closer.
The bent-knee version, which reaches the soleus. Worth doing both — lighter on the left.

items.name: Contract–relax: hamstring
items.why: Loaded lengthening — the real answer to a nervous system guarding a range.

fields.tool: Belt, strap, or towel
fields.release: Lie on your back. Loop the strap around the arch of one foot and raise that leg toward the ceiling, knee softly bent — never locked straight. Raise until you feel the first real tension. Press your heel DOWN into the strap at 25–50% effort for 8 seconds. Resist with your arms so nothing actually moves. Relax, exhale long, and draw the leg closer to you. 3 rounds, then swap sides.
fields.notice: Forward fold goes deeper — with soft knees, which is the version that counts.
fields.careful: Knee softly bent throughout. This drill is the safe route to the range you want; locking the knee out to gain a few degrees is the unsafe one.

photos.caption: On your back, knee softly bent. Yours uses a strap round the arch — press the heel down into it for 8 seconds, then draw the leg closer.

fields.release: Kneel facing away from a wall. Place one foot against the wall behind you (top of foot on wall, knee on floor close to wall). Step the other foot forward into a lunge. Squeeze the glute on the back leg side. This is an intense hip flexor stretch — ease into it.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hip flexors, quads, psoas.

levels.name: easy
levels.note: Knee further from wall, smaller stretch

levels.name: standard
levels.note: Knee close to wall, upright torso

levels.name: advanced
levels.note: Knee against wall, reach arms overhead

items.name: Couch Stretch (Hip Flexor)
items.why: Rear foot up against wall or couch, squeeze glute, stand tall

fields.release: Kneel with your back to a wall or couch and place the top of one foot against it behind you, knee on the floor. Step your other foot forward into a lunge position. Squeeze the glute on the back leg and stand tall to deepen the stretch. You should feel an intense stretch through the hip flexor and quad of the rear leg. Hold and breathe steadily.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors, quads.

items.name: Criss-Cross
items.why: Cross arms at elbows on every other jump, uncross on return

fields.release: While jumping rope, cross your arms in front of your body at the elbows as the rope comes overhead, then jump through the crossed loop. On the next revolution, uncross your arms back to normal position. Alternate between crossed and uncrossed on each jump. Cross at the elbows rather than the wrists for a wide enough loop to jump through.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, calves.

items.name: Cupping
items.why: Increases blood flow, releases fascial tension, supports detox pathways

items.name: DB Bench Press
items.why: Feet flat, arch slightly, press to lockout above chest

fields.release: Lie on a flat bench with feet planted on the floor. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at chest level and press them straight up above your chest to full lockout, then lower back down with control. Maintain a slight natural arch in your lower back and keep your shoulder blades pinched together against the bench for stability.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, triceps, shoulders.

levels.name: Single-Arm
levels.note: One arm at a time, brace core

items.name: DB Bulgarian Split Squat
items.why: Rear foot on bench, front knee tracks over toes, torso upright

fields.release: Stand about two feet in front of a bench and place the top of your rear foot on the bench behind you. Hold a dumbbell in each hand. Lower your body by bending your front knee until your rear knee nearly touches the floor, keeping your torso upright. Drive through your front heel to stand back up. Make sure your front knee tracks over your toes, not inward.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

levels.name: Deficit
levels.note: Front foot elevated for more ROM

items.name: DB Chest Fly
items.why: Slight bend in elbows, wide arc, squeeze at top

fields.release: Lie on your back on the floor or a bench, holding a dumbbell in each hand above your chest with a slight bend in your elbows. Open your arms in a wide arc, lowering the weights to the sides until you feel a stretch across your chest, then squeeze your chest to bring them back together. Keep the elbow angle fixed throughout and avoid turning this into a press.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest.

items.name: DB Clean & Press
items.why: Clean DB to shoulder, press overhead, reverse with control

fields.release: Start with a dumbbell hanging at your side. In one motion, pull the dumbbell up to your shoulder (the clean), then press it overhead to full lockout. Reverse the motion with control back to your side. The clean uses hip drive and a quick arm pull; the press should be smooth from shoulder to overhead. This is a full-body compound movement.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, legs, core.

items.name: DB Curl
items.why: Elbows pinned, supinate at top, no swinging

fields.release: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, arms fully extended at your sides with palms facing forward. Curl the weights up toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows, squeezing your biceps at the top, then lower slowly. Keep your elbows pinned to your sides and avoid swinging your body to generate momentum.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: biceps.

items.name: DB Floor Press
items.why: Elbows touch floor each rep, press to lockout

fields.release: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a dumbbell in each hand and press them up above your chest. Lower the weights until your elbows gently touch the floor, pause briefly, then press back to lockout. The floor limits your range of motion, making this a shoulder-friendly pressing option.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, triceps.

items.name: DB Incline Press
items.why: Prop upper back on pillows or backpack for incline angle

fields.release: Prop your upper back on a stack of pillows, a backpack, or an incline bench so your torso is angled roughly 30-45 degrees. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at chest level and press them upward, then lower with control. This angle shifts emphasis to the upper chest and front shoulders compared to a flat press.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, shoulders.

items.name: DB Lateral Lunge
items.why: Wide step to side with DBs, sit back into hip, push back up

fields.release: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Take a wide step to one side, sit your hips back, and bend the stepping leg while keeping the trailing leg straight. Push through the bent leg to return to the starting position. Keep the dumbbells close to your body and your chest up throughout. You should feel this in your adductors, quads, and glutes.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: adductors, quads, glutes.

items.name: DB Overhead Press
items.why: Brace core, press straight overhead, full lockout

fields.release: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height with palms facing forward. Brace your core and press both dumbbells straight overhead until your arms are fully extended. Lower them back to shoulder height with control. Avoid arching your lower back excessively; if you find yourself leaning back, reduce the weight.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, triceps.

levels.name: Single-Arm
levels.note: One arm at a time, anti-lateral flexion

items.name: DB Pullover
items.why: Hips low, stretch arms overhead, pull DB back over chest

fields.release: Lie perpendicular across a bench with your upper back supported, feet flat on the floor, and hips slightly lower than the bench. Hold one dumbbell with both hands above your chest, arms slightly bent. Lower the weight in an arc behind your head until you feel a deep stretch in your lats and chest, then pull it back over your chest.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lats, chest, triceps.

items.name: DB Row
items.why: Flat back, pull elbow past torso, squeeze shoulder blade

fields.release: Place one hand and knee on a bench for support, keeping your back flat and parallel to the floor. Hold a dumbbell in the other hand with arm hanging straight down. Pull the dumbbell up by driving your elbow past your torso and squeezing your shoulder blade toward your spine, then lower with control. Avoid rotating your torso as you pull.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: back, biceps.

items.name: DB Skull Crusher
items.why: Lower DBs beside ears, elbows fixed, extend to lockout

fields.release: Lie on a bench and hold a dumbbell in each hand with arms extended above your chest. Keeping your upper arms vertical and elbows fixed in place, bend at the elbows to lower the weights down beside your ears. Extend back to lockout by squeezing your triceps. Avoid letting your elbows flare outward during the movement.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: triceps.

items.name: DB Snatch
items.why: One motion floor to overhead, explosive hip drive, lock out

fields.release: Stand over a dumbbell with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width. Hinge down, grab the dumbbell with one hand, and in one explosive motion drive it from the floor to overhead using your hips, pulling it close to your body and punching through to lockout at the top. Lower with control. This is a powerful full-body movement that builds explosive strength.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, hips.

items.name: DB Step-Up (Bench Height)
items.why: Full foot on bench, drive up without pushing off back leg

fields.release: Stand in front of a bench with a dumbbell in each hand. Place your entire foot on the bench and drive up through that leg to stand on the bench, bringing the other foot up.
