Step down with control. Avoid pushing off with your bottom leg; all the work should come from the leg on the bench. This is an excellent single-leg strength builder.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

items.name: DB Sumo Squat
items.why: Wide stance, toes out, hold DB between legs, sit deep

fields.release: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width apart, toes turned out about 45 degrees. Hold a dumbbell vertically between your legs with both hands. Push your hips back and squat down as deep as you can while keeping your chest tall and knees tracking over your toes. Drive through your heels to stand back up. You should feel this in your inner thighs, quads, and glutes.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, adductors, glutes.

items.name: DB Swing (Kettlebell Style)
items.why: Hold one end of DB, hip hinge and swing like a kettlebell

fields.release: Hold one end of a dumbbell with both hands, letting the other end hang down. Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width. Hinge at your hips and swing the dumbbell between your legs, then snap your hips forward to drive it up to chest height, just like a kettlebell swing. Let it swing back and repeat. All the power should come from your hip snap.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hamstrings.

items.name: DB Tricep Extension
items.why: Keep elbows close to head, full stretch and lockout

fields.release: Stand or sit and hold a dumbbell overhead with both hands or one hand. Keeping your upper arm vertical and elbow pointed at the ceiling, lower the weight behind your head until you feel a deep stretch in the triceps. Extend your arm back to full lockout. Avoid flaring your elbows outward or arching your back.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: triceps.

levels.name: Two-Arm Overhead
levels.note: Hold one DB with both hands

items.name: Dead Bug
items.why: Low back pressed into floor, extend opposite arm and leg slowly

fields.release: Lie on your back with arms extended toward the ceiling and knees bent at 90 degrees above your hips. Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Slowly extend one arm overhead and the opposite leg toward the floor, then return to the starting position and switch sides. If your lower back lifts off the floor, you have gone too far.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, deep core.

items.name: Dead Hang
items.why: Relax into hang, shoulders by ears, breathe deeply

fields.release: Grab a pull-up bar with an overhand grip and let your body hang with arms fully extended. Relax your shoulders up by your ears and breathe deeply. This decompresses the spine, builds grip endurance, and stretches the lats and shoulders. Aim to accumulate time rather than rushing.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: forearms, lats, shoulders.

levels.name: Two-Arm Hang
levels.note: Just hang as long as possible

levels.name: Scapular Shrug
levels.note: Pull shoulder blades down while hanging

items.name: Deep breathing 5 min
items.why: Parasympathetic activation — calms fight-or-flight

items.name: Deep in the back of the hip — the figure-four position
items.why: Underneath the big buttock muscle sits a fan of small muscles running from the tailbone area out to the top of the thigh bone. They turn the leg outward and they sit right next to the big nerve that runs down the leg, which is why they get blamed for so much.
items.equipment: A ball, and a chair or the floor

fields.tool: A ball, seated on a firm chair or lying on the floor.
fields.release: Sitting, cross the ankle of the working side over the opposite knee — the figure-four. That position puts the deep rotators on stretch and brings them nearer the surface. Now place a ball under that buttock, roughly midway between the tailbone and the bony knob at the side of the hip, and lean into it. Hunt for the tender point. Once you have it, slowly let the crossed knee rise and lower a few inches while keeping the contact.
fields.notice: Whether the crossed position itself is very restricted on one side. Whether the tenderness is deeper than the surface buttock work you may have done before — it should feel like a different layer.
fields.careful: This is the region the big leg nerve passes through. Tenderness is fine; shooting, electric or burning sensation down the back of the leg, or numbness, means come off immediately. Do not chase leg symptoms with more pressure — that is the one wrong move here, and persistent leg symptoms belong with a clinician.
fields.load: Outward rotation of the hip against resistance, and single-leg balance work — these muscles are also position sensors and they get quiet when they stop being used.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: the figure-four takes a mobile hip a long way. Keep the crossing modest and support the knee; the point is access to the muscle, not the depth of the position. Orthostatic: the seated version needs no floor transfer.

levels.name: On the floor
levels.note: More pressure available. Harder to get out of quickly.

loadAfter.name: Hip outward rotation against a band
loadAfter.note: Match at S5; author if absent.

evidence.grade: Undetermined for the self-administered form; clinician-delivered versions have small trials against comparators.
evidence.basis: Clinician-applied pin-and-stretch approaches have been compared against other manual techniques in small trials with mixed results. Nothing I found tests the self-administered version specifically. The rationale — that tissue moving under a fixed contact restores glide between layers — is a mechanism story, not a demonstrated finding, and is written here as such.

items.name: Deep squat hang
items.equipment: A doorframe, post, or the edge of a heavy table
items.dose: 30–60 seconds, daily. This is one you can do every day.
items.why: Loaded lengthening — the real answer to a nervous system guarding a range.

fields.tool: A doorframe, post, or the edge of a heavy table
fields.release: Hold the doorframe with both hands at about waist height. Sink into the deepest squat you can while keeping your heels down. Let your arms carry as much of your weight as they need to. Relax into it. Rock gently side to side. Let your knees drift out over your feet. Breathe into your belly and the back of your ribs the whole time.
fields.notice: Over weeks you need less and less arm support. That is the progression — not more depth, but how much of your own weight you can hold down there.
fields.careful: Heels stay down. If they lift, the ankle is the limiter — do the calf work and take more weight through your arms in the meantime.

photos.caption: The squat pattern. Yours is a hang from a doorframe: the progression is needing less arm support, not more depth.

items.name: Deep Squat Hold
items.why: Sit deep, heels down, chest up, breathe and relax into it

fields.release: Lower yourself into the deepest squat position you can while keeping your heels on the floor. Hold the position, keeping your chest upright and breathing deeply to relax into the stretch. If your heels rise, widen your stance or hold onto a support. This opens up the hips, ankles, and thoracic spine. Aim to accumulate time rather than rushing.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hips, ankles, quads, adductors.

items.name: Depth Drop
items.why: Step off box, absorb landing with bent knees, stick it

fields.release: Stand on a box and step off (do not jump) the edge. Land on both feet with bent knees, absorbing the impact as quietly as possible, and hold the landing position. The goal is to train your body to absorb force efficiently. Start with a low box and increase height gradually. This is an important prerequisite for depth jumps.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, calves.

items.name: Dip
items.why: Lean slightly forward, elbows back, full depth

fields.release: Place your hands on parallel bars or the edge of a sturdy bench behind you and support your body weight with arms extended. Lower yourself by bending your elbows until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor, then press back up to lockout. Lean your torso slightly forward to emphasize your chest, or stay upright to target triceps more. Avoid shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, triceps, shoulders.

levels.name: Weighted Dip
levels.note: Add DB between feet or in backpack

items.name: Doorway Chest Stretch
items.why: Forearms on door frame, step through and lean

fields.release: Stand in a doorway. Place forearms on the door frame at 90° (elbows at shoulder height). Step one foot through and lean forward until you feel the stretch across your chest. Adjust arm height to target different pec fibers — higher hits upper chest, lower hits lower.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, anterior deltoids.

levels.name: Gentle Lean
levels.note: Gentle lean, arms at shoulder height

levels.name: Unilateral
levels.note: One arm at a time for deeper unilateral stretch

items.name: Double-Under
items.why: Jump higher, flick wrists fast for two rotations per jump

fields.release: Jump slightly higher than normal while flicking your wrists quickly to pass the rope under your feet twice per jump. Keep your elbows tight to your body and use wrist speed rather than arm swings. Jump with a straight body and pointed toes. This is a challenging skill that requires coordination and timing. Practice single reps first before stringing them together.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, shoulders, forearms.

levels.name: Single Practice
levels.note: One at a time with resets

items.name: Downward Dog
items.why: Inverted V, push hips up and back, press heels toward floor

fields.release: Start in a high plank and push your hips up and back to form an inverted V shape. Spread your fingers wide, press through your palms, and work on pushing your heels toward the floor. Keep your head relaxed between your arms. You should feel a stretch through your hamstrings, calves, and shoulders. Bend your knees slightly if your hamstrings are tight.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hamstrings, calves, shoulders, spine.

items.name: Dragon Flag
items.why: Grip behind head, lift body as one rigid line, lower with control

fields.release: Lie on a bench or the floor and grip something sturdy behind your head. Brace your core and lift your entire body (from shoulders down) as one rigid line, pivoting at the upper back. Lower your body slowly toward the floor with control. This is an extremely advanced core exercise. Start with tucked knees and negative-only reps to build the necessary strength.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, core.

items.name: Dry brushing
items.why: Stimulates lymphatic drainage, exfoliates skin, improves circulation

items.name: Eccentric heel drops
items.equipment: A step or stair with a rail
items.dose: Start at 5 reps per side, twice a week. Build toward 8.
items.why: Loaded lengthening — the real answer to a nervous system guarding a range.

fields.tool: A step or stair with a rail
fields.release: Stand with the balls of both feet on the edge of a step, heels hanging off. Hold the rail. Rise up onto both toes. Shift all your weight onto ONE leg. Lower that heel slowly, counting 5 seconds, until it is well below the level of the step. Put the other foot back down and use BOTH legs to come back up. Never come up on one leg. That is one rep.
fields.notice: Calves get stronger and longer at the same time. This is how you get range that holds instead of range you have to keep re-earning. You will be sore 24–48 hours later. That is the drill working, and it is also why the starting dose is deliberately low.
fields.careful: Eccentrics cause real delayed soreness, and delayed is the operative word: if you are someone who pays for exertion a day or two later, this is a drill that can set that off. Start at half the volume you think you need and watch the following two days before adding any.

photos.caption: The foot position and the balance support. Yours is the edge of a stair with a rail: rise on BOTH, shift to ONE, lower that heel over a slow count of 5 well below the step, then come back up on BOTH. Never up on one leg.

items.name: Elbow Strike
items.why: Short range, explosive, rotate through the elbow

fields.release: From your fighting stance, rotate your torso and drive the tip of your elbow through the target in a short, explosive arc. Elbow strikes can travel horizontally, diagonally, or vertically depending on the variation. Keep your fist tight and your opposite hand guarding your face. The power comes from hip and core rotation, not just the arm.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core.

items.name: Extended exhale
items.dose: Run it during every single release hold. Plus 5 minutes before sleep.
items.why: Breathing is upstream of most of it. Everything else on this list is downstream effect.

fields.tool: None
fields.release: In through the nose for a count of 4. Out through the nose or pursed lips for a count of 6 to 8. No force, no strain, no holding at the top.
fields.notice: Tissue lets go faster under release when you are doing this than when you are not. Test it on a spot you know well. Slowing. This is the mechanism behind the melt-into-the-floor response you already get.
fields.careful: If the count feels like a struggle, shorten both numbers and keep the ratio. 3 in, 5 out is fine.

items.name: Eye drills — how to run them
items.why: These train how well your eyes aim, follow, and refocus. Read this once; it applies to every eye drill in this section.

fields.tool: Two sticky notes with a + drawn on each, and a pen.
fields.release: The head stays still in all of them. Only the eyes move. If your neck starts doing the work, stop and reset — that is the drill quietly turning into something else.
fields.notice: Whether your eyes land cleanly on a target or overshoot and correct. Whether they follow a moving target smoothly or in small jumps. That noticing is the point as much as the reps are.

levels.name: Read it
levels.note: One read is enough. It stays here to come back to.

evidence.grade: established as a rehabilitation approach for vestibular and oculomotor dysfunction; not studied specifically in POTS
evidence.basis: Vestibular rehabilitation is standard care for peripheral vestibular hypofunction and PPPD. In POTS, vestibular symptoms are common and examination is recommended, but no POTS-specific trial exists.

items.name: Eye jumps — side to side
items.why: Trains your eyes to land accurately on a target instead of overshooting and correcting.
items.equipment: Two sticky notes with a + on each

fields.tool: Two sticky notes, each with a + drawn on it.
fields.release: Put one target at the far left edge of your vision and one at the far right. They stay put. Head still. Jump your eyes from one + to the other, refocusing on each as fast as you can.
fields.notice: Do your eyes land right on the +, or overshoot and slide back? Small corrections before you arrive are the thing being looked for.
fields.careful: This can bring on dizziness or nausea. Mild, settling discomfort is expected. A ramp that keeps climbing is a stop.

levels.name: As demonstrated
levels.note: 30 seconds. Position (seated or standing) not yet confirmed — ask.

items.name: Eye jumps — up and down
items.why: Same skill as the side-to-side version, in the plane that usually gets less practice.
items.equipment: Two sticky notes with a + on each

fields.tool: Two sticky notes, each with a + drawn on it.
fields.release: One target high, one low, both at the edges of your vision. They stay put. Head still. Jump your eyes between them, refocusing each time.
fields.notice: Same as side to side — landing clean, or overshooting and correcting.
fields.careful: Can bring on dizziness or nausea. Mild and settling is expected; a climbing ramp is a stop.

items.name: Farmer's Carry
items.why: Shoulders packed, chest tall, walk with purpose

fields.release: Pick up a heavy dumbbell in each hand and stand tall with your shoulders pulled down and back (packed). Walk forward in a controlled manner, keeping your chest up and core braced. Avoid leaning to either side. This builds grip strength, trap endurance, and core stability. Walk until your grip gives out or you reach your target distance.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: forearms, traps, core.

items.name: Feet
items.equipment: Firm lacrosse ball, or a golf ball for finer work
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Firm lacrosse ball, or a golf ball for finer work
fields.release: Ball under the arch — seated first, standing when you want more. Roll the whole sole slowly: heel, arch, ball of foot. Then park on the tender spots. 60–90 sec per foot.
fields.load: Short foot — gently dome the arch without curling the toes, hold 5 sec ×10. Then barefoot balance, eyes open, 30 sec per side.
fields.notice: The ground feels more detailed. Balance steadier. Calves loosen without being touched.
fields.careful: Tender because they're deconditioned, not damaged. Daily and light beats hard and occasional.

photos.caption: Ball under the arch, seated first. Roll heel, arch, ball of foot slowly, then park on the tender spots.

items.name: Figure-4 Stretch
items.why: Cross ankle over opposite knee, pull thigh toward chest

fields.release: Lie on your back and cross one ankle over the opposite knee, creating a figure-4 shape. Reach through and grab the uncrossed leg behind the thigh, then pull that thigh toward your chest. You should feel a deep stretch in the glute and outer hip of the crossed leg. Keep your head on the floor and breathe into the stretch.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, piriformis.

items.name: Finding a spot, and how to press it
items.why: Read once. It applies to every point in this section, and most of the skill is in here rather than in any single spot.

fields.tool: A thumb, a knuckle, or a small ball. Nothing sharp, nothing motorised.
fields.release: Press slowly until you meet something that feels tender out of proportion to how hard you are pressing. That mismatch is the find — not the hardest pressure you can stand. Hold steady contact rather than rubbing. Somewhere between 20 and 90 seconds, most spots either soften under your finger or they don't; both are answers.
fields.notice: Three things. Tenderness that doesn't match the pressure. Sensation that spreads somewhere other than where you are pressing. And whether the spot eases while you hold it. Easing under sustained pressure is the response worth chasing; more pain the longer you hold is a reason to come off.
fields.careful: Never press into a pulse, into the front of the throat, or hard onto bone. Numbness, pins and needles, or electric sensation means you are on a nerve — come off and move. Bruising means too hard.
fields.load: A point that eases is a door opened. Use the range afterward — move the joint it crosses, or load the muscle — or it closes again.

levels.name: Read it
levels.note: Comes back here whenever a point card says 'how do I do this again?'

evidence.grade: phenomenon: established as observable · mechanism: contested
evidence.basis: That tender spots exist, spread sensation, and soften under sustained pressure is uncontroversial and self-verifiable. Why they exist is unresolved in the literature.

items.name: Finding the deep abdominal layer
items.why: The load partner for the trunk and low-back release items. The deepest abdominal layer wraps around like a wide belt. It is not a six-pack muscle and it does not produce a crunch — it produces tension, and most people have never located it deliberately.

fields.tool: Your own fingertips as a monitor.
fields.release:
Lying on your back, knees bent. Put fingertips just inside the front points of your pelvis, an inch in and down. Breathe out and gently draw the lower abdomen inward and slightly upward, as if narrowing your waist a fraction — a very small effort. Under your fingers you should feel a gentle tensioning, not a hard bulge and not the belly hollowing dramatically. Hold it while you breathe normally.

Breathing normally while holding it is the whole point. If you can only produce it by holding your breath, you have produced something else.
fields.notice: Whether you can find it at all, and whether you can keep breathing while it is on. Whether you brace hard instead — that is the substitute pattern and it is very common. Whether your back flattens or your ribs flare.
fields.careful: Gentle. No sucking the belly in hard, no bearing down, no holding your breath. If your back or pelvis hurts doing this, stop and get it looked at.
fields.load: This is the load. Later rungs add limb movement while it stays on.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this kind of deep, low-effort control work is more valuable for you than heavy trunk exercise, and progressing to limb movement while it holds is the part that transfers. Slower progression than the rungs suggest is normal, not a failure.
items.dose: [undetermined] — hold time and repetitions are a clinician's number, not an app's.

levels.name: Find it
levels.note: Locate the gentle tension under your fingertips. That is the rung.

levels.name: Hold it and keep breathing
levels.note: The hard part, and the useful part.

levels.name: Hold it while a leg moves
levels.note: Keep the tension while slowly sliding one heel away and back. Losing it means back a rung.

levels.name: Standing and walking
levels.note: The same quiet tension upright. This is where it stops being an exercise and starts being how you are built.

evidence.grade: Established as standard rehabilitation content; the claim that this specific muscle must be trained in isolation is contested.
evidence.basis: Deep abdominal and multifidus training appears in trials of motor control exercise for low back pain, with results favouring motor control approaches over some passive modalities. What is genuinely contested is the stronger version of the story — that a specific isolated activation of one deep muscle is necessary, or that its timing explains back pain. This card teaches the skill of producing low-level trunk tension while breathing, which is useful regardless of how that debate settles, and does not make the stronger claim.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Fold and hold — releasing by shortening, not stretching
items.why: The backwards one, and the reason it is in this library. Everything else here lengthens or presses. This shortens the muscle until the tender spot stops being tender, and waits there. For anything too irritable to press or stretch, it is often the only door left open.
items.equipment: Pillows or cushions to hold the position

fields.tool: Props. The whole technique depends on the position being effortless, so you will use more cushions than you expect.
fields.release: Find the tender spot and keep a light finger on it — light enough to monitor, not enough to treat. Then slowly move the body part around until the tenderness under your finger drops substantially. Usually that means folding toward the tender spot, shortening the muscle, and it often looks like a strange slumped position. Prop yourself so you can stay there without effort, and wait. Then come out of the position slowly and passively — you move yourself out; do not let the muscle contract its way out.
fields.notice: The tenderness under the finger is your instrument. You are hunting for the position where it drops most, and small adjustments matter more than big ones. Coming out slowly matters as much as going in.
fields.careful: This should never hurt. If a position increases the tenderness, it is the wrong position — keep looking. Do not hold positions that compress the front of the neck or that you cannot get out of without help.
fields.load: Gentle, and later than usual. Something irritable enough to need this family is not ready for immediate hard loading — move the joint through easy range first, and put real load on it on a later day.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: positions of ease can be deep positions, and a lax joint can end up at end-range without any stretch sensation to warn you. Prop the joint rather than letting it settle to its limit. PEM/pacing: this is a low-exertion family and one of the few genuinely available on a bad day.
items.dose: The osteopathic tradition this comes from uses holds of roughly 90 seconds [practitioner convention — the figure is conventional in the technique's own literature and is not established by trials]. Number of positions per session: [undetermined].

levels.name: Find one position of ease
levels.note: One spot, one position, well propped. Finding it is the skill.

levels.name: Refine the position
levels.note: Small adjustments in several directions to find where tenderness drops furthest.

evidence.grade: Very low certainty. Some effect on tender-point pain, mainly as an addition to other treatment; not supported as a standalone.
evidence.basis: A meta-analysis of the technique's effect on tender-point palpation pain found a pooled benefit from low-quality studies. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in low back pain graded the certainty as very low and found benefit when combined with other treatment but not as a standalone. It is in this library because it is gentle, it opens a door for irritable tissue that tolerates nothing else, and its risk profile is close to zero — not because the evidence is strong. Tier: exploratory.

items.name: Following a moving target
items.why: Trains your eyes to follow something continuously instead of chasing it in small jumps.
items.equipment: One sticky note with a + on it

fields.tool: One sticky note with a + drawn on it.
fields.release: Hold the note out in front of you. Head still. Move the note slowly side to side and follow the + the whole way with your eyes — following it, not jumping ahead to where it is going.
fields.notice: Whether the follow is smooth or your eyes jump and catch up. That difference is exactly what an examiner watches for.
fields.careful: Can bring on dizziness or nausea. Mild and settling is expected; a climbing ramp is a stop.

items.name: Forward fold
items.why: Re-test: Every 2 weeks. Lower is better.

fields.release: Stand, knees SOFT — never locked back. Fold and let the arms hang. Measure fingertips to floor. A smaller number is more range. Locking the knees to gain a few centimetres invalidates it and is the exact thing you are trying not to do.
fields.notice: Recorded in cm.

items.name: Frog Stretch
items.why: Wide knees, hips push back, feel inner thigh stretch

fields.release: Start on all fours and spread your knees as wide as comfortable with your shins and the inside of your feet on the floor. Push your hips back toward your heels while keeping your chest down near the floor. You should feel a deep stretch in your inner thighs and groin. Breathe deeply and ease further into the stretch with each exhale.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: adductors, groin, hips.

items.name: Front of hip
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Firm lacrosse ball
fields.release: Lie face down, ball at the front-outside of the hip just inside the hip bone. Sink onto it slowly. Wait for the guard to let go, then a little more. 60–90 sec. Start with the tighter side; the other side lighter.
fields.load: Glute bridge ×10 slow, squeeze at the top. Then standing hip extension ×10 each side. The flexor let go; the glute has to take the job.
fields.notice: Knee-to-chest goes further with less pinch. Clicking quiets. Relaxation runs down the leg.
fields.careful: If a hip clicks, catches or feels like it slides, release is the opener and stability is the fix — do not chase depth.

photos.caption: Half-kneeling hip flexor — the safer swap for the kneeling lean-back the card warns about. Tuck the pelvis under.
The load. Slow, squeeze at the top. The flexor let go; the glute has to take the job.

items.name: Front of the hip — contract and let go
items.why: A different family applied to a region the library already has a pressure card for. Contract-relax reaches the deep hip flexor in a way a ball never will, and it builds control at the same time — which suits a hip that is tight because it is unstable rather than because it is short.
items.equipment: A cushion for the back knee

fields.tool: A half-kneeling position, cushion under the back knee.
fields.release:
Half kneeling, back knee down on a cushion, front foot flat. Tuck your tailbone under slightly — that is what actually puts the deep hip flexor on stretch, and without it you are just leaning forward. Shift your weight forward only until you feel the first honest sensation at the front of the back hip.

Now gently press the back knee down into the floor, as if trying to drag it toward your front foot, without moving. Hold lightly. Then let go completely on an out-breath, keep the tailbone tucked, and shift a little further forward. Repeat.
fields.notice: Whether you can keep the tailbone tucked as you shift forward — most people lose it immediately, and once it is lost the position stops working. Whether the sensation is at the front of the hip or in the low back; low back means the tuck has gone.
fields.careful: Gentle contraction, not a maximal push. Cushion under the knee. If the front of the hip pinches rather than stretches, come back and reduce the range.
fields.load: The same muscle working at its short end — knee lifts, or holding a knee up unsupported.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is a good family for you because the contraction builds control in the range you open. Keep the shift small; the tuck matters far more than the distance. Orthostatic: kneeling and standing up again is a position change — use support to get up.

levels.name: Find the tuck
levels.note: Half kneeling, tailbone tucked, no forward shift at all. Many people feel plenty here.

levels.name: Contract and release
levels.note: Add the gentle press and let-go, taking up slack afterward.

levels.name: Add the arm overhead
levels.note: Reach the arm on the back-leg side overhead and slightly across. Reaches the front of the trunk as well.

loadAfter.name: Slow knee lifts, lying or standing
loadAfter.note: Match at S5.

evidence.grade: Established for acute range of motion; no better than other stretching methods; mechanism is largely increased tolerance to stretch.
evidence.basis: Meta-analysis across stretching types finds contract-relax, static and dynamic stretching all improve range of motion acutely and over training periods, with no significant difference between them. A 2025 meta-analysis of static stretching mechanisms across 65 studies found range gains track increased tolerance to the stretch far more than any change in muscle length or stiffness. So: it works, and it works by changing what you will allow, not by lengthening tissue.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Different technique family from the imported 'Front of hip' pressure card.

items.name: Front of thigh
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Foam roller
fields.release: Roller down the front of the thigh, weight regulated through your arms. Slow.
fields.load: Bodyweight squat to a box or chair ×10, strict form. Then step-downs ×8 each side, slow and controlled.
fields.notice: Less pull on the kneecap. The deep squat comes easier.
fields.careful: The kneeling lean-back stretch is intense on a knee in deep flexion. Keep it propped and short — or swap it for a half-kneeling hip flexor stretch with the pelvis tucked under. Same chain, far more control.

photos.caption: Roller down the front of the thigh, weight regulated through the arms. Slow.

items.name: Front Raise
items.why: Raise to eye level, thumbs up, no swinging

fields.release: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging in front of your thighs with thumbs pointing forward. Raise one or both arms straight out in front of you to eye level, then lower with control. Keep your core braced and avoid swinging the weight; if you need momentum, the weight is too heavy.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders.

items.name: Front-of-thigh glide — half kneeling
items.why: The upright sibling for the same nerve, for people who cannot get comfortably onto their side or who want it in a standing routine.
items.equipment: A cushion for the knee; something to hold

fields.tool: A folded towel or cushion under the kneeling knee, and a wall or chair for one hand.
fields.release:
Half kneeling: one knee down on the cushion, the other foot flat in front of you, hand on a support.

Together: shift your weight forward a small amount so the front of the kneeling-side hip opens AND lift your chin. Then reverse together: shift back AND drop the chin toward your chest.

Inches of weight shift, not a lunge. The kneeling knee stays where it is.
fields.notice: The same front-of-thigh sensation, and whether it changes with the head. If the head makes no difference at all, you are stretching a hip flexor rather than gliding a nerve — which is fine, but it is a different module.
fields.careful: Do not let the low back arch to create the movement; the weight shift comes from the hips. Hand stays on the support. Stop for numbness or pins and needles at the front of the thigh.
fields.load: Stand up from the half-kneeling position without using your hands if you can, once or twice. That is the range being used.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: kneeling puts a lot on the front of the knee; a thicker cushion is not fussiness. And the low back will arch to give you the range your hip is not providing — if you cannot tell whether it is, use the side-lying version instead where the floor tells you. Orthostatic: getting down and up is the risky part, not the drill; take it in stages with a hand on support.

levels.name: Weight shift and head
levels.note: Add the chin lifting and dropping.

loadAfter.name: Hip flexors working at their short end

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.name: Front-of-thigh glide — side lying
items.why: The nerve at the front of the hip, serving the front of the thigh and the inner shin. The whole library talks about the back of the leg; this is the one that covers the front, and it is the one to think about when the front of the thigh is where the symptoms are.

fields.tool: The bed or floor, and a pillow between the knees if that is more comfortable.
fields.release:
Lie on your side, bottom knee bent up for stability. Reach back and hold the top ankle or trouser leg, drawing that knee gently backward behind you — a small amount.

Together: draw the knee a little further back AND lift your chin, looking slightly up. Then reverse together: bring the knee forward AND drop your chin toward your chest.

Small at the hip. This nerve does not need much, and the front of the hip is easy to overdo.
fields.notice: A sensation down the front of the thigh, sometimes toward the inner side of the shin, that changes as your head moves. That last part is the giveaway — a muscle at the front of the thigh does not care what your head is doing.
fields.careful: Keep your back from arching to make room; if your low back is doing the work, the range is too big. Stop for any pins and needles or numbness at the front of the thigh. Never hold the end position.
fields.load: Roll onto your back and bring the knee up toward your chest against light resistance a few times, or stand and take a few slow steps.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: hips that extend a long way will let the knee travel back much further than intended, and the low back will happily arch to add to it — set the ceiling by sensation, not by available movement. Orthostatic: lying item; sit up in stages.

levels.name: Knee only
levels.note: Head still, tiny range at the hip.

levels.name: Knee and head opposing
levels.note: Chin up as the knee draws back, chin down as it comes forward.

loadAfter.name: Hip flexors working at their short end

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.name: Getting used to busy visual scenes
items.why: For people whose dizziness is set off by a supermarket aisle, scrolling, or traffic — the system leaning too hard on vision, so busy vision overwhelms it.
items.equipment: A moving scene — a video of a crowd or traffic, or a real one

fields.release: Seated, feet flat. Watch a moving scene for a short, fixed time — start under a minute. Let your eyes rest on it rather than chasing any one thing. Stop at the time you set, not at the point where you feel bad.
fields.notice: Where the discomfort starts, and how long it takes to fade afterward. The fade time is the number worth watching over weeks; if it shortens, that is the change you were after.
fields.careful: Set the duration before you start and hold to it — this is a drill people overdo because the effect arrives late. Not while standing, not while driving, and not before something you need to be well for. If it triggers a headache or a migraine pattern, this is one to raise with a clinician rather than push through.
fields.load: Nothing. Sit until it settles.

levels.name: Short and seated
levels.note: 30–60 seconds, a scene you choose. Note how long the after-effect lasts.

levels.name: Longer
levels.note: Extend only when the after-effect from rung 1 is brief.

levels.name: Real environments
levels.note: A shop or a busy street, briefly, with a way to sit down.

evidence.grade: established as a component of vestibular rehabilitation for visually-provoked dizziness; not studied in POTS
evidence.basis: Habituation to visual motion is standard practice for persistent postural-perceptual dizziness, where over-reliance on vision is part of the picture. Whether it helps when the dizziness is orthostatic in origin is untested — which is why the card above it matters.

items.authoringNote: worth asking whether it fits his plan given the orthostatic findings.

items.name: Glute & back of hip
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Firm lacrosse ball
fields.release: Sit on the floor, ball under one glute, that ankle crossed over the opposite knee. Roll slowly to find the tender spot, then stop and let the pressure build. 60–90 sec each side.
fields.load: Side-lying clamshells ×12 each side, or standing banded abduction. Light band — this is about finding the muscle, not loading it.
fields.notice: Hips sit more level. Less low-back ache when standing.
fields.careful: Deep glute work can catch the sciatic nerve. Numbness or shooting down the leg means move the ball, not push harder.

photos.caption: Ball or roller under one glute, that ankle crossed over the opposite knee. Roll to the tender spot, then stop and let the pressure build.
Further round the side, if the tenderness sits on the outer hip rather than deep in the glute.
A harder bridge once the two-leg version is easy. Light band optional — this is about finding the muscle.

items.name: Glute Bridge
items.why: Drive hips up, squeeze glutes hard at top, feet flat

fields.release: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Drive through your heels to lift your hips toward the ceiling, squeezing your glutes as hard as you can at the top. Lower your hips back down with control. Avoid pushing from your lower back; the movement should come from your glutes. You should feel a strong contraction in your glutes at the top.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hamstrings.

items.name: Glute/Piriformis Roll
items.why: Sit on roller, cross one ankle over knee, lean into glute

fields.release: Sit on the foam roller with both feet on the floor. Cross one ankle over the opposite knee in a figure-4 position and lean toward the crossed side to target that glute. Roll slowly over the glute and piriformis area, pausing on tight or tender spots. Support yourself with your hands behind you. This is especially helpful for relieving sciatic tension and hip tightness.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, piriformis.

items.name: Gratitude / journaling
items.why: Mental clarity, emotional processing, stress reduction

items.name: Grounding / earthing
items.why: Bare feet on earth — reduces inflammation, improves sleep

items.name: Hamstrings
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Foam roller or firm ball
fields.release: Under the hamstring, seated on the floor with the leg out. Slow. Once you're on a spot, straighten and bend the knee a few times under the pressure.
fields.load: Glute bridge with the feet further out ×10. Then a bodyweight hip hinge with soft knees ×10 — slow, back flat.
fields.notice: The forward fold goes further with the knees soft.
fields.careful: Chase the fold with knees in soft neutral, never locked back. Range here is a fair target; knee hyperextension is not.

photos.caption: Under the hamstring, seated, leg out. Once you are on a spot, bend and straighten the knee under the pressure.
The load. Bridge with the feet further out than usual.

items.name: Hanging Leg Raise
items.why: No swinging, controlled raise, curl pelvis at top

fields.release: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms fully extended. Raise your legs in front of you by engaging your abs and hip flexors. At the top, curl your pelvis upward to fully contract the abs. Lower your legs back down with control, avoiding any swinging. Start with knee raises if straight legs are too difficult.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, hip flexors.

levels.name: Windshield Wiper
levels.note: Legs up, rotate side to side

items.name: Heat first — and when it makes things worse
items.why: A modifier rather than a technique — it changes what any of the other families feel like. Included because 'apply heat first' is advice everybody has heard and almost nobody has been told the limits of.
items.equipment: A heat pack, a shower, a bath

fields.tool: Moist heat, a warm shower, or a warm room. Comfortable warmth, not hot.
fields.release: Warm the area for a few minutes, then do the release work while it is still warm. Everything tends to feel less guarded and more tolerable.
fields.notice: Whether heat actually helps you, or whether it makes you feel worse afterward. Both happen, and which one you are is worth knowing before you build a routine around it.
fields.careful: Comfortably warm, never hot enough to redden skin. Not on a numb area, and not on a fresh injury with swelling.
fields.load: Heat changes how the work feels; it does not replace the loading step.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: heat is one of the most reliable triggers for symptoms in people with blood-pressure instability — hot showers, hot baths and heat packs all count. If standing in a hot shower makes you grey out, heat before release work is not a neutral addition for you, and cool or neutral is the better default. PEM/pacing: heat exposure is itself a load for some people.
items.dose: [undetermined] — this library does not have a derived warming time.

levels.name: Try it once, deliberately
levels.note: Same release item, one session with heat and one without, and compare honestly.

evidence.grade: Undetermined as a modifier to self-release specifically. Heat has its own small evidence base for musculoskeletal pain.
evidence.basis: Heat before soft-tissue work is standard practice and appears as a comparator inside some trials rather than as a tested variable of its own, so its contribution has not been isolated. The orthostatic caution above is not from this literature — it is the well-described heat sensitivity in orthostatic intolerance, and it is why this card exists at all.

items.name: High Knees
items.why: Drive knees to waist height, pump arms, stay on toes

fields.release: Run in place, driving your knees up to waist height with each step. Stay on the balls of your feet and pump your arms as you would while sprinting. Keep your torso upright and avoid leaning back. Start at a comfortable pace and increase speed as you warm up. This builds hip flexor endurance and elevates your heart rate quickly.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors, quads.

items.name: High-Knee Jump
items.why: Drive knees high with each jump, maintain rhythm

fields.release: While jumping rope, drive your knees up toward your chest with each revolution, alternating legs like you are running with high knees. Maintain a steady rhythm with the rope and land on the balls of your feet. This elevates the intensity significantly compared to basic jumping and builds hip flexor strength and cardiovascular fitness.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors, calves.

items.name: Hindu Push-Up
items.why: Dive from downward dog through low sweep to upward dog

fields.release: Start in a downward-dog position with hips high. Swoop your body forward and down, skimming your chest close to the floor, then press up into an upward-dog position with your chest open and hips low. Reverse the motion back to downward dog. This flowing movement works the chest, shoulders, and back while building flexibility.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, shoulders, back.

items.name: Hip CARs
items.why: Slow controlled circles at the hip, biggest circle possible

fields.release: Stand on one leg or kneel on all fours. Lift one knee and slowly draw the biggest circle possible with your hip joint, moving through flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction. Make smooth, controlled circles in both directions. This maintains hip joint range of motion and highlights any areas of tightness.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hips, hip flexors, glutes.

items.name: Hip Flexor Release
items.why: Face down, roller under hip crease, gentle pressure and breathe

fields.release: Lie face down and place the foam roller under one hip crease, where the front of your thigh meets your pelvis. Apply gentle pressure and breathe deeply, allowing the tight hip flexor muscles to release. You can gently rock side to side or bend and straighten your knee to work different fibers. Be careful with pressure here as this area can be very sensitive.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors.

levels.name: Leg Movement
levels.note: Bend and straighten knee while on spot

items.name: Hip flexors working at their short end
items.why: The load partner for the hip flexor release items. A hip flexor that feels tight is often not short — it is working at the wrong length and never asked to produce force where it is shortest. Stretching it and walking away leaves the reason untouched.

fields.tool: Nothing.
fields.release:
Lying on your back, knees bent. Lift one knee toward your chest as far as it will comfortably go using your own muscle, then take your hands away and hold it there without help. That is the short end, and holding it there is what the muscle has probably not been asked to do in years. Lower slowly. Then the other side.

Standing version: bring one knee up to hip height and hold, standing tall, near something to hold onto.
fields.notice: Whether the knee drops as soon as you take your hands away. How much higher your hands can put it than your own muscle can. That gap is the finding, and closing it matters more than gaining stretch.
fields.careful: Slow and controlled. Any pinching at the front of the hip means lower the knee until it stops. Standing version near support.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: your hands can take the joint much further than your muscle can hold, and that gap is bigger for you than for most people — which makes this item unusually valuable and makes chasing more range unusually pointless. Orthostatic: use the lying version, or stand near support.

levels.name: Lying, hold at your own end range
Standing knee hold
levels.note: Upright, near support. Also a balance item, which is a bonus rather than an accident.

evidence.grade: Established as standard rehabilitation content.
evidence.basis: Active hip flexor work at inner range is routine in rehabilitation, and the general principle — that range gained passively is retained better when the muscle is loaded in the new range — is consistent with how range-of-motion training is understood. Specific doses are protocol-dependent and are not reproduced here.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Hip Thrust
items.why: Upper back on bench, drive hips up, squeeze glutes at top

fields.release: Sit on the floor with your upper back resting against a bench. Place your feet flat on the floor about hip-width apart, knees bent at roughly 90 degrees. Drive through your heels and push your hips up until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees, squeezing your glutes hard at the top. Lower with control. Place a dumbbell on your hips for added resistance.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hamstrings.

items.name: Holding a target while your head moves
items.why: The opposite of the eye drills. There, the head stays still and the eyes move. Here the eyes stay locked and the head moves — which is the reflex that keeps the world from sliding around when you walk, turn, or look over your shoulder.
items.equipment: A card or sticky note with a letter or + on it

fields.tool: A target you can hold at arm's length — a letter is better than a dot, because you can tell whether it stays sharp.
fields.release: Seated. Hold the target at arm's length and keep your eyes locked on it. Turn your head slowly side to side while the target stays still and stays in focus. The head moves; the target doesn't; your gaze doesn't leave it. Then the same with a nodding motion.
fields.notice: Whether the letter stays sharp or smears as your head turns. Smearing means the reflex isn't keeping up — slow the head down until it stays sharp, and that speed is your starting point.
fields.careful: This one provokes more than the head-still drills. Seated first, always. Short — build up from well under a minute. Mild dizziness that settles within a few minutes afterward is expected; dizziness that keeps climbing, or nausea, is a stop. If you are prone to migraine, start shorter still.
fields.load: Nothing to load. Sit for a minute afterward before standing up.

levels.name: Seated, side to side
levels.note: Start at 15–20 seconds and only extend if it settles cleanly. Slow enough that the letter stays sharp.

levels.name: Standing, near support
levels.note: Same drills upright. Only once the seated versions are comfortable.

evidence.grade: established for vestibular hypofunction and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness; not studied in POTS specifically
evidence.basis: Gaze stabilization is a core component of standard vestibular rehabilitation and has a real trial base in those populations. No trial has tested it in orthostatic intolerance, where symptoms overlap but the mechanism differs.

items.authoringNote: worth asking him whether he wants this in the mix yet, since it is a step up in provocation from the head-still drills he started with.

items.name: Hollow Body Hold
items.why: Low back glued to floor, arms and legs hovering, tight body

fields.release: Lie on your back and press your lower back into the floor. Lift your arms overhead and your legs off the floor so both hover a few inches above the ground, creating a slight banana shape with your body. Squeeze every muscle tight and hold. If your lower back peels off the floor, tuck your knees or raise your legs higher to make it easier.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, hip flexors.

levels.name: Hollow Rock
levels.note: Rock back and forth in hollow

items.name: Hook
items.why: Rotate hips and shoulders, elbow at 90 degrees, snap through

fields.release: From your boxing stance, keep your elbow bent at roughly 90 degrees and rotate your hips and shoulders explosively to swing your fist in a horizontal arc toward the target. Your power comes from the hip rotation, not the arm. Pivot on your lead foot and keep your other hand up guarding your face throughout the punch.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques, shoulders, hips.

levels.name: Lead Hook Slow
levels.note: Slow lead hook, focus on form

items.name: Humming & gargling
items.equipment: Your voice, and a glass of water
items.dose: Daily. It combines with the soft palate work — same drills, two purposes.
items.why: Direct downregulation. Cheap, and most of it needs no equipment at all.

fields.tool: Your voice, and a glass of water
fields.release: Hum on the lowest comfortable pitch, drawing the exhale out as long as it will go. Feel the vibration in your throat and chest. 5 minutes, or about 20 long hums. Gargle water loudly for 30 seconds, ×3.
fields.notice: The vagus nerve supplies the larynx, so this is about as direct as non-invasive vagal stimulation gets without a device.
fields.careful: None.

items.name: Incline DB Curl
items.why: Lean back on incline, let arms hang, curl with full stretch

fields.release: Set a bench to a 45-degree incline and sit back with a dumbbell in each hand, letting your arms hang straight down behind your torso. Curl the weights up toward your shoulders, then lower all the way back to a full stretch. The incline angle creates a longer range of motion and a deeper stretch at the bottom, which makes this one of the best bicep exercises.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: biceps.

items.name: Inside the armpit — the cuff muscle nobody reaches
items.why: One rotator cuff muscle sits on the front surface of the shoulder blade, between the blade and the ribs. You can only reach a sliver of it, from inside the armpit — and that sliver is often startlingly tender in anyone whose shoulders sit rounded forward.

fields.tool: The fingers of your opposite hand. No tool reaches here.
fields.release:
Let the arm hang relaxed, or rest it on a table. Reach across with the other hand and find the back wall of your armpit — the thick fold you can pinch between fingers and thumb. Now slide your fingers just in front of that fold, toward the front of the shoulder blade, and press gently backward and outward against the flat surface you find there. Hold, and let the arm stay completely relaxed. Then move your fingers a little and repeat.

The arm being relaxed is not a detail. This muscle is under the blade and you cannot reach it through a shoulder that is holding itself up.
fields.notice: How tender it is compared with what you expected. Whether sensation spreads to the back of the shoulder or down the back of the arm. Whether reaching overhead feels different immediately afterward.
fields.careful: Gentle, and stay against the flat surface of the shoulder blade rather than poking into the middle of the armpit — nerves, vessels and lymph nodes sit in the hollow. Tingling into the arm or hand means come off immediately. If you find a firm tender lump that is new, that is something to have looked at rather than to release.
fields.load: External rotation — the opposite action — at a range you control. Release this without loading the other side of the joint and it will be back.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: shoulder instability is common with hypermobility and this muscle may be gripping for a reason. Release plus loading, never release alone, and if your shoulder subluxes or gives way, this belongs with a clinician before it belongs in a routine.

levels.name: Find it, arm supported
levels.note: Locating the surface with the arm fully rested. Finding it is a legitimate whole session.

levels.name: Sustained contact
levels.note: Gentle hold, moving to a few spots along it.

levels.name: Add slow rotation
levels.note: Hold contact and slowly turn the palm up and down, letting the tissue move underneath. Pin-and-move.

loadAfter.name: Turning the arm out, under control

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Inverted Row
items.why: Body straight, pull chest to bar or table edge

fields.release: Lie under a sturdy table or low bar, grab the edge with an overhand grip, and hang with your body straight and heels on the floor. Pull your chest up to the bar or table edge by squeezing your shoulder blades together, then lower with control. Keep your body rigid like a reverse plank. The more horizontal your body, the harder the exercise.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: back, biceps.

levels.name: Feet Elevated
levels.note: Feet on bench for extra load

items.name: IT Band Roll
items.why: Lie on side, roll from hip to knee, pause on tender spots

fields.release: Lie on your side with the foam roller under your outer thigh, just below your hip. Support yourself with your hands and opposite foot. Slowly roll from your hip down to just above your knee, pausing on any tender spots for 20-30 seconds. Control the pressure by shifting more or less weight onto the roller. This can be intense; start with light pressure.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: IT band, outer thigh.

items.name: Jab-Cross
items.why: Snap jab, rotate hips on cross, return hands to guard

fields.release: From a boxing stance, extend your lead hand straight out in a snapping motion (jab), then immediately follow with your rear hand, rotating your hips and rear foot for power (cross). Return both hands quickly to your guard position after each punch. The jab is fast and light; the cross should carry your full body rotation behind it.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core, hips.

items.name: Jaw — bite gently, then let go
items.why: The no-hands jaw item. Useful when the cheek is too sore to press, and useful in public, where pressing your own face is conspicuous and this is not.

fields.tool: Your own jaw. Optionally a knuckle resting under the chin as a gentle resistance.
fields.release: Let your jaw hang so the teeth are slightly apart. Now clench very gently — a fraction of what you could do — hold briefly, then let go completely and let the jaw drop open a little further than it was. Feel the weight of your jaw hanging. Repeat a few times. Then a second version: rest a knuckle under your chin and try to open your mouth gently against it, hold, then release and let the jaw open freely.
fields.notice: Where your teeth sit when you are not thinking about it. They are meant to be slightly apart, with the tongue resting on the roof of the mouth and the lips closed. Most people discover their teeth are touching, and often that they are lightly clenched.
fields.careful: Gentle clench, never hard — a maximum bite is exactly what this is meant to undo. If your jaw clicks, locks, or shifts to one side when it opens, keep everything small and take it to a dentist or clinician. Do not do this with something between your teeth.
fields.load: The resting position itself is the load partner here, plus slow tracking — opening and closing while keeping the jaw travelling straight.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: jaw joints move further and click more often in hypermobile people, and jaw problems are common. Keep the opening well short of maximum, avoid wide yawning stretches, and treat locking or a jaw that shifts off line as a clinical question rather than something to work through.

levels.name: Clench and let go
levels.note: Gentle. Learn what a released jaw feels like.

levels.name: Open against a knuckle
levels.note: Light resistance to opening, then release.

levels.name: Carry it into the day
levels.note: Set the resting position deliberately several times during the day. This is where the change actually happens.

loadAfter.name: Jaw resting position and straight tracking

evidence.grade: Established for acute range of motion; no better than other stretching methods; mechanism is largely increased tolerance to stretch.
evidence.basis: Meta-analysis across stretching types finds contract-relax, static and dynamic stretching all improve range of motion acutely and over training periods, with no significant difference between them. A 2025 meta-analysis of static stretching mechanisms across 65 studies found range gains track increased tolerance to the stretch far more than any change in muscle length or stiffness. So: it works, and it works by changing what you will allow, not by lengthening tissue.

items.name: Jaw resting position and straight tracking
items.why: The load partner for every jaw item. Releasing a jaw and then returning it to the same clenched default is a door you open every day and never walk through.

fields.tool: A mirror for the tracking part.
fields.release: Two pieces. **The resting position:** tongue resting broad on the roof of the mouth just behind the front teeth, teeth slightly apart, lips closed, breathing through the nose. Set it deliberately and notice how long it lasts before you drift. **Tracking:** in front of a mirror, open and close your mouth slowly, watching whether your chin travels straight down or veers to one side. If it veers, rest a fingertip lightly on the chin and use it as a reminder to keep the path straight — a guide, not a force.
fields.notice: How quickly the resting position is lost. Whether the jaw tracks straight, and whether it veers in the same direction each time. Where a click, if there is one, happens in the movement.
fields.careful: Never force the jaw straight and never open to maximum. Locking, a jaw that will not close, or pain with opening is a clinician's question. If tracking practice makes things worse, stop.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: jaw joint problems are common with hypermobility, and wide opening is where they show up. Keep opening moderate, do not practise big yawns as a stretch, and treat repeated locking as a clinical issue.

levels.name: Set the resting position
levels.note: Just finding it, several times a day.

levels.name: Add tracking in a mirror
levels.note: Slow open and close, watching the path.

levels.name: Hold it through a task
levels.note: Keep the resting position through something that normally makes you clench — driving, typing, a difficult conversation.

evidence.grade: Established as standard conservative jaw care; the specific resting-position instruction is convention.
evidence.basis: Resting-position and controlled-opening advice is routine in conservative jaw management. The precise tongue position taught is a convention across clinical traditions rather than a trial-derived parameter, and is stated here as such.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Jaw, tongue and throat — letting the whole floor go
items.why: The jaw, the tongue, the floor of the mouth and the throat hold tension as a set, not individually, and they are wired into the same protective response as everything else that braces. Releasing them one muscle at a time misses how they behave.

fields.tool: Breath and attention.
fields.release: Sitting or lying. Breathe in through your nose, letting the belly and lower ribs widen. On the way out, let go of four things in order: the teeth come apart, the tongue goes heavy and wide and rests on the roof of the mouth, the floor of the mouth under the chin goes soft, and the throat opens. Then breathe in again without re-gripping any of them. Several breaths.
fields.notice: Which of the four you cannot let go of. Almost everyone has one that resists. Notice too whether the soft area under your chin is tight — put a thumb lightly under there and feel whether it is firm; it should be soft when you are not swallowing or speaking.
fields.careful: If deliberate breathing makes you lightheaded, make the breaths smaller and shorter. Nothing forced, nothing held.
fields.load: Nose breathing during the day, tongue resting on the roof of the mouth, teeth apart. That is the load for this one — the position becomes the default rather than an exercise.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: do this seated or lying. Slow deep breathing makes lightheadedness worse in some people; shorten the breath rather than dropping the item.

levels.name: Find which one resists
levels.note: Teeth, tongue, floor of mouth, throat. Identifying the sticky one is the rung.

levels.name: All four on each exhale
levels.note: Several consecutive breaths, releasing the whole set each time.

levels.name: Set it during the day
levels.note: The same release, briefly, at ordinary moments — at a red light, before a meeting, on hold.

loadAfter.name: Jaw resting position and straight tracking

evidence.grade: Expert consensus and small clinical series for down-training overactive muscle; not established as a strengthening method.
evidence.basis: For the high-tone pelvic floor specifically, expert consensus and treatment algorithms place relaxation-focused work — diaphragmatic breathing, paced exhale, graded desensitisation — as a first-line element, supported by pilot studies and clinical series rather than large trials. A separate and important finding: breathing-based approaches used alone are not effective for pelvic floor strengthening. Down-training and strengthening are different jobs and this family does the first one.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Overlaps deliberately with the existing tongue-posture and airway cards — this is the release-side entry into that material, not a replacement for it.

items.name: Jump Rope Tabata
items.why: 20 seconds max effort, 10 seconds rest, repeat

fields.release: Follow the Tabata protocol with your jump rope: perform 20 seconds of maximum effort jumping followed by 10 seconds of rest, and repeat for the prescribed number of rounds. Use any jump rope skill you are comfortable with. The short rest periods make this an extremely effective cardiovascular workout. Push hard during each work interval.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: full body.

items.name: Just below the ear
items.why: Where the jaw hinge and the muscles around it sit — often tender, and often connected to ear fullness and jaw noise.

fields.tool: One or two fingertips.
fields.release: Find the hollow just in front of your earlobe. Open and close your jaw and you will feel the hinge move under your finger. Press gently into the soft tissue just below and behind that, not onto the joint itself.
fields.notice: Whether the jaw tracks straight when it opens or veers to one side. Whether there is a click, and if so, where in the movement.
fields.careful: Not on the joint, and not hard. Clicking, locking, or a jaw that shifts out of line is a clinician's question, not something to press harder on — this is more common in hypermobile people, and pressure is not the answer to it.
fields.load: Slow open and close with the tongue held on the roof of the mouth — it guides the jaw straight.

items.name: KB Around the World
items.why: Pass KB around body at waist level, keep hips still

fields.release: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a kettlebell in one hand at waist level. Pass the bell behind your back, switch hands, and bring it back around to the front. Keep your hips still and core braced as the bell circles your body. This warms up the grip, shoulders, and core. Switch directions each set for balanced training.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: core, shoulders.

items.name: KB Bottoms-Up Press
items.why: Hold KB upside down, crush grip, press overhead with control

fields.release: Hold a kettlebell upside down (bottom up) by the handle with a crushing grip. The bell should be balancing above your fist. From the rack position, press the kettlebell overhead with control, keeping it balanced the entire time. This requires intense grip strength, shoulder stability, and core engagement. Use a much lighter weight than your normal press.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, forearms, core.

items.name: KB Clean
items.why: Pull from floor to rack position, punch hand around bell, soft catch

fields.release: Start with the kettlebell on the floor between your feet. Hinge at the hips, grab the handle, and pull the bell upward close to your body. As it rises past your chest, punch your hand around the handle to catch it in the rack position against your forearm and chest. The key is a smooth catch; avoid letting the bell slam against your wrist by keeping it close.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: forearms, shoulders, hips.

items.name: KB Front Rack Carry
items.why: KB in rack position against chest, stand tall, walk with control

fields.release: Clean one or two kettlebells to the rack position, resting them against your chest and forearms with elbows tucked. Stand tall, brace your core, and walk with controlled, purposeful steps. The weight challenges your core stability and breathing while building endurance. Keep your shoulders down and chest up throughout the carry.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: core, shoulders, forearms.

items.name: KB Goblet Squat
items.why: Hold KB at chest, sit deep, elbows inside knees, chest tall

fields.release: Hold a kettlebell by the horns (sides of the handle) at chest level, close to your body. Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width. Squat deep, keeping your chest tall and letting your elbows track inside your knees. Drive through your whole foot to stand back up. The goblet position naturally promotes good squat form.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

items.name: KB Halo
items.why: Circle KB around head, keep core tight, smooth path

fields.release: Hold a kettlebell upside down by the horns at chest level. Circle it around your head in a smooth path, keeping it close to your head and your core braced. Complete several reps in one direction, then switch. Keep your torso still and avoid leaning. This builds shoulder mobility and stability while engaging the core.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core.

levels.name: Half-Kneeling
levels.note: Kneel on one knee for stability

items.name: KB Snatch
items.why: One motion floor to overhead, punch through at top, lock out

fields.release: Swing the kettlebell from between your legs and, in one powerful motion, drive it overhead to a locked-out position. At the top, punch your hand through the handle so the bell rests gently against the back of your forearm. This combines a swing and an overhead press into one explosive movement. Master the swing and clean before attempting snatches.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, hips, core.

items.name: KB Swing
items.why: Hip hinge, snap hips forward, float the bell, arms are ropes

fields.release: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width and the kettlebell on the floor in front of you. Hinge at the hips, grab the bell, and hike it back between your legs. Explosively snap your hips forward to drive the kettlebell up to chest or shoulder height. Let it swing back between your legs and repeat. Your arms are just ropes; all the power comes from your hips.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hamstrings, core.

items.name: KB Turkish Get-Up
items.why: Eyes on bell at all times, move through each position deliberately

fields.release: Lie on your back with a kettlebell pressed overhead in one hand. Move through a series of deliberate positions to transition from lying down to standing while keeping the bell locked out overhead. Keep your eyes on the kettlebell at all times. This is a full-body exercise that builds stability, mobility, and strength. Learn each position slowly before adding weight.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: full body.

items.name: KB Windmill
items.why: KB overhead, hinge sideways, eyes on bell, touch floor

fields.release: Press a kettlebell overhead with one arm and lock it out. Turn your feet slightly away from the loaded side. Keeping your eyes on the bell, hinge at the hips and slide your free hand down your front leg toward the floor. Your torso rotates open as you descend. Stand back up by driving through your hips. This challenges oblique strength, hip mobility, and shoulder stability.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques, shoulders, hips.

items.name: Kick Check (Shin Block)
items.why: Lift leg to block with shin, toes pointed down, stay balanced

fields.release: From your fighting stance, lift your lead leg by bending the knee and turning the shin outward to block an incoming kick. Point your toes downward and raise your knee to at least waist height. Keep your hands up to protect your head and stay balanced on your supporting leg. Return to your stance quickly after the check.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors, calves.

items.name: Knee Strike
items.why: Drive knee upward, pull with hips, squeeze at top

fields.release: From your fighting stance, drive your rear or lead knee upward toward the imaginary target, pulling your hips into the strike. Rise onto the ball of your supporting foot and squeeze at the top of the motion. In a clinch position, you would pull the opponent into the knee. Keep your guard up and core engaged throughout the strike.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors, core.

items.name: Knee to wall
items.why: Re-test: Every 2 weeks. Higher is better.

fields.release: Big toe pointing at the wall, foot square. Slide the foot back until your knee only just touches the wall with the heel still down. Measure from the wall to the big toe. Same foot position, same bare feet, every time.
fields.notice: Recorded in cm.

items.name: Knee-to-chest pinch
items.why: Re-test: Every 2 weeks. Lower is better.

fields.release: On your back, draw one knee to your chest. Rate the PINCH at the front of the hip, 0 to 10 — not the stretch behind. Same depth each time, so stop at the point where the pinch first appears rather than pulling to end range.
fields.notice: Recorded in 0–10.

items.name: L-Sit
items.why: Hands on floor beside hips, lift legs parallel, lock arms

fields.release: Sit on the floor with legs straight in front of you and place your hands flat on the floor beside your hips. Lock your arms and press down to lift your entire body off the floor, holding your legs straight and parallel to the ground. This requires significant core, hip flexor, and tricep strength. Start with a tucked position if you cannot hold straight legs.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, hip flexors.

levels.name: One Leg Extended
levels.note: Extend one leg at a time

items.name: Lat & back of armpit
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Firm ball, side-lying
fields.release: Lie on your side, arm overhead, ball in the back wall of the armpit. Small movements, not long rolls.
fields.load: Lat squeeze isometric — arms at your sides, squeeze the armpits down toward the hips, 5 sec ×10. Then assisted hang, feet partly down, 20–40 sec, pulling the shoulder blades DOWN.
fields.notice: Ribs stop flaring. Belly breath comes easier. Traps quieten.
fields.careful: If a shoulder subluxes or feels unstable overhead, keep the feet partly on the ground during hangs until the scapular base is solid.

photos.caption: Side-lying, arm overhead, in the back wall of the armpit. Small movements, not long rolls.
