The load. Hang, then raise yourself a few inches WITHOUT bending the arms — a reverse shrug that depresses the shoulder blades. This is the "pull the blades DOWN" cue, and it is the exact drill rather than an approximation.

items.name: Lat Roll
items.why: Lie on side, roller under armpit, roll up and down lat

fields.release: Lie on your side with the foam roller positioned under your armpit area. Extend the bottom arm overhead and slowly roll from your armpit down to the bottom of your ribcage. Pause on tender areas for 20-30 seconds. Control pressure with your feet and opposite hand. This releases tightness in the lats, which improves overhead reach and shoulder mobility.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lats.

items.name: Lateral Bound
items.why: Push off one leg, land on the other, absorb and stick

fields.release: Stand on one leg, push off explosively to the side, and land on the opposite foot. Absorb the landing by bending your knee and hip, sticking the position for a moment before bounding back. Keep your hips and chest facing forward throughout. This builds lateral power, ankle stability, and single-leg landing mechanics.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, quads, ankles.

items.name: Lateral Lunge
items.why: Wide step to side, sit hips back, keep trailing leg straight

fields.release: Stand with feet together, then take a wide step to one side. Sit your hips back and bend the stepping leg while keeping the trailing leg straight. Push through the bent leg to return to the starting position. Keep your chest up and your weight in your heel on the working side. You should feel this in your inner thighs and glutes.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: adductors, quads, glutes.

levels.name: Cossack Squat
levels.note: Full depth, raised toes on straight leg

fields.release: Step wide to the right, bending right knee and pushing hips back while keeping left leg straight. Keep both feet flat. Sit into the bent knee side. Feel the stretch in the straight leg's inner thigh. Hold, then switch sides.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: adductors, groin, hamstrings, quads.

levels.name: easy
levels.note: Shallow lunge, hands on thigh for support

levels.name: advanced
levels.note: Transition into Cossack squat — heel on straight leg lifts

items.name: Lateral Raise
items.why: Slight bend in elbows, raise to shoulder height, control down

fields.release: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. With a slight bend in your elbows, raise both arms out to the sides until they reach shoulder height, then lower slowly. Avoid swinging or using momentum, and do not raise above shoulder level. You should feel this in the sides of your shoulders.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders.

levels.name: Banded
levels.note: Use a light band for resistance

items.name: Leg Raise
items.why: Low back pressed to floor, raise legs to 90 degrees, lower slow

fields.release: Lie on your back with legs straight and hands at your sides or under your hips for support. Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Raise both legs together to 90 degrees, then lower them slowly toward the floor without letting your lower back arch up. If your back lifts off the floor, bend your knees slightly or do not lower your legs as far.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, hip flexors.

items.name: Legs Up the Wall
items.why: Butt near wall, legs straight up, arms relaxed

fields.release: Sit with one hip against a wall, then swing your legs up as you lie back. Scoot your butt as close to the wall as comfortable. Arms at sides or on belly. Close your eyes. This inverts blood flow, calms the nervous system, and gently stretches hamstrings.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings, lower back, nervous system.

levels.name: Away From Wall
levels.note: Butt a few inches from wall

levels.name: Straddle
levels.note: Straddle legs wide for adductor stretch

items.name: Letting the deep hip flexor go — without touching it
items.why: The deepest hip flexor runs from the lumbar spine through the pelvis to the top of the thigh. Reaching it manually means pressing through the abdomen, which is a genuinely poor idea for most people. This position removes its job entirely and waits, which costs nothing and risks nothing.
items.equipment: Floor and a wall or chair; a small cushion

fields.tool: The floor, and something to rest your lower legs on.
fields.release: Lie on your back with your lower legs resting on a chair seat, hips and knees at roughly right angles. Or lie with knees bent and feet flat, close to your seat, and let the knees lean gently against each other so nothing is held. Arms wherever they are comfortable. Then stop. Not stretching, not breathing in a special way, not scanning your body. Several minutes of the muscle having no job at all.
fields.notice: How long it takes before anything actually lets go. Often several minutes — much longer than most people ever wait. Whether one hip feels different from the other once things settle.
fields.careful: Nothing should go numb. If your low back is uncomfortable flat on the floor, put a small cushion under it or use the legs-on-a-chair version. Get up slowly.
fields.load: The hip flexors need to work at their short range afterward, not just be released — a slow knee lift while lying, or holding one knee up without the hands. That teaches the muscle it can produce rather than only tighten.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: legs-elevated is usually well tolerated and often actively welcome; come up in stages. PEM/pacing: genuinely close to free — this is a real protocol item on a day when nothing else is possible, not a rest day dressed up.
items.dose: [undetermined] — traditions using this position suggest several minutes to twenty; nothing here is derived.

levels.name: Longer
levels.note: Time is the only variable that changes.

loadAfter.name: Slow knee lifts, lying
loadAfter.note: Match against existing hip flexor strength content at S5.

evidence.grade: Undetermined. No trial base as a standalone intervention. Risk close to zero.
evidence.basis: This family has not been tested as an intervention in its own right, so there is no grade to report and none is invented here. It is in the library because it is the only release approach that costs nothing in capacity, which matters in a population where capacity is the binding constraint. Judge it against your own experience, not against evidence that does not exist.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Deliberately offered instead of deep abdominal pressure on this muscle, which this library does not teach.

items.name: Letting the floor drop on the out-breath
items.why: The entry point for the whole region. You cannot reach this muscle with a ball, so breath is the tool — and it turns out to be the more effective one anyway, because the floor already moves with breathing whether you attend to it or not.
items.equipment: None; a cushion under the knees helps

fields.tool: Breath, and a position where nothing has to hold you up.
fields.release:
Lie on your back with knees bent, or on your side, or sit well supported. Breathe in slowly through the nose and let the belly and the lower ribs widen sideways — not a big breath, a wide one. As you breathe in, imagine the base of the pelvis softening and dropping very slightly, like a hammock taking weight. On the out-breath, let it return without pushing it anywhere. Then repeat, and let each in-breath find a little more give.

The common mistake is trying. This is a letting-go instruction, and effort is the opposite of the thing.
fields.notice: Whether there is any sense of movement at all. Whether your belly moves but nothing lower does — that disconnect is very common and it is the thing this item is aimed at. Whether you grip somewhere else instead: buttocks, inner thighs, jaw, or the top of the shoulders. Almost everyone grips somewhere.
fields.careful: No bearing down and no pushing. If you feel pressure downwards or a bulging sensation, you have gone from releasing to straining — stop, and if that happens repeatedly, take it to a pelvic floor physiotherapist. Lightheadedness means the breaths are too big; make them smaller.
fields.load: A gentle lift and a full release, which is the activation item in this file. Down-training alone is half the job; a floor that can let go also needs to be able to produce.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: lying is the friendliest position and slow deep breathing can provoke symptoms in some people — smaller breaths, and come up in stages. PEM/pacing: about as low-exertion as this library gets, and available on almost any day. Hypermobile: see the opening card — the case for a real assessment is stronger for you.
items.dose: [undetermined] — breath counts and session lengths in the down-training literature vary by clinic and are not standardised.

levels.name: Just breathe wide
levels.note: Belly and lower ribs widening. Do not chase the pelvic floor at all yet.

levels.name: Add the drop
levels.note: Attention on the base of the pelvis softening as you breathe in.

levels.name: In a lengthening position
levels.note: The same breathing inside one of the supported positions below, which gives the floor more room to give.

loadAfter.name: A lift, and a full let-go

evidence.grade: Expert consensus and small clinical series for down-training overactive muscle; not established as a strengthening method.
evidence.basis: For the high-tone pelvic floor specifically, expert consensus and treatment algorithms place relaxation-focused work — diaphragmatic breathing, paced exhale, graded desensitisation — as a first-line element, supported by pilot studies and clinical series rather than large trials. A separate and important finding: breathing-based approaches used alone are not effective for pelvic floor strengthening. Down-training and strengthening are different jobs and this family does the first one.

items.name: Lifting the arch, and calf raises that use it
items.why: The load partner for the deep calf and foot items. An arch is held up by muscles, not by shoe inserts, and the muscles that do it are ones most people cannot consciously find.
items.equipment: None; a step for the later rungs

fields.tool: Nothing. Bare feet.
fields.release:
Seated, foot flat on the floor. Without curling your toes and without lifting your heel or the ball of your foot, try to shorten the distance between your heel and the base of your big toe — the arch domes upward a small amount. Toes stay long and flat. It is a small movement and most people cannot produce it at first; that is normal and it comes with practice.

Then: calf raises with the weight kept toward the big-toe side so the arch has to hold rather than collapse. Slow up, slower down.
fields.notice: Whether you can produce the arch lift at all, and whether your toes cheat by curling. Whether your ankle rolls inward as you rise onto your toes — that is the collapse the arch work is aimed at.
fields.careful: Small movements, no toe curling. Slow calf raises, holding something for balance if needed.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: flat or collapsing arches are common with hypermobility and the passive support is not going to change — the active support is the part you can build. Frequent and small beats occasional and heavy. Orthostatic: the seated arch lift needs no standing at all; add calf raises near support.

levels.name: Standing arch lift
levels.note: Same movement with weight on the foot. Much harder.

levels.name: Calf raises holding the arch
levels.note: Slow up, slower down, weight toward the big toe.

levels.name: Single-leg calf raises
levels.note: Near support. Only once the arch holds through rung 3.

evidence.grade: Established direction for foot intrinsic strengthening; specific arch-lift protocols vary and the transfer to symptoms is less settled.
evidence.basis: Foot intrinsic muscle training is standard content in foot and ankle rehabilitation, and there is trial evidence that it changes foot posture and balance measures. Whether it resolves any given person's foot symptoms is a treatment claim this card does not make.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Long holds — settling into a position and waiting
items.why: The quietest family in the library. No tool, no effort, and it is the one most compatible with a low-capacity day.
items.equipment: Props to support the position — cushions, a wall, a bolster

fields.tool: Whatever holds you in the position so your muscles don't have to. If you are working to stay there, it is not a long hold.
fields.release: Find a position that puts a mild stretch on the target and set yourself up so gravity and props do the work. Stay for minutes rather than seconds. Breathe normally. The sensation typically rises, plateaus and then fades — that fade is the thing you came for, and rushing out before it means the hold did not happen.
fields.notice: Whether the sensation actually fades, or climbs. Climbing means too much position; back off and let it settle. Where you feel it — a stretch that has migrated into a joint rather than a muscle belly is a position problem, not a tolerance problem.
fields.careful: Never at the edge of your range — mild is the target, and the long duration is what makes it work, not the depth. Come out of long holds slowly; tissue that has been still is not ready for a sudden load.
fields.load: The most-skipped step in this family. After a long hold, move the joint actively through the new range under your own power a few times, or the position was a nap.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this family carries the most risk of being unhelpful for you, because long passive holds at range are exactly what a lax joint does not need. Use a much smaller position than feels like a stretch, favour holds that support the joint rather than hang from it, and treat the loading step as non-optional. Orthostatic: lying positions are generally the friendliest here; come up slowly. PEM/pacing: this is often the family that still works on a bad day.
items.dose: Hold durations for this style commonly run in minutes rather than seconds [practitioner convention — the long-hold traditions have no controlled dose literature]. Exact durations, and how many positions per session: [undetermined].

levels.name: Supported, brief
levels.note: Fully propped, short. Learn where the sensation settles.

levels.name: Supported, longer
levels.note: Same setup, more time. Time is the variable, not depth.

levels.name: Less support
levels.note: Take a prop away so the position asks slightly more. Not more range — less help.

evidence.grade: Established for range of motion; the change is mostly in stretch tolerance, not tissue length.
evidence.basis: A 2025 systematic review with meta-regression covering 65 studies and over 1,500 adults found that range-of-motion improvements after static stretching track changes in tolerance to passive stretch, with much weaker association to measured stiffness or fascicle length. The practical reading: you are training your nervous system's willingness to go there, which is real and useful — and is a different claim from lengthening tissue.

items.name: Lunge
items.why: Long step, knee hovers above floor, drive through front heel

fields.release: Stand tall and take a long step forward. Lower your body by bending both knees until your rear knee hovers just above the floor and your front thigh is roughly parallel to the ground. Drive through your front heel to return to standing. Keep your torso upright throughout and avoid letting your front knee shoot past your toes.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes, hamstrings.

items.name: Mace 10-to-2
items.why: Swing mace like a pendulum from 10 o'clock to 2 o'clock

fields.release: Hold the mace at the end of the handle and swing it behind your head like a pendulum, moving the mace head from the 10 o'clock position to the 2 o'clock position and back. Keep your core braced and control the arc. This is a simpler variation of the 360 that builds the same shoulder endurance and grip strength with less range of motion.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core.

items.name: Mace 360
items.why: Swing mace behind head in full 360, tight core, control the arc

fields.release: Hold the mace at the end of the handle with both hands near your chest. Swing the mace head behind your head in a full 360-degree circle, controlling it as it passes behind your neck and back to the front. Keep your core tight and your elbows close to your head. The momentum of the mace head makes this a challenging shoulder and grip exercise.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core, grip.

items.name: Mace Barbarian Squat
items.why: Squat while pressing mace overhead, keep chest up

fields.release: Hold the mace at chest level and squat down while pressing the mace overhead. As you stand, bring the mace back to chest level. Keep your chest upright and core braced throughout. The offset weight of the mace challenges your stability more than a balanced weight would. This is a full-body compound movement.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, shoulders.

items.name: Mace Flow
items.why: Chain mace movements together in smooth continuous flow

fields.release: Link multiple mace exercises together into one continuous sequence without stopping. For example, combine a 360 into a grave digger into a paddle swing. Focus on smooth transitions between movements and maintaining control of the mace throughout. This builds shoulder endurance, coordination, and full-body conditioning. Start with two movements and add more as you gain confidence.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: full body.

items.name: Mace Grave Digger
items.why: Shovel-like motion, rotate through core, control the mace

fields.release: Hold the mace with a staggered grip and perform a diagonal shoveling motion, rotating through your core as if digging with a shovel. Drive the movement from your hips and core, not your arms. Control the mace through the entire range of motion. This builds rotational core strength and mimics real-world functional movements.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques, core.

items.name: Mace Lunge + Reach
items.why: Lunge forward while reaching mace overhead or to the side

fields.release: Hold the mace in both hands and step into a lunge position. As you lunge, reach the mace overhead or rotate it to one side to add an upper-body and core challenge to the lower-body movement. The offset weight of the mace creates an additional stability demand. Keep your front knee tracking over your toes and your torso upright.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes, shoulders.

items.name: Mace Paddle Swing
items.why: Swing mace side to side like paddling, rotate from hips

fields.release: Hold the mace with a staggered grip and swing it from side to side in a paddling motion, as if paddling a canoe. Rotate through your hips and core to drive each swing. Keep the movement smooth and controlled. This targets the obliques and builds rotational endurance. Switch your grip and dominant side each set.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques, core.

items.name: Mace Uppercut
items.why: Drive mace upward in uppercut motion, rotate and brace

fields.release: Hold the mace with a staggered grip and drive it upward in an uppercut-like motion, rotating your hips and core to generate power. Brace your core as you punch the mace head upward. Control the mace as you return to the starting position. This combines rotational core work with shoulder and arm engagement.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: core, shoulders.

items.name: Median glide — lying down, arm supported
items.why: The smallest, least provocative version in the module. Lying down takes the shoulder, the neck and gravity out of the equation, which leaves only the movement you are actually trying to make.

fields.tool: The bed itself as the support. A pillow under the upper arm if the shoulder does not like resting flat.
fields.release:
Lie on your back. Arm out from the body at about forty-five degrees, elbow bent, upper arm resting on the bed, palm facing the ceiling.

Together: straighten the elbow along the bed while the wrist drops back, AND turn your head away from that arm — a small turn. Then reverse together: bend the elbow, relax the wrist, turn the head back toward the arm.

The upper arm never leaves the bed. If it lifts, the range has got away from you.
fields.notice: How much less this takes than the upright versions. If the seated version has been giving you symptoms and this one does not, that is useful — it usually means the shoulder position, not the wrist, was the provocative part.
fields.careful: Stop if the hand tingles. Keep the arm low — the further the arm goes above shoulder height, the more provocative this whole family becomes, and lying down makes it easy not to notice that you have drifted upward.
fields.load: Squeeze and release a fist a few times before you get up, then use the hand normally.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: a shoulder that rests in more external rotation than most is already partway into the provocative position before you start — begin with the elbow bent further than the instructions suggest. Orthostatic: this is a lying-down item, so stand up in stages afterwards; the module is not the cause but the position is.

levels.name: Elbow only
levels.note: Wrist stays neutral, head stays still.

levels.name: Elbow and wrist
levels.note: Add the wrist dropping back as the elbow straightens.

levels.name: Elbow, wrist and head
levels.note: The full version, still with the upper arm on the bed.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.name: Median glide — the desk version
items.why: The thumb-side nerve, done small enough to run at a desk without looking like anything. The library's existing median card takes the arm out to the side; this one keeps it in front of you, which is both more discreet and a much easier range to keep small.

fields.tool: A flat surface to rest the forearm on, so the shoulder does nothing.
fields.release:
Forearm resting on the desk, palm up, elbow bent to about a right angle. Fingers and thumb loosely curled.

Now, together: open the hand and let the wrist drop back so the fingers point away from you, AND tip your head gently toward that arm. Then reverse, together: curl the fingers and thumb back in, let the wrist come to neutral, AND tip your head away from that arm.

About two seconds each way. The elbow stays where it is; this is a wrist-and-neck drill and the small range is the whole reason it exists.
fields.notice: Whether the sensation runs from the palm up toward the elbow and moves as you go. Compare sides — most people find one side has a great deal more to say than the other.
fields.careful: Head tilt is a small tilt, not a stretch of the neck. If the fingers start tingling, you have gone past useful — reduce the wrist range first, and the head range second. Never hold either end.
fields.load: Use the hand for something ordinary straight afterwards — gripping a mug, typing a sentence — rather than letting it sit still.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: wrists that drop back a long way make it easy to reach a provocative wrist position with no sense of effort. Set your ceiling by what the fingers report, not by what the wrist can do. Orthostatic: none specific — this one is seated and small, which makes it the module's safest entry point.

levels.name: Wrist only
levels.note: Leave the head out of it entirely until you know what the arm does on its own.

levels.name: Wrist and a small head tilt
Wrist, head, and the elbow opening a little
levels.note: Let the elbow straighten slightly as the wrist drops back. This is the largest version this card offers.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.name: Median nerve glide
items.why: Different tissue, different rules. Some of what reads as muscle tightness is neural.

fields.tool: None
fields.release: Arm out to the side at shoulder height, elbow bent, palm facing up near your shoulder. Straighten the elbow out to the side while bending the wrist back so the fingers point down and behind you — and at the same time tilt your head AWAY from that arm. Reverse: bend the elbow back in, relax the wrist, and tilt your head TOWARD the arm. Slow and smooth, about 2 seconds each way.
fields.notice: Arm symptoms that come and go with position are usually neural rather than muscular. This tests that directly.
fields.careful: Start with a much smaller range than feels necessary, and smaller still for anyone who already gets numbness or tingling into the hand. If it reproduces those symptoms, halve the range. Never push into symptoms.

photos.caption: The arm and wrist position. Yours is a GLIDE, not this held stretch — move in and out continuously, about 2 seconds each way, and never park at the end position.

items.name: Meditation
items.why: Even 5 minutes reduces cortisol and improves focus

items.name: Mid & upper back
items.why: Manual release paired with the loading that keeps it.

fields.tool: Foam roller
fields.release: Roller across the mid-back, arms crossed over the chest. A few passes, then park on a stiff segment and drape backwards over it. Breathe into it. Don't crank.
fields.load: Cat-cow ×8 with real attention to the cow — that's the direction you've lost. Then prone Y-raises ×10, light.
fields.notice: Standing tall stops being effort. Head sits back over the shoulders.
fields.careful: Extend from the mid-back, not the low back. If it hinges down low, move the roller up.

photos.caption: Roller across the mid-back, arms crossed over the chest. Park on a stiff segment and drape back over it.
Cat-cow. Give real attention to the cow direction — that is the one you have lost.

items.name: Morning sunlight 10 min
items.why: Sets circadian rhythm, boosts vitamin D, improves sleep

items.name: Mountain Climber
items.why: Plank position, drive knees to chest, hips low and stable

fields.release: Start in a high plank position with hands under shoulders. Rapidly drive one knee toward your chest, then switch legs in a running motion while keeping your hips low and stable. Avoid letting your hips bounce up and down. The faster you go, the more cardiovascular demand. Keep your core braced to maintain a flat back throughout.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, hip flexors.

items.name: Movement 20–30 min
items.why: Lymph needs muscle movement — walk, bike, play, anything counts

items.name: Muay Thai Stance + Movement
items.why: Tall stance, hands high, weight on balls of feet, stay balanced

fields.release: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, dominant foot slightly back. Keep your hands high near your temples with elbows pointed down to protect your ribs. Stay on the balls of your feet with weight evenly distributed. Unlike boxing, the Muay Thai stance is more upright to facilitate kicking and knee strikes. Practice moving forward, back, and laterally.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, core.

items.name: Muscle-Up
items.why: Explosive pull, transition over bar, press to lockout

fields.release: Hang from a pull-up bar and perform an explosive pull-up, generating enough height to transition your chest over the bar. Once above the bar, press your body up to a straight-arm support position. This is an advanced movement that combines a pull-up and a dip. Build the prerequisite strength with high pull-ups and chest-to-bar pull-ups first.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lats, chest, triceps.

items.name: Near and far shifts
items.why: Trains the eyes to converge and refocus between something close and something far — the skill that gets used every time you look up from a screen.
items.equipment: Two sticky notes with a + on each

fields.tool: Two sticky notes, each with a + drawn on it.
fields.release: One target close to your face, one across the room. Head still. Shift your eyes between them, letting each come into focus before moving on.
fields.notice: How long each one takes to sharpen. Whether one direction is harder than the other.
fields.careful: Can bring on dizziness or nausea. Mild and settling is expected; a climbing ramp is a stop.

_undetermined: whether this belongs in its own category rather than with the eye jumps — mechanically it is focusing, not jumping

items.name: Neck isometrics — pushing without moving
items.why: The load partner for the side and back of the neck. Nothing moves, so there is no range to lose control of — which makes it the safest way to ask a neck to get stronger.
items.equipment: Your own hand, or a wall

fields.tool: A hand against your head, or your head against a wall with a folded towel between.
fields.release: Head in a neutral position, chin very slightly tucked. Press your head gently into your hand — forward, then backward, then each side — without letting the head move at all. Gentle effort, not maximum. Breathe throughout; holding your breath is the most common error here and it turns a quiet item into a strain.
fields.notice: Which direction is weakest. Whether you can keep the effort steady, or whether it comes in a surge and fades. Whether your jaw clenches as soon as your neck works — very common, and worth uncoupling.
fields.careful: Gentle. This is not a strength test and there is no benefit to maximum effort. Keep the head in neutral rather than at the end of any range. Stop for dizziness, visual change, or any symptom into the arms.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: isometric work is the friendliest way to load a hypermobile neck, since the joint never travels. Start lighter and progress slower than the instructions suggest, and keep it strictly in neutral.
items.dose: [undetermined] — hold time, number of directions, rounds. Another good thing to get a number for from a clinician.

levels.name: Longer holds
levels.note: Same gentle effort, more time. Time before force.

evidence.grade: Established as standard neck rehabilitation content.
evidence.basis: Isometric neck strengthening is routine in neck-pain rehabilitation and in return-to-activity programmes. Doses vary by protocol and none is reproduced here.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Neck Stretch
items.why: Tilt ear to shoulder, keep opposite shoulder down

fields.release: Sit or stand tall. Tilt right ear toward right shoulder. Gently place right hand on top of head for light overpressure. Keep left shoulder down. Hold 15-20 seconds. For the front of the neck, look up and slightly to one side. Switch sides.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: neck, upper traps.

levels.name: Nerve Glides
levels.note: All positions with gentle nerve glides

items.name: Neck-crack urge
items.why: Re-test: Count on a normal day, monthly. Lower is better.

fields.release: Rough count of how many times in a day you want to crack your neck. Count the urge, not the act. This is the behaviour the base-of-skull work is meant to replace.
fields.notice: Recorded in /day.

items.name: Nerve glides — different tissue, different rules
items.why: Read this before any item in this module. Everything else in this library rewards doing a little more than you did last time. This is the one category where that instinct is the problem.

fields.tool: Nothing. This one is reading.
fields.release:
A nerve is not a rope tied at both ends. It runs from your spine out to your fingers or your toes through a series of tunnels — between muscles, under bands of tissue, past joints — and every time you move, it has to slide a little inside those tunnels. Bend your elbow and the nerve on the inside of it has to accommodate; straighten your knee and the nerve down the back of your leg has to as well.

A glide is built on that. You lengthen the nerve's path at one end of the body while shortening it at the other, at the same time, then reverse. Straighten the knee and tip the head back; bend the knee and drop the chin. The nerve moves, but it never gets pulled tight from both ends at once. That is the entire distinction between this and a stretch, and it is the reason none of these are held.

The pull you feel should MOVE as you go. That travelling sensation is the point. A pull that sits in one place and stays there is a muscle, and you are in the wrong module.
fields.notice: Where the sensation actually is, and whether it moves. And whether the arm or leg feels different for a few minutes afterwards — lighter, or clearer, or nothing at all. Nothing at all is a completely acceptable answer.
fields.careful: Never hold the end position. Never push into pins and needles, numbness, burning or electricity — those are not the sensation you are working toward, they are the sign you have gone past the useful range. If the drill reproduces your symptoms, make the movement smaller until it does not. If symptoms are still there an hour later, or worse the next day, that is too much, and less next time is the correction, not more. This is the one module where the honest instruction is that more is worse.
fields.load: Nothing to load — this is an explanation, not a technique.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: nerve symptoms in hypermobile people are frequently not a mechanical problem at all. Studies of hypermobile people with suspected nerve pain find small-fibre neuropathy in a large majority — a problem of the smallest nerve fibres in the skin, which no amount of gliding will move. Burning, patchy numbness, temperature that feels wrong, symptoms in both hands or both feet: that pattern belongs in a clinician's hands for a diagnosis, not in this module. Orthostatic: a controlled trial in healthy volunteers found that both halves of this technique family raised sympathetic nervous system markers during and after the session. In a body that already runs hot on the sympathetic side, that is worth knowing before you add these to an evening routine.

levels.name: Read it, then find one nerve on yourself
levels.note: The map card next door tells you which nerve serves which part of your hand or leg. Finding one on your own body is what makes the rest of the module mean anything.

evidence.grade: Anatomy and an instruction, not an intervention.
evidence.basis: That peripheral nerves slide within their surroundings during limb movement is standard anatomy and has been shown directly with ultrasound imaging. Nothing on this card is a treatment claim; the claims and their grade live on the technique guide.

items.name: Nerve gliding — moving a nerve without pulling on it
items.why: The family guide for this module. Every item here inherits its evidence grade from this card, and every item's instructions assume you have read the two rules below.
items.equipment: None for anything in this module.

fields.tool: Your own limb, and a chair or a bed for the supported versions.
fields.release:
**The mechanic.** Two joints at opposite ends of the nerve's path move at the same time, in opposite directions. One end lengthens the path; the other shortens it by the same sort of amount. The nerve slides through its tunnels; the net tension on it barely changes. Reverse, and it slides back. That is one repetition, and it should take a couple of seconds each way — slow, smooth, continuous, no pause at either end.

**The two rules.** Never hold the end position. Never work in a range that reproduces your symptoms.

**The other half of this family, which this library does not offer.** The same drills can be run with both ends lengthening at once, which does put the nerve under tension. Those are called tensioners, and they are a legitimate clinical technique in the right hands. They are not in this module, for three reasons: the head-to-head trials do not agree on whether they beat sliders, the one clear signal is that they are the more provocative of the two, and the population this library is built for is exactly the one that overshoots end range without noticing. If a clinician who has examined you prescribes tensioners, do those instead of these; the app is not the better judge of your case.
fields.notice: Whether the sensation travels. A pull that moves along the limb as you go is the nerve. A pull that sits in one place is a muscle, and a muscle wants a different module.
fields.careful: Small range first, always — smaller than feels necessary. Stop the session, do not just ease off, if you get pins and needles, numbness, burning or an electric quality. Judge the dose by the next day, not by the session: symptoms that are still raised an hour later, or louder the following morning, mean the last session was too much. In this family the correction for a bad response is less, never more.
fields.load: Not load in the usual sense. If a glide gives you range — a straighter knee, an arm that reaches further — use that range in the next few minutes with something ordinary and unloaded, or the body will quietly take it back. Each item names what to use.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: two separate cautions. First, joints that travel further than most make it easy to reach a provocative position without feeling like you did anything, so the range that is small enough for you is smaller than the instructions imply. Second, and more important: nerve symptoms in hypermobile people are often small-fibre rather than mechanical — one hospital cohort of hypermobile people referred for suspected nerve pain found definite small-fibre neuropathy in well over half, on both testing and skin biopsy — and small-fibre symptoms do not respond to gliding a nerve trunk. Persistent burning or patchy numbness is a reason for a diagnosis, not for more repetitions. Orthostatic: a randomised controlled trial in 90 healthy volunteers measured a clear rise in sympathetic markers with both sliders and tensioners, sustained into the rest period afterwards, with the tensioner slightly higher. It was healthy people and a laboratory measure, not a symptom outcome, so it does not predict how you will feel — but if your system already leans sympathetic, put these earlier in the day and watch what follows. PEM: these are low in physical cost and can still be provocative to a sensitised nervous system; the pacing rule applies to the nervous system's response, not to the effort.
items.dose: [undetermined] for self-administered use, and left blank deliberately. For reference only, and not a recommendation: trial protocols in this family typically use sets of roughly ten to twenty repetitions, and at least one comparative sciatica protocol held the end position for five seconds [derived — a published slider-versus-tensioner sciatica protocol]. That end-position hold contradicts the first rule on this card; the trial was clinician-supervised in people with an established diagnosis, which is not this module's situation. The library's two legacy cards say ten repetitions, two sets — provenance for that number is [undetermined]; it is in the library, not derived from anything on file. A defensible number for self-administered use will come from real use, or not at all.

levels.name: Quarter range, one set, one side
levels.note: Learn what a travelling sensation feels like before you learn anything else. Then wait a day and see what happened.

levels.name: Half range, both sides
levels.note: Only once level 1 produced no next-day increase in symptoms.

levels.name: Comfortable range, and use the range afterwards
levels.note: Full available range still means the range that does not reproduce symptoms — that ceiling never lifts.

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. If you have had an examination, the examiner's instructions outrank this card.

items.name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
items.why: Anchor feet, slowly lower body forward, fight with hamstrings

fields.release: Kneel on the floor with your feet anchored under something heavy or held by a partner. Keeping your body straight from knees to head, slowly lower yourself forward toward the floor by extending at the knees while resisting with your hamstrings. Lower as far as you can with control, then push yourself back up from the floor. This is an extremely difficult hamstring exercise; start with negatives only.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings.

levels.name: Negative Only
levels.note: Slow lower, push up from floor

items.name: Nose only, all day
items.dose: All day, imperfectly. It is a default you are rebuilding, not a rule you are passing or failing.
items.why: Breathing is upstream of most of it. Everything else on this list is downstream effect.

fields.tool: Awareness
fields.release: Mouth closed at rest. Lips sealed, teeth slightly apart, tongue on the roof of the mouth. Nose breathing on walks. If you have to open your mouth, slow down until you do not. Notice when you break the seal. Stress, concentration, and reaching for something are the usual triggers.
fields.notice: Reaching for the mouth constantly is data, not failure — it points at nasal obstruction, which is already on your list.
fields.careful: Do not tape your mouth at night. That advice is everywhere in this space and it is specifically wrong for you: you can reproduce your own airway collapse, and taping removes the escape route.

items.name: Nose-only walk
items.why: Re-test: Monthly. Higher is better.

fields.release: Walking at a normal pace, time until you have to open your mouth. Flat ground, same route. This one is as much a readout on nasal obstruction as on fitness.
fields.notice: Recorded in min.

items.name: Oil pulling
items.why: Swish coconut oil 10–20 min — oral microbiome support

items.name: Out along the shoulder blade
items.why: The middle band of the big back muscle runs horizontally out from the spine across the shoulder blade's ridge. Different angle, different job, different spot from the strip beside the spine — which is why it gets its own item rather than being lumped in.
items.equipment: A ball and a wall, or a roller

fields.tool: A ball against a wall for spots, a foam roller across the upper back for the broad version.
fields.release: Ball version: place it out along the bony ridge of the shoulder blade and just above and below it, working outward from the spine toward the point of the shoulder. Roller version: lie with the roller across your upper back below the shoulder blades' ridges, hands supporting your head, and move slowly with pauses. Keep your ribs down rather than arching over the roller.
fields.notice: Whether you arch your low back to get over the roller — very common and it means the thoracic spine is not the thing moving. Whether the tenderness runs along the ridge or sits below it.
fields.careful: Not on the neck with the roller. Keep the roller below the level of the shoulders and support your head with your hands so the neck is not hanging. Don't roll the low back.
fields.load: Setting the shoulder blade, and holding it while the arm works.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: arching over a roller takes a mobile spine a long way; keep the ribs down and treat the roller as pressure, not as an extension stretch. Orthostatic: the wall version needs no floor transfer.

levels.name: Roller with arm movement
levels.note: Hold a position and slowly bring the arms overhead and back.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back
loadAfter.note: Cross-file reference to release-neck-jaw.json.

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Pallof Press
items.why: Press band straight out from chest, resist rotation

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to your side. Hold the band at your chest with both hands and stand or kneel perpendicular to the anchor. Press the band straight out in front of you and hold, resisting the rotational pull of the band. Return to your chest and repeat. This trains your core anti-rotation muscles, which are essential for athletic performance and spinal health.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: core, anti-rotation.

items.name: Parallel Bar Dip
items.why: Elbows back, lean forward for chest emphasis, full depth

fields.release: Grip a set of parallel bars and support your body with arms locked out. Lower yourself by bending your elbows until your upper arms are at least parallel to the floor, then press back up to lockout. Lean forward to place more emphasis on your chest, or stay upright to target your triceps. Avoid shrugging your shoulders at the bottom.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, triceps, shoulders.

items.name: Parallel Bar L-Sit
items.why: Lock arms, lift legs parallel to floor, point toes

fields.release: Support yourself on parallel bars with arms fully locked out. Lift your legs straight in front of you until they are parallel to the floor and hold this position. Point your toes and keep your arms straight. This demands significant core and hip flexor strength. Start with a tucked position if holding straight legs is too difficult.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, hip flexors, triceps.

levels.name: One Leg Extended
levels.note: Extend one leg at a time

items.name: Parallel Bar Swing
items.why: Controlled swing, tight core, shoulders stable

fields.release: Support yourself on parallel bars with arms locked out. Initiate a controlled forward and backward swinging motion using your core and shoulders. Keep your body tight and maintain stable shoulders throughout. This builds shoulder stability and body control, and serves as a foundation for more advanced parallel bar skills.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core.

items.name: Pec / Shoulder Roll
items.why: Face down, roller under chest/shoulder, roll gently

fields.release: Lie face down at a slight angle with the foam roller under the front of one shoulder and chest area. Use your feet and opposite arm to control pressure and slowly roll across the pec and front deltoid area. Pause on any tender spots and breathe into them. This is especially beneficial for people who sit at desks or have rounded shoulder posture.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: pecs, anterior deltoids.

items.name: Percussion — massage guns and vibration
items.why: New to this library. A device does the repetitive part so your hands don't have to, which for anyone with limited grip strength or limited energy is a real accessibility gain rather than a gadget.

fields.tool: A handheld percussive device. The soft round head is the default; the pointed heads are for people who know exactly what they are aiming at, which is most of the way to not needing them.
fields.release: Keep it moving over the muscle belly rather than parking it in one place. Let the device's weight do the work — pressing it in adds nothing that matters and adds bruising that does. Short passes along the muscle. If it hurts rather than feeling strong, turn the speed down.
fields.notice: Whether the muscle actually feels different afterward or whether you just feel buzzed. That distinction is easy to lose with this tool and worth holding onto.
fields.careful: Muscle bellies only. Never on bone, joints, the front or sides of the neck, the throat, the abdomen, the spine itself, or anywhere with numbness, a recent injury, or unexplained swelling. Injuries have been reported from aggressive use — the risk here is not zero, and there is no agreed safety standard for these devices.
fields.load: Same as everything else: the range or ease you gain needs something asked of it afterward.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: easy bruising and fragile tissue argue for the lowest speed, the softest head, and short passes. Do not use it on or near a joint that subluxes. Orthostatic: sit for it. PEM/pacing: the device removes the effort of self-massage, which can make this the family that costs least on a low day — but the tissue is still receiving a real dose, so it is not free.
items.dose: Trial applications range from about 30 seconds to several minutes per site [derived — the range reported across a 2023 systematic review of 13 studies]. No standard exists. Frequency: [undetermined].

levels.name: Low speed, soft head, short
levels.note: Large muscle, lowest setting, brief passes.

levels.name: Longer passes
levels.note: More time, same pressure — the device's weight, not yours.

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term. Comparable to static stretching for acute flexibility; repeated use reduces reported pain; no consensus safety standards.
evidence.basis: A 2023 systematic review of thirteen studies found single applications associated with acute gains in flexibility and in some strength measures, and multiple applications with reduced musculoskeletal pain. A randomised comparison found percussion and static stretching produced similar acute hamstring flexibility gains. A 2025 critical appraisal noted the absence of agreed indications, precautions and contraindications for consumer devices, which is why this card carries a longer careful field than most.

items.name: Percussion on the front of the thigh
items.why: The percussion family's first appearance here, on the biggest and most forgiving muscle in the body. If a device is going to be useful to you at all, this is where you will find out — and it is the option that costs you no grip strength and no floor transfer.

fields.tool: A percussive device with the soft round head. Low speed to start.
fields.release: Seated with the leg relaxed and supported. Move the head slowly along the front of the thigh from above the knee up toward the hip, then across the outer and inner portions. Let the device's own weight do the work — pressing it in adds bruising and nothing else. If it hurts rather than feeling strong, turn the speed down.
fields.notice: Whether the muscle feels genuinely different afterward or whether you just feel buzzed. That distinction is easy to lose with this tool and is worth holding onto deliberately.
fields.careful: Muscle belly only. Not on the kneecap, not on the bony points at the hip, not over a joint. Not on any area with numbness, a recent injury, or unexplained swelling. If you are on blood thinners or bruise easily, this family carries more risk for you than a ball does.
fields.load: Knee extension work and squatting through a range you control.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: lowest speed, softest head, short passes, and stay well away from the knee itself. Orthostatic: seated throughout, which makes this one of the easier release items for you to reach at all. PEM/pacing: the device removes the effort of self-massage, which genuinely lowers the cost — but the tissue still receives a real dose, so it is cheaper, not free.
items.dose: Applications in trials range from about 30 seconds to several minutes per site [derived — the range reported across a 2023 systematic review of thirteen studies]. No standard exists.

levels.name: Low speed, short passes
levels.note: Front of the thigh only, device weight only.

levels.name: Cover the whole thigh
levels.note: Outer and inner portions too, same pressure.

loadAfter.name: Sit-to-stand or knee extension through a controlled range
loadAfter.note: Match against existing leg strength content at S5.

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term. Comparable to static stretching for acute flexibility; repeated use reduces reported pain; no consensus safety standards.
evidence.basis: A 2023 systematic review of thirteen studies found single applications associated with acute gains in flexibility and in some strength measures, and multiple applications with reduced musculoskeletal pain. A randomised comparison found percussion and static stretching produced similar acute hamstring flexibility gains. A 2025 critical appraisal noted the absence of agreed indications, precautions and contraindications for consumer devices, which is why this card carries a longer careful field than most.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Sibling to the imported 'Front of thigh' pressure card — same target, different family, and a swap when your hands or your energy are the limit.

items.name: Pigeon Stretch
items.why: Front shin across body, square hips, ease into stretch

fields.release: From a kneeling position, bring one shin across your body in front of you with the knee angled outward. Extend your other leg straight behind you. Square your hips toward the front and ease your torso down toward the floor. You should feel a deep stretch in the front hip and glute. Use your hands for support and breathe into the stretch.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: glutes, hip flexors, piriformis.

items.name: Pike Push-Up
items.why: Hips high, head between arms, touch nose to floor

fields.release: Start in a downward-dog position with your hips piked high and hands shoulder-width apart. Bend your elbows and lower the top of your head toward the floor between your hands, then press back up. Keep your hips high throughout so the movement targets your shoulders rather than your chest. You should feel this primarily in your front and side deltoids.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, triceps.

levels.name: Feet Elevated Pike
levels.note: Feet on bench for steeper angle

items.name: Pin and move — hold the spot, move the joint
items.why: The single highest-yield upgrade to ball work, and most people have never been shown it. You are not pressing harder — you are making the tissue slide underneath the pressure.
items.equipment: Ball, thumb, or knuckle — the same tools as sustained pressure

fields.tool: Whatever you were already using for sustained pressure.
fields.release: Find the spot and hold it still. Then, without letting the contact drift, move the joint that muscle crosses through its range — slowly, a few times. The pressure stays put; the tissue moves under it. Bend and straighten, or rotate, depending on what the muscle does. Most people find this far more productive than adding pressure, and it is easier on the tissue.
fields.notice: Whether the tenderness changes through the range — it usually spikes at one point in the movement, and that point is more informative than the resting tenderness. Whether the muscle glides under your contact or drags.
fields.careful: The joint movement should be slow and within a range you own comfortably. If pinning makes the movement painful rather than just tender, ease the pressure before you shrink the movement. Never force the joint against the pin.
fields.load: This one pairs naturally: you are already moving the joint, so finish by moving it under load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: keep the joint movement well inside your range and do not use the pin as leverage to push further. The point is tissue glide, not end-range. Somebody with lax joints can easily turn this into an end-range stretch without meaning to.
items.dose: [undetermined] — no trial base for the self-administered version; repetitions of the joint movement are a judgment call, not a prescription.

levels.name: Small movement
levels.note: Pin the spot, move the joint through a short middle-range arc.

levels.name: Full available range
levels.note: Same, taking the joint through everything you comfortably own.

levels.name: Active, then loaded
levels.note: Move under the pin, then come off and do the same movement against resistance.

evidence.grade: Undetermined for the self-administered form; clinician-delivered versions have small trials against comparators.
evidence.basis: Clinician-applied pin-and-stretch approaches have been compared against other manual techniques in small trials with mixed results. Nothing I found tests the self-administered version specifically. The rationale — that tissue moving under a fixed contact restores glide between layers — is a mechanism story, not a demonstrated finding, and is written here as such.

items.name: Pistol Squat
items.why: One leg extended forward, sit all the way down and stand

fields.release: Stand on one leg with the other leg extended straight in front of you. Lower yourself by bending the standing leg until you reach the bottom of a full squat, then drive back up to standing. Keep your extended leg off the floor throughout. This demands significant single-leg strength, balance, and ankle mobility. Use a support or box to build up.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes, ankle stability.

levels.name: Negative Only
levels.note: Slow lower, stand with both legs

items.name: Plank
items.why: Straight line from head to heels, squeeze everything tight

fields.release: Get into a forearm plank position with elbows directly under shoulders and feet together or hip-width apart. Your body should form a perfectly straight line from head to heels. Squeeze your abs, glutes, and quads to maintain the position. Avoid letting your hips sag toward the floor or pike upward. Breathe steadily throughout.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, obliques, shoulders.

items.name: Positional rest — letting gravity unload a region
items.why: The lowest-effort family in the library and the honest answer to 'I have nothing today.' You arrange the body so a region is asked to do nothing at all, and stay.

fields.tool: Furniture and gravity.
fields.release: Set the region up so it is fully supported and has no job — back on the floor with calves on a chair, or side-lying with the top arm propped. Then do nothing for several minutes. Not stretching, not breathing exercises, not scanning. The instruction is genuinely to stop.
fields.notice: How long it takes before anything actually lets go — often several minutes, which is longer than most people ever give it. Whether some part of you keeps switching back on. That part is worth knowing about.
fields.careful: Nothing should be numb or pins-and-needles when you get up. Change position if it is.
fields.load: Come out slowly and move the region deliberately before asking anything of it — tissue that has been fully unloaded for ten minutes is not ready to be strong.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: legs-elevated positions are usually well tolerated and often welcome; get up in stages. PEM/pacing: this is the family that is still available when nothing else is, and it is genuinely a rung of the protocol rather than a rest day.
items.dose: [undetermined] — no controlled dose evidence exists for this. Traditions using it suggest several minutes to twenty; nothing here is derived.

levels.name: A few minutes
levels.note: Set up, stay, get up. Short.

levels.name: Longer
levels.note: Extend the stay. Time is the only variable.

evidence.grade: Undetermined. No trial base as a standalone intervention. Risk close to zero.
evidence.basis: This family has not been tested as an intervention in its own right, so there is no grade to report and none is invented here. It is in the library because it is the only release approach that costs nothing in capacity, which matters in a population where capacity is the binding constraint. Judge it against your own experience, not against evidence that does not exist.

items.name: Positions that give the floor room
items.why: Some positions open the base of the pelvis and some close it. If you are trying to let a floor go, doing it in a position that has already shortened everything around it is working uphill.
items.equipment: Cushions, a wall, a strap or towel

fields.tool: As many cushions as it takes. If you are holding yourself in the position, it is the wrong position or not enough props.
fields.release:
Three positions, all with the breath work from the previous item running underneath. **Knees wide, soles together, lying on your back** — cushions under each outer thigh so the legs are not hanging. **Knees drawn toward the armpits, lying on your back** — hold behind the thighs or use a strap; the low back stays down. **A supported squat** — heels down, holding a doorframe or with your back against a wall and a rolled towel under the heels, only as deep as is comfortable.

In any of them, settle, then breathe wide and let the base of the pelvis go on each in-breath. Stay for minutes rather than seconds.
fields.notice: Which position gives most. Whether the inner thighs let go or grip. Whether the low back has to arch to make a position work, which means it is too much position for today.
fields.careful: Mild positions, fully propped. Nothing at the end of range. Come out of the squat slowly and hold something. If any position produces downward pressure, a bulging feeling, or pain, come out of it.
fields.load: The lift-and-release item, and hip work — a floor sits between two hips, and hips that cannot support it leave it doing their job.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: these are all positions where a lax hip will happily go far past where the muscle work stops. Use fewer degrees and more cushions, and treat 'how far the position goes' as irrelevant — the breathing inside it is the item. Orthostatic: the squat means getting up and down; skip it or use the lying versions. Legs-elevated variants are usually well tolerated. PEM/pacing: the lying versions cost almost nothing.

levels.name: Knees wide, fully propped
levels.note: The gentlest, and enough on its own for many people.

levels.name: Knees toward the armpits
levels.note: More opening at the back of the floor.

levels.name: Supported squat
levels.note: Most opening, most demand on the ankles and knees. Support required.

loadAfter.name: A lift, and a full let-go

evidence.grade: Established for range of motion; the change is mostly in stretch tolerance, not tissue length.
evidence.basis: A 2025 systematic review with meta-regression covering 65 studies and over 1,500 adults found that range-of-motion improvements after static stretching track changes in tolerance to passive stretch, with much weaker association to measured stiffness or fascicle length. The practical reading: you are training your nervous system's willingness to go there, which is real and useful — and is a different claim from lengthening tissue.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. The three positions are standard relaxation postures used in pelvic floor down-training programmes; described here from anatomy in the app's own words.

items.name: Prone Y-T-W Raise
items.why: Lie face down, lift arms in Y, T, then W shapes

fields.release: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended. Lift your arms off the ground into a Y shape (overhead and angled out), then a T shape (straight out to the sides), then a W shape (elbows bent, pulled toward ribs). Hold each position for a beat. These target the upper back, rear delts, and rotator cuff muscles important for posture.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: upper back, rear delts.

items.name: Pseudo Planche Push-Up
items.why: Hands by waist, lean forward, protract shoulders at top

fields.release: Set up in a push-up position but place your hands further back, near your waist, with fingers pointing forward or slightly outward. Lean your body forward over your hands and perform push-ups from this position. Push your shoulder blades apart (protract) at the top of each rep. This variation heavily loads the shoulders and core.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, shoulders, core.

items.name: Pull-Up
items.why: Full dead hang to chin over bar, no kipping

fields.release: Grab a pull-up bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder-width. Start from a full dead hang with arms completely straight. Pull yourself up until your chin clears the bar, then lower back to a full dead hang. Avoid swinging or kipping; the movement should be smooth and controlled. Engage your lats by thinking about pulling your elbows down to your hips.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lats, biceps, forearms.

levels.name: Weighted
levels.note: Add weight via backpack or DB

items.name: Push-Up
items.why: Chest to floor, full lockout, body in straight line

fields.release: Start in a plank position with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, body forming a straight line from head to heels. Lower your chest to the floor by bending your elbows, then press back up to full arm extension. Keep your core tight and avoid letting your hips sag or pike up. You should feel the work in your chest, shoulders, and triceps.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: chest, shoulders, triceps.

levels.name: Archer Push-Up
levels.note: One arm extended to the side

items.name: Quad Roll
items.why: Face down, roller under thighs, roll from hip to knee

fields.release: Lie face down in a forearm plank position with the foam roller under the front of your thighs. Roll slowly from your hips down to just above your knees, pausing on tender areas. Support yourself with your forearms and control the pressure with your arms. For more pressure, stack one leg on top of the other to roll one quad at a time.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads.

levels.name: Cross-Friction
levels.note: Rock side to side on tight spots

items.name: Radial glide — hand resting on the thigh
items.why: The seated, supported version of the same nerve, with the shoulder given nothing to do. This is the one to use if the standing version keeps turning into a shoulder movement.

fields.tool: Your own thigh as the shelf.
fields.release:
Sitting. Rest the back of your hand on your thigh, palm up, elbow comfortably bent and the upper arm hanging at your side.

Together: curl the fingers and thumb in and let the wrist turn so the palm rolls away from you, AND tilt the head away from that arm — small. Then reverse: open the hand, roll the palm back up, head back to centre.

The forearm stays on the thigh throughout.
fields.notice: Whether the sensation is in the same place as the standing version. If the standing one gives you shoulder sensation and this one gives you forearm sensation, the standing one was too big.
fields.careful: Small head tilt only. Stop if the back of the hand goes numb or buzzes.
fields.load: Press the back of the hand down into the thigh for a couple of seconds, a few times.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: thumb joints that fold a long way will take the movement instead of the wrist — curl the whole hand as a unit rather than folding the thumb in first.

loadAfter.name: Turning the arm out, under control

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.name: Radial glide — the back of the hand
items.why: The third arm nerve, wrapping around the back of the upper arm to serve the back of the hand and the thumb web. It is the one people miss, and the one to think about when the back of the hand is the loud part.

fields.tool: Nothing.
fields.release:
Arm down by your side, slightly behind the line of your body, palm facing backward.

Together: let the wrist and fingers curl down and in, thumb tucked, while the arm turns inward — AND tilt your head away from that arm. Then reverse together: open the hand, let the wrist come back to neutral, turn the arm out a little, AND bring the head back toward the arm.

The arm stays low the whole time. It does not lift, and it does not go far behind you.
fields.notice: A sensation across the back of the forearm and the back of the hand. It is often vaguer than the other two arm nerves — a heaviness rather than a line.
fields.careful: The shoulder is easy to cheat with here. If your shoulder is doing the work of moving the arm backward, the range is too big — bring the arm forward until the sensation comes from the hand and forearm instead. Never combine a big head tilt with the arm pulled back; that combination is the one people flare themselves with.
fields.load: Lift the back of the hand against your other hand's light resistance a few times, or press the back of the hand into a wall.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: shoulders that travel far backward will let this arm go somewhere the instructions never intended. Keep the upper arm alongside your body. Orthostatic: standing item — do it near a wall or seated first.

levels.name: Hand and wrist only, arm alongside you
Add the head tilt
levels.note: The full version. The head is the last thing added, not the first.

loadAfter.name: Turning the arm out, under control

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
