items.name: Reaching — the shoulder blade wrapping the ribs
items.why: The load partner for the serratus and rhomboid items, and the movement that most people have never separated out. Almost everyone can push. Far fewer can push and let the shoulder blade travel forward around the ribcage while they do it, which is what the movement actually requires.

fields.tool: A wall to start with.
fields.release:
Stand facing a wall, hands on it at chest height, arms straight. Without bending your elbows, push the wall away and let your upper back round slightly — your shoulder blades slide apart and forward around your ribs. Hold. Then let them come back together. Elbows stay straight the whole time; if they bend, it has turned into a push-up.

On hands and knees, the same movement: push the floor away without bending the elbows, letting the upper back round.
fields.notice: Whether the blades actually move or whether your whole trunk shifts instead. Whether the shoulders shrug up toward the ears — different muscle, wrong one.
fields.careful: Elbows straight, shoulders down. Small range at first. Any pinching in the front of the shoulder means reduce it.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: a shoulder blade that wings away from the ribs is common with hypermobility, and this is the direct answer to it. Small range, frequent, and progress by control rather than by moving to harder positions.

levels.name: On hands and knees
levels.note: More load, and the blade has to hold against gravity.

levels.name: In a plank position
levels.note: Full bodyweight. Only when rung 2 is clean and the shoulders stay down.

evidence.grade: Established as standard shoulder rehabilitation content.
evidence.basis: Serratus anterior activation exercises are routine in shoulder rehabilitation, and this progression is a common one across programmes. Doses are protocol-dependent and are not reproduced here.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Renegade Row
items.why: Plank on DBs, row one arm at a time, minimize hip rotation

fields.release: Get into a high plank position with each hand gripping a dumbbell on the floor. With a wide foot stance for stability, row one dumbbell up to your hip by pulling your elbow past your torso, then lower and repeat on the other side. The key is minimizing hip rotation as you row. Keep your core braced tight and avoid rocking side to side.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: back, core.

items.name: Rolling — foam roller and roller stick
items.why: The broad-area version of sustained pressure. Covers a whole muscle rather than a spot, and it is the more sensible starting tool for large muscles.
items.equipment: Foam roller, or a handheld roller stick

fields.tool: A roller uses your bodyweight, so pressure is set by how much of you is on it. A roller stick uses your arms instead, which means you control the pressure precisely and never have to get on the floor — that is not a lesser option, it is a different one, and for anyone with orthostatic symptoms it is often the better one.
fields.release: Move slowly. Slower than feels productive. Cover the length of the muscle in unhurried passes, and when you find somewhere that bites, stop there and hold rather than rolling back and forth over it. Fast rolling is mostly sensation; slow rolling with pauses is where the change is.
fields.notice: Where along the length the muscle changes character — most muscles have one or two spots that are unlike the rest. Whether the tender area is where you assumed it would be. It usually isn't.
fields.careful: Roll muscle, not bone and not joints. Skip the back of the knee, the front of the neck, and the lower back's soft flank directly. If you feel it in the joint rather than the muscle, you have drifted off the target.
fields.load: Rolling opens range; if nothing then asks the muscle to work in that range, the range does not stay.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: bodyweight on a firm roller is a lot of pressure to control. A roller stick or a softer roller gives you a dial that a firm foam roller does not. Orthostatic: getting up and down from the floor repeatedly is its own load — a stick, standing against a wall, or a seated version avoids it entirely.
items.dose: Rolling durations in the literature vary widely and duration appears to matter more than the tool's texture [derived — comparative foam-roller studies on delayed-onset soreness]. Per-muscle time and weekly frequency: [undetermined].

levels.name: Roller stick or soft roller
levels.note: Pressure fully under your control, no floor required.

levels.name: Foam roller, partial weight
levels.note: On the floor with a hand or foot taking some of your weight.

levels.name: Foam roller, full weight, slow passes with holds
levels.note: Full bodyweight, slow, stopping where it bites.

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and recovery; no evidence of lasting tissue change.
evidence.basis: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis find rolling produces acute range-of-motion improvement without impairing strength, and shows some benefit for post-exercise soreness. Effects on measured tissue stiffness are small and short-lived, which again points at a nervous-system effect rather than a structural one.

items.name: Romanian Deadlift
items.why: Soft knees, hinge at hips, slide DBs along legs, flat back

fields.release: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding dumbbells in front of your thighs. With a slight bend in your knees, hinge at the hips and push your butt back, sliding the dumbbells down along your legs. Lower until you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings, keeping your back flat throughout. Squeeze your glutes to drive your hips forward and return to standing.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings, glutes, lower back.

items.name: Roundhouse Kick
items.why: Turn hip over, kick through target with shin, pivot base foot

fields.release: From your fighting stance, pivot on your base foot while turning your hip over and swinging your leg in a circular arc, striking with your shin. Your base foot should rotate so your toes point away from the target. Keep your hands up and swing your arm on the kicking side slightly back for counterbalance. The power comes from the hip rotation, not just the leg.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hips, quads, obliques.

items.name: Russian Twist
items.why: Lean back, rotate torso side to side, keep chest up

fields.release: Sit on the floor with knees bent and lean your torso back about 45 degrees. Clasp your hands together or hold a weight in front of your chest. Rotate your torso to tap your hands on the floor beside each hip, alternating sides. Keep your chest lifted and avoid rounding your back. Lift your feet off the floor for an added challenge.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques.

items.name: Scapular Push-Up
items.why: Arms locked, only shoulder blades move — protract and retract

fields.release: Get into a high plank position with arms fully locked out. Without bending your elbows, let your chest sink between your shoulder blades (retract), then push the floor away and round your upper back (protract). Only your shoulder blades should move. This exercise strengthens the serratus anterior and improves shoulder stability.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: serratus anterior, shoulders.

items.name: Sciatic glide
items.dose: 10 reps × 2 sets per side. Daily is fine.
items.why: Different tissue, different rules. Some of what reads as muscle tightness is neural.

fields.tool: A chair
fields.release: Sit on the edge of a chair with your hands on your thighs. Slouch. Let your low back round. This is deliberate, not sloppy. Now, at the same time: straighten one knee out in front of you AND tip your head BACK. Then reverse, at the same time: bend the knee back down AND drop your chin to your chest. That is one rep. About 2 seconds each direction, smooth and continuous.
fields.notice: If your hamstring range improves from this when stretching has not moved it, the restriction was never muscular. A pull down the back of the leg that MOVES as you go. That movement is the nerve sliding, which is the whole point.
fields.careful: This is flossing, not stretching — never hold the end position. If it reproduces pain, tingling, or numbness, reduce the range until it does not. More is not better here; this is one of the few drills where overdoing it clearly makes things worse.

items.name: Sciatic glide — lying on your back
items.why: The lying-down sibling of the library's seated slump glide. Your hands hold the thigh, which means you control the range with your arms instead of with your hamstring's opinion — much easier to keep small.

fields.tool: Your own hands behind the thigh, and the floor or bed taking your back.
fields.release:
Lie on your back, both knees bent. Bring one knee up toward your chest and hold behind that thigh with both hands, keeping the thigh still.

Together: straighten that knee toward the ceiling — as far as it goes without the sensation changing character — AND pull your toes up toward your shin. Then reverse together: bend the knee back down AND point the toes away.

The thigh does not move. Only the knee and the ankle. Two seconds each way.
fields.notice: A pull down the back of the thigh and calf that travels as the knee straightens. Compare with what a held hamstring stretch feels like — the difference between a moving sensation and a parked one is the thing this module is teaching you to feel.
fields.careful: Never straighten into the position and stay there. The moment you hold it, you have converted this into a stretch of an irritated nerve, which is the opposite of the intent. Shooting pain, tingling or numbness down the leg means the range is too big — bend the knee more, and if that does not fix it, stop.
fields.load: Roll to your side, get up, and do a few unloaded hip hinges or a short walk. Range that is not used goes back.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: knees that hyperextend can reach past straight without the nerve ever telling you, and the hamstring will not stop you either. Use the point where the sensation starts to travel as your ceiling, and never the point where the knee runs out of movement. Orthostatic: this is a lying-flat item and then a getting-up item — sit on the edge before standing. PEM: the leg items cost more than the arm items; one side per session is a reasonable start.

levels.name: Knee and ankle opposing
levels.note: Toes up as the knee straightens, toes down as it bends.

levels.name: Add the head
levels.note: Chin to chest as the knee bends, head back to the pillow as it straightens. This is the largest version and the one to arrive at last.

loadAfter.name: Side-lying leg raises — the side of the hip working

items.name: Sciatic glide — standing, heel on a step
items.why: The version that fits into a day without lying down. It is also the hardest of the three to keep small, which is why it is last in the group rather than first.
items.equipment: A step, a low chair, or a kerb; something to hold

fields.tool: A low step for the heel and a wall, rail or counter for the hand.
fields.release:
Stand with one hand on something solid. Put the other heel on a low step in front of you, that knee slightly bent, toes up.

Together: hinge forward a little from the hip AND lift your chin, looking slightly up. Then reverse together: come upright AND drop your chin toward your chest.

The forward hinge is small — inches, not a bow. If your back is rounding a long way, it is too big.
fields.notice: The same travelling pull down the back of the leg, now with your body weight in the picture. If this version produces something the lying version does not, that is the standing position adding to it, not new information about the nerve.
fields.careful: Keep a hand on something the whole time. Keep the standing knee soft, never locked back. This is the one item in the module that combines a forward hinge with looking up, and if your neck objects to looking up, do not do this version at all — the lying one is there for exactly this reason.
fields.load: Walk for a minute or two straight afterwards. That is the whole load partner: use the leg in the range you just found.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: soft standing knee, always — a locked, hyperextended standing leg turns this into a joint at its end range holding your body weight. And if looking up brings on headache, visual change or dizziness, skip this version and raise it with a clinician. Orthostatic: standing plus a forward hinge plus looking up is a combination that can drop blood pressure; hand on support throughout, and do the lying version instead on a bad day. This is the module's least suitable item for anyone with orthostatic symptoms and it should not be anyone's first.

levels.name: Hinge only, head still
levels.note: Small hinge, head neutral, hand on support.

levels.name: Hinge with the chin dropping and lifting

loadAfter.name: Side-lying leg raises — the side of the hip working

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.

items.name: Scorpion Stretch
items.why: Lying face down, reach foot toward opposite hand behind you

fields.release: Lie face down with arms extended out to the sides. Lift one leg and reach it across your body toward the opposite hand behind you, rotating through your hips and thoracic spine. Keep the opposite shoulder pressed into the floor. Return to the start and repeat on the other side. This opens up the hip flexors and thoracic spine simultaneously.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hip flexors, thoracic spine, chest.

items.name: Scraping — a smooth edge drawn across tissue
items.why: New to this library. A blunt-edged tool is drawn across the skin over a muscle. It reaches broad, flat areas — shins, forearms, the outside of the hip — that balls handle badly, and it needs no grip strength.
items.equipment: A smooth-edged tool: a purpose-made scraping tool, or the edge of a spoon

fields.tool: Anything with a smooth blunt edge. Sharp edges have no place here, and neither does anything that could break.
fields.release: Lotion or oil on the skin first — dry scraping tears skin. Draw the edge across the tissue at a shallow angle with light-to-moderate pressure, in short strokes, following or crossing the direction of the muscle fibres. Cover the area rather than digging one line. Stop well before the skin is raw.
fields.notice: Areas that feel gritty or catch under the tool. That sensation is real and consistently reported, but what causes it is not established, and it is not a reading of scar tissue — treat it as a place to spend more time, not as a diagnosis.
fields.careful: Light pressure. This family reddens skin quickly and can bruise; redness is not the goal and more redness is not more result. Never over broken skin, a rash, a mole, or a bony ridge. Not over the front of the neck.
fields.load: Unchanged: use the area afterward.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: fragile skin, and this technique acts directly on skin. Very light, short, with lubricant, and stop at the first sign of marking. Of all the new families here this is the one most likely to leave a mark you did not want.
items.dose: [undetermined] — stroke counts and treatment times vary by system with no established standard for self-application.

evidence.grade: Mixed. Roughly comparable to massage; less effective than skilled manual techniques for range; the mechanism story is presumed rather than shown.
evidence.basis: Systematic review evidence places instrument-assisted soft tissue work similar to massage and flossing for range of motion, below specific manual techniques and joint mobilisation, and equal or better than most passive modalities for pain and function. The traditional explanation — that the tool detects and breaks down scar tissue and adhesions — is a presumption in the technique's own literature rather than a demonstrated finding, and this library does not repeat it as fact.

items.name: Scraping the forearm
items.why: The forearm is flat, broad, easy to see, and takes a scraping tool better than almost anywhere. It is also the region where thumb-and-ball work runs out fastest, because the hand doing the work gets as tired as the arm receiving it.
items.equipment: A smooth-edged tool or a spoon, and lotion

fields.tool: Any smooth blunt edge — a purpose-made tool, or the edge of a spoon. Lotion or oil first.
fields.release: Rest the forearm on a table, palm down. Draw the edge along the muscle from below the elbow toward the wrist at a shallow angle, with light pressure and short strokes, covering the whole outer forearm rather than digging one line. Then turn the arm over and do the palm side. Stop well before the skin is raw.
fields.notice: Places where the tool feels gritty or catches. That sensation is consistently reported and its cause is not established — treat it as somewhere to spend a bit more time, not as a diagnosis of what is under there.
fields.careful: Light. Redness is not the goal and more redness is not more result. Lotion always — dry scraping tears skin. Not over the bony ridge on the outside of the elbow, and not over the inner crease of the elbow or the wrist creases where vessels and nerves are close to the surface.
fields.load: Grip and release work, wrist movement in both directions against light resistance, and finger spreading.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this family acts directly on skin, and yours may mark more easily than most. Very light, short, well lubricated, and stop at the first sign of marking. If you want the same region without the marking risk, the thumb and ball items in entry-points.json cover it.

loadAfter.name: Wrist and grip work against light resistance
loadAfter.note: Match at S5; entry-points.json also carries hand loading in prose.

evidence.grade: Mixed. Roughly comparable to massage; less effective than skilled manual techniques for range; the mechanism story is presumed rather than shown.
evidence.basis: Systematic review evidence places instrument-assisted soft tissue work similar to massage and flossing for range of motion, below specific manual techniques and joint mobilisation, and equal or better than most passive modalities for pain and function. The traditional explanation — that the tool detects and breaks down scar tissue and adhesions — is a presumption in the technique's own literature rather than a demonstrated finding, and this library does not repeat it as fact.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Sibling to the forearm pressure items in the tender-point entry set — same target, different family, and a swap option when your hands are the thing that is tired.

items.name: Screen-free wind-down
items.why: No screens 30–60 min before bed — protects melatonin production

items.name: Seated Forward Fold
items.why: Sit with legs extended, hinge at hips, reach for toes

fields.release: Sit with legs extended straight in front of you. Sit tall first, then hinge at the hips and reach toward your toes. Keep your back as flat as possible — don't round excessively. Use a strap around feet if needed. Breathe and relax deeper on each exhale.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings, lower back, calves.

items.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back
items.why: The load partner for the upper trapezius and levator items. Those two muscles overwork because the lower half of the shoulder blade has nothing holding it down. Release them without addressing that and they are tight again by evening — which is the counterforce idea in its most visible form.

fields.tool: Nothing.
fields.release: Sit or stand tall. Without shrugging, slide the shoulder blade gently down your back and slightly toward your spine — the feeling is your shoulder blade settling into a back pocket. Hold it there and breathe normally. The top of your shoulder should stay relaxed the whole time; if it lifts, you have recruited the muscle you were trying to give a rest.
fields.notice: Whether the top of the shoulder can stay quiet while the lower part works. For most people it cannot, at first — that is the finding and the reason to do this at all.
fields.careful: No forced squeezing of the shoulder blades together, no puffed chest. This is a small, quiet, low-effort position, and effort is usually the sign it has gone wrong.
fields.load: This is the load. Later rungs add arm movement and then resistance.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: your shoulder blade may sit further out or lower at rest than the standard picture, and 'down and back' can take you into a position that does not suit your anatomy. Aim for a position you can hold quietly, not a textbook one, and if your shoulder feels less stable in the position rather than more, that is worth asking a clinician about.

levels.name: Find and hold
levels.note: Just the position, with the top of the shoulder staying quiet.

levels.name: Hold while the arm moves
levels.note: Keep the blade set and slowly raise and lower the arm. The blade holding while the arm moves is the actual skill.

levels.name: Against resistance
levels.note: The same, with a band or a light weight. Raise load only when rung 2 is quiet.

evidence.grade: Established as standard rehabilitation content; the specific 'correct' scapular position is contested.
evidence.basis: Scapular control training is routine in shoulder and neck rehabilitation. What is not settled is that any one scapular resting position is correct or that deviation from it causes symptoms — the card therefore teaches a position you can hold quietly rather than a position you should have.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Shadowbox Round
items.why: Stay light on feet, mix punches, movement, and defense

fields.release: Shadowboxing is practicing punches, kicks, movement, and defense against an imaginary opponent. Stay light on your feet, keep your hands up, and mix combinations of strikes with footwork and head movement. Visualize an opponent in front of you and react to imaginary attacks. This builds technique, endurance, and coordination.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: full body.

items.name: Shoulder CARs
items.why: Fist tight, move arm in biggest circle possible, stay controlled

fields.release: Stand tall and make a tight fist with one hand. Slowly raise your arm in front of you, continue overhead, then behind you and back down, tracing the biggest circle possible with a straight arm. Move very slowly and with control. Repeat in the opposite direction. This helps maintain shoulder mobility and highlights any restrictions in your range of motion.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: shoulders, rotator cuff.

items.name: Shoulder Tap
items.why: Minimize hip rotation, keep hips square to floor

fields.release: Start in a high plank position with hands directly under shoulders and feet slightly wider than hip-width apart. Lift one hand and tap the opposite shoulder, then return it to the floor and repeat on the other side. The key challenge is keeping your hips perfectly still and square to the floor; widen your stance to make this easier.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, core.

items.name: Side Plank
items.why: Stack feet, hips high, straight line from head to ankles

fields.release: Lie on your side and prop yourself up on your forearm with your elbow directly under your shoulder. Stack your feet and lift your hips so your body forms a straight line from head to ankles. Hold this position, keeping your hips high. Avoid letting your hips drop toward the floor. You should feel this in your obliques and the side of your hip.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques, shoulders.

levels.name: Copenhagen
levels.note: Top foot on bench, bottom leg free

items.name: Side-lying leg raises — the side of the hip working
items.why: The load partner for the side-of-hip, IT band and low-back-corner items — three release items pointing at one piece of strength, which tells you where the actual problem usually is.

fields.tool: Nothing. A wall behind you is a useful honesty check.
fields.release:
Lie on your side with your back against a wall, knees and hips slightly bent, top leg straight. Keeping your heel lightly in contact with the wall, lift the top leg toward the ceiling. The wall stops you swinging the leg forward, which is the cheat almost everybody does without noticing — and the moment your heel leaves the wall you have stopped using the muscle you came for.

Standing version: stand on one leg, level pelvis, and hold. Then notice whether the hip on the free side drops.
fields.notice: How small the honest range is with the heel on the wall. Whether one side is much weaker. Whether you feel it at the side of the hip or in the front corner — the front corner means the small overworking muscle has taken over again, so make the range smaller.
fields.careful: Small, clean range beats a big sloppy one. If the front corner of the hip cramps or takes over, reduce the height until it stops.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is one of the highest-value items in the hip module for you, because side-to-side pelvic control is exactly what less passive support costs you. Progress by hold time and cleanliness rather than by adding weight.

levels.name: Side-lying against a wall
levels.note: Heel on the wall the whole time. Small and honest.

levels.name: Hold at the top
levels.note: Same, holding rather than repeating. Time under load.

levels.name: Standing, level pelvis
levels.note: Single-leg stand with the free hip staying level. This is the one that transfers to walking.

evidence.grade: Established as standard rehabilitation content for hip and low back complaints.
evidence.basis: Hip abductor strengthening is routine in rehabilitation for hip, knee and low back problems and has a substantial trial literature behind the general approach. Specific doses vary by protocol and none is reproduced here.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Side-lying rib opener
items.equipment: Foam roller or a rolled towel
items.dose: 8 breaths per side. Daily if you like it.
items.why: This works what pulls on the rib cage, not the cage itself.

fields.tool: Foam roller or a rolled towel
fields.release: Lie on your side with the roller under your bottom ribs, running across your body. Stretch the top arm overhead and bring the top leg forward for balance. Breathe INTO the upside ribs — the ones facing the ceiling. Feel them open. 8 breaths, then swap sides.
fields.notice: Rotation and side-bending get easier. Pairs naturally with the lat work.
fields.careful: Roller under the ribs, not the waist. If it presses into soft belly, move it up.

photos.caption: Side-lying with the top arm overhead. Yours adds a roller under the bottom ribs and eight breaths into the upside ribs.

items.name: Single leg, eyes closed
items.why: Re-test: Every 2 weeks. Higher is better.

fields.release: Barefoot, counter within reach. Stop the clock the moment the foot moves or you touch down. Cap it at 60 — past that it is measuring patience, not balance.
fields.notice: Recorded in sec.

items.name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
items.why: One foot, full stretch at bottom, peak squeeze at top

fields.release: Stand on one foot, ideally on the edge of a step so your heel can drop below the surface. Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, squeezing your calf at the top, then lower slowly below step level for a full stretch. Hold a wall or railing for balance. This isolates one calf at a time for better strength development.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves.

items.name: Single-Leg Hop
items.why: One leg, controlled hop, soft landing, stay balanced

fields.release: Stand on one leg and hop in a controlled manner, landing softly on the same foot each time. Keep your knee slightly bent and focus on balance and a quiet landing. This builds single-leg power, ankle stability, and proprioception. Start with small hops in place and progress to forward, lateral, and multi-directional hops.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, quads, ankles.

items.name: Single-leg progression
items.equipment: Bare feet, and a wall or counter within reach
items.why: Proprioception training — the direct route to knowing where your body is and what it is doing.

fields.tool: Bare feet, and a wall or counter within reach
fields.release: Only move up a level when the current one is boring.
fields.notice: Your foot will be visibly working — toes gripping, arch adjusting constantly. That is the foot-to-brain conversation you are trying to restart.
fields.careful: Stay within reach of a counter. The Level 3 head turns can bring on dizziness in anyone whose balance or blood pressure is unreliable — if the room moves, sit down and come back to it another day at a slower speed.

levels.name: Single leg, eyes closed, 15–30 seconds
levels.note: This is a big jump; vision was doing most of the work.

levels.name: Single leg, eyes open, with slow head turns left and right ×10, then up and down ×10
Single leg standing on a folded towel or pillow, eyes open
Single leg on the pillow, eyes closed

photos.caption: Balance training on an unstable surface — roughly Level 4 of your progression. Levels 1–3 come first and need nothing but bare feet and a counter within reach.

items.name: Sissy Squat
items.why: Lean back, knees forward, lower on toes, keep hips extended

fields.release: Stand on your toes with your body upright. Lean your torso back while pushing your knees far forward, lowering yourself toward the ground. Keep your hips fully extended throughout so your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Use a support for balance while learning. This intensely isolates the quads.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads.

items.name: Skater Squat
items.why: Single leg, rear knee taps floor behind you, arms for balance

fields.release: Stand on one leg with the other leg bent behind you, knee pointing down. Lower yourself by bending the standing leg until your rear knee gently taps the floor, then stand back up. Extend your arms in front for counterbalance. This is a challenging single-leg exercise that builds quad and glute strength. Hold onto a support while learning.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

levels.name: To Box
levels.note: Lower to a box or target

items.name: Skin gliding — the layer above the muscle
items.why: New to this library, and the gentlest thing in it. Nothing is pressed. You lift and shift the skin and the loose layer beneath it and notice where it moves freely and where it does not. Often the only tolerable option over a sensitive or painful area.

fields.tool: Your fingers.
fields.release: Take a fold of skin between your fingers and thumb and lift it slightly away, or place a flat hand and move the skin over what is underneath without sliding across it. Explore an area systematically. Where it lifts and moves easily, move on; where it feels stuck or thick, stay a while with the gentlest sustained shift in the direction that resists.
fields.notice: The map of where it moves and where it doesn't. It is usually asymmetric, and often the stuck areas are places you would never have pressed. This is at least as much an assessment as a treatment.
fields.careful: No pinching hard, no dragging across dry skin. Should be comfortable throughout.
fields.load: Move the region normally afterward.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: skin that stretches unusually far is part of the picture, so what 'normal glide' feels like for you is your own baseline, not a textbook one. Compare left to right rather than against any standard. Do not lift to the limit of what the skin will do. PEM/pacing: near-zero exertion, and available on almost any day.
items.dose: [undetermined] — no dose literature exists for the self-administered form.

levels.name: Map an area
levels.note: Explore and notice. No treatment goal at this rung.

levels.name: Stay where it resists
levels.note: Gentle sustained shift into the restricted direction.

evidence.grade: Undetermined. Grouped with manual myofascial approaches in reviews; no separate trial base for the self-administered version.
evidence.basis: Reviews of fascia-targeted manual work include superficial-layer techniques within the broader category but do not test them separately, and nothing I found evaluates self-applied skin gliding. So there is no grade, and none is invented. It earns a place on gentleness and information value, not on evidence.

items.name: Skipping for Height
items.why: Drive knee up, push off hard, get maximum height each skip

fields.release: Skip forward with an emphasis on getting as high off the ground as possible with each skip. Drive your knee explosively upward and push hard off the ground with your opposite foot. Pump your arms to generate additional height. This develops explosive hip extension and improves vertical power for jumping sports.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, quads.

items.name: Sleep routine
items.why: Consistent bedtime, cool room, dark environment

items.name: Slip + Roll
items.why: Move head off centerline, slip to each side, roll under

fields.release: From your boxing stance, practice moving your head off the centerline to avoid imaginary punches. To slip, bend slightly at the waist to move your head to one side. To roll, bend your knees and rotate under an imaginary hook. Keep your hands up and eyes forward throughout. Start slowly and focus on staying balanced during each movement.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: core, quads.

items.name: Soft palate & throat
items.dose: Daily. Fold it into brushing your teeth so you do not have to remember it separately.
items.why: Myofunctional therapy. Real evidence for mild apnea and upper-airway resistance, and rarely offered.

fields.tool: A glass of water
fields.release: Say an exaggerated 'ahh' and hold it, feeling the back of the throat lift. ×10. Gargle water properly and loudly for 30 seconds. ×3. Aggressive enough that your eyes water slightly. Hum on a low pitch with a long exhale until you feel the buzz in your throat and chest.
fields.notice: Doubles as direct vagal work — the vagus nerve supplies the larynx. It is also relevant to the voice thread.
fields.careful: Nothing to speak of. This is the safest thing in the whole document.

items.name: Split Squat Jump
items.why: Lunge position, jump and switch legs mid-air, land soft

fields.release: Start in a lunge position with one foot forward and the other back. Explosively jump upward and switch your legs mid-air, landing in a lunge with the opposite foot forward. Land softly with your knees bent, keeping your torso upright. Avoid letting your back knee slam into the ground on landing.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

items.name: Sprint Drill (Wall Drive)
items.why: Hands on wall, lean forward, drive knees alternating

fields.release: Place your hands on a wall at about chest height and lean forward at roughly a 45-degree angle with your body in a straight line. Alternately drive your knees toward the wall, focusing on a powerful hip extension on the push-off leg and a quick knee drive on the other. This drill teaches proper sprint mechanics and develops hip drive power.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: glutes, hip flexors.

items.name: Squat
items.why: Knees track over toes, hips below parallel, chest up

fields.release: Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart, toes pointing slightly outward. Push your hips back and bend your knees to lower your body as if sitting into a chair, going at least until your thighs are parallel to the floor. Keep your chest up and knees tracking over your toes. Drive through your whole foot to stand back up.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes, hamstrings.

items.name: Squat Jump
items.why: Sit back, explode up, land soft, immediately reload

fields.release: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Lower into a squat, then explode upward as high as you can, swinging your arms for momentum. Land softly with bent knees, absorbing the impact, and immediately lower into the next squat to reload. Focus on both the height of your jump and the quality of your landing.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

items.name: Squat support needed
items.why: Re-test: Monthly. Higher is better.

fields.release: Deep squat hold. 0 = arms carrying most of you. 1 = a firm pull. 2 = light fingers. 3 = hands off entirely. This is the progression — not depth.
fields.notice: Recorded in 0–3.

items.name: Standing balance — the ladder
items.why: Balance is a skill that rebuilds with practice, and it is the one your ankles, hips and eyes are all doing at once. Each rung takes away one source of information so the others have to work harder.
items.equipment: A counter or wall within reach; later, a wobble board

fields.tool: Something to catch yourself on. Not optional — the whole ladder assumes it is there.
fields.release: Work at the rung where you can hold steady for about 30 seconds with only occasional touches for support. Not the hardest rung you can survive — the hardest one you can do well. When 30 seconds is easy and quiet, move up.
fields.notice: Which direction you drift, and whether one side is worse. Whether your toes claw the floor — that is your foot gripping because something upstream isn't holding. Whether closing your eyes changes everything, which tells you how much of your balance is running on vision.
fields.careful: Near a counter, every rung, every time. Knees soft — if yours snap back past straight, keep a small bend and treat that as part of the drill. If you have a history of ankle instability, earn each rung rather than skipping to the boards.
fields.load: Calf raises and single-leg hip work on the same days. Balance is a skill, but it still needs something underneath it that can hold.

levels.name: Feet together
levels.note: Stand with feet touching, arms relaxed. 30 seconds. Harder than it sounds if it has been a while.

levels.name: Heel to toe
levels.note: One foot directly in front of the other, heel touching toe. 30 seconds each way.

levels.name: One leg
levels.note: Other foot off the floor, not resting on the standing leg. 30 seconds a side.

levels.name: One leg, eyes closed
levels.note: Same, eyes shut. This is where most people find out how much they were using vision. Expect a big drop — that is the point of the rung.

levels.name: One leg, head turning
levels.note: Eyes open, turn your head slowly side to side, then up and down, while balancing. The first rung where the balance system and the eyes have to negotiate.

levels.name: Unstable surface
levels.note: Wobble or dome board, eyes open, two feet first and one foot later. Counter within reach.

levels.name: Foot board, single foot
levels.note: The two-section board with the forefoot and rearfoot moving separately. Start in its most stable configuration and free it up as you go.

evidence.grade: established direction, small trials
evidence.basis: Exercise programmes including balance and proprioceptive work in hypermobility syndromes improve balance, proprioception, strength and pain across a small set of trials, with no adverse effects reported. The trials are few and small; the direction is consistent.

items.authoringNote: Rungs 6 and 7 use equipment already owned.

items.name: Standing Forward Fold
items.why: Hinge at hips, let gravity pull you down, relax neck

fields.release: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at the hips and fold your torso forward, letting gravity pull you down. Relax your neck and let your arms hang heavy. Bend your knees slightly if your hamstrings are tight. Breathe deeply and allow yourself to sink a little deeper into the stretch with each exhale. You should feel this in your hamstrings and lower back.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hamstrings, lower back, calves.

items.name: Standing Hamstring Stretch
items.why: Foot on low surface, hinge forward with flat back

fields.release: Place one foot on a low step or bench (or just extend in front of you). Keep the elevated leg straight. Hinge at the hips and lean forward with a flat back until you feel the stretch behind the thigh. Keep hips square. Hold and switch.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings, calves.

levels.name: Low Surface
levels.note: Foot on low surface, slight lean

levels.name: Bench Height
levels.note: Foot on bench height, deeper lean

levels.name: Flex Foot
levels.note: Flex foot, pull toes toward you

items.name: Standing Quad Stretch
items.why: Stand on one leg, pull heel toward glute

fields.release: Stand on one leg (hold wall if needed). Bend the other knee and grab your foot behind you, pulling heel toward glute. Keep knees close together and push hips slightly forward. You should feel the stretch in the front of your thigh.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, hip flexors.

levels.name: Backbend
levels.note: Add slight backbend for deeper hip flexor stretch

items.name: Step-Up
items.why: Drive through top foot, minimal push from bottom leg

fields.release: Stand facing a box or sturdy step. Place one foot fully on top of the box. Drive through the top foot to step up, bringing your body to a standing position on the box. Avoid pushing off with your bottom foot. Step down with control. Keep your torso upright and use a box height that allows your knee to bend to about 90 degrees.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes.

items.name: Strength training
items.why: Build muscle, support metabolism, improve bone density

items.name: Stretch/yoga 10+ min
items.why: Circulation + stress reduction

items.name: Suction cups — pulling tissue up instead of pressing it down
items.why: New to this library, and mechanically the opposite of everything else in it. Every other family compresses. This lifts. For anyone who cannot tolerate pressure — which includes a lot of people with fragile or irritable tissue — that reversal is the whole reason it is worth knowing about.
items.equipment: Soft silicone cups (the squeeze kind, not fire cupping)

fields.tool: Soft silicone cups you squeeze and place. No flame, no pump, nothing that stays on unattended.
fields.release: A little oil or lotion on the skin. Squeeze the cup, place it on a muscle belly, release so it grips. You can leave it still, or — usually better — glide it slowly along the muscle. Keep the suction gentle enough that you could pull it off easily. Short applications.
fields.notice: Whether the tissue underneath feels different afterward. Whether particular areas grip differently — some parts of a muscle will pull up readily and others hardly at all.
fields.careful: Static cups leave marks; gliding cups mostly don't, which is one good reason to prefer gliding. Never over broken skin, a mole, a vein you can see standing up, or an area that is numb. Not on the front of the neck or the abdomen. If you bruise easily, this family will mark you — decide in advance whether that is acceptable.
fields.load: Same law: the tissue you decompressed needs something asked of it.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this family marks fragile skin readily and the marks can last. Gliding rather than static, minimum suction, short. On the other hand, it may be more tolerable than deep pressure — the trade is bruising risk against pressure tolerance, and that is your call to make knowingly.
items.dose: [undetermined] — application times in the literature vary widely and no standard exists for self-applied silicone cups.

levels.name: Gliding, light suction
levels.note: Moving the cup along the muscle, gentlest setting. The default.

levels.name: Static, brief
levels.note: Cup left in place for a short time. Expect a mark.

evidence.grade: Limited. Some benefit for musculoskeletal pain and function, occasionally on par with standard care; mechanism plausible but unconfirmed.
evidence.basis: Reviews of cupping for musculoskeletal complaints report reductions in pain and improvement in function, sometimes comparable to usual care. A pilot randomised trial compared cupping against heat plus foam rolling for hamstring flexibility. The mechanism claim — that negative pressure lifts and separates fascial layers — is anatomically plausible and has imaging support of an unclear clinical significance. Grade reflects small studies and high variability in how the technique is applied.

items.name: Suction on the back of the shoulder
items.why: A pressure-free option for a region that gets a lot of pressure. The back of the shoulder is broad, flat, easy to reach and one of the easiest places to try a cup, which makes it the sensible first experiment with that family.
items.equipment: A soft silicone cup and a little oil or lotion

fields.tool: One soft silicone cup. Lotion or oil on the skin first.
fields.release: Oil the back of the shoulder and the area over the shoulder blade. Squeeze the cup, place it on the muscle, release so it grips — gently enough that you could pull it off easily. Then glide it slowly along the muscle rather than leaving it still: along the back of the shoulder, out across the blade, up toward the ridge. Slow passes. Take it off well before the skin darkens.
fields.notice: Whether the tissue feels different afterward compared with how it feels after ball work. That comparison is the reason to have both families available.
fields.careful: Gliding rather than static — static cups leave marks that last days. Never over broken skin, a mole, or a visible standing vein. Not on the front of the neck. If you bruise easily, expect marks and decide before you start whether that is acceptable.
fields.load: External rotation and setting the shoulder blade, same as the pressure items.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: fragile skin marks readily with this family. Gliding only, minimum suction, short. The trade-off is real — less pressure on the tissue, more risk of a visible mark — and it is your call to make knowingly.

levels.name: Gliding, light suction
levels.note: Moving, gentlest setting. The default and often the only rung needed.

levels.name: Brief static
levels.note: Cup left in place briefly. Expect a mark.

loadAfter.name: Turning the arm out, under control

evidence.grade: Limited. Some benefit for musculoskeletal pain and function, occasionally on par with standard care; mechanism plausible but unconfirmed.
evidence.basis: Reviews of cupping for musculoskeletal complaints report reductions in pain and improvement in function, sometimes comparable to usual care. A pilot randomised trial compared cupping against heat plus foam rolling for hamstring flexibility. The mechanism claim — that negative pressure lifts and separates fascial layers — is anatomically plausible and has imaging support of an unclear clinical significance. Grade reflects small studies and high variability in how the technique is applied.

items.name: Suitcase Carry
items.why: DB in one hand, stand tall, resist leaning to that side

fields.release: Hold a dumbbell in one hand at your side and walk forward with an upright posture. The challenge is resisting the pull of the weight, which tries to make you lean sideways. Keep your shoulders level and core braced throughout. This builds oblique strength, grip endurance, and teaches your core to resist lateral forces.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques, core, forearms.

items.name: Superman
items.why: Lift arms and legs off floor, squeeze glutes and back

fields.release: Lie face down with arms extended overhead and legs straight. Simultaneously lift your arms, chest, and legs off the floor by squeezing your glutes and lower back muscles. Hold briefly at the top, then lower with control. Keep your neck neutral by looking at the floor rather than cranking your head up.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lower back, glutes.

levels.name: Hold
levels.note: Static hold, arms and legs up

levels.name: Reverse Snow Angel
levels.note: Sweep arms from front to hips

levels.name: W-Raise
levels.note: Pull elbows down into W shape

fields.release: Lie on your back. Cross right ankle over left knee (making a "4" shape). Reach through and pull the left thigh toward your chest. You should feel a deep stretch in the right glute/hip. Keep head on the floor. Hold and switch.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: glutes, piriformis, hips.

levels.name: easy
levels.note: Keep bottom foot on floor, just cross ankle

levels.name: advanced
levels.note: Press crossed knee away while pulling thigh closer

items.name: Supine Hamstring Stretch
items.why: Lie on back, lift one leg, hold behind thigh or calf

fields.release: Lie on your back. Lift one leg and hold behind the thigh or calf (use a towel or strap if needed). Keep the leg as straight as possible. Keep the other leg flat on the floor. Pull gently to deepen the stretch. Hold and breathe.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hamstrings.

levels.name: Deeper
levels.note: Pull closer, point/flex foot for different fibers

items.name: Supine Spinal Twist
items.why: Lie on back, pull knee across body, keep shoulders down

fields.release: Lie on your back, arms in a T. Pull one knee to chest, then guide it across your body to the opposite side. Let gravity pull the knee toward the floor. Keep both shoulders pressed down. Look in the opposite direction of the knee. Breathe and melt into it.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: spine, obliques, glutes, chest.

levels.name: Easy Twist
levels.note: Knee does not need to touch floor

levels.name: Full Twist
levels.note: Both shoulders stay down, breathe into twist

levels.name: Straight Leg
levels.note: Straighten crossing leg for deeper twist

items.name: Sustained pressure — ball, thumb, knuckle
items.why: The workhorse. Most release items in this library are some version of this, so it is worth learning properly once.
items.equipment: A ball, your thumb, a knuckle. Nothing motorised, nothing sharp.

fields.tool: Firmness matters more than brand. A tennis ball is forgiving, a lacrosse ball is sharp, a soft inflatable ball is the gentlest option and the right starting point for most people who are new to this or who bruise easily.
fields.release: Sink in slowly until you meet something tender out of proportion to how hard you are pressing. That mismatch is the find — not the hardest pressure you can tolerate. Then hold still. Do not grind, do not rub, do not chase. Breathe out into it. Somewhere in the hold, the spot either softens under the contact or it doesn't; both are answers, and neither means push harder.
fields.notice: Whether the pressure eases while you hold it. Whether sensation spreads somewhere other than where you are pressing. Whether one side is worse than the other — that difference is usually your best single finding of the session.
fields.careful: Never into a pulse, the front of the throat, the front of the neck, the kidney area, or hard onto bone. Numbness, pins and needles, or an electric sensation means you are on a nerve — come off and move slightly. Bruising means it was too hard. Pressure that keeps climbing the longer you hold is a stop.
fields.load: Whatever you opened, use. A spot that eases is a door that closes again if you walk away from it.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: fragile tissue and easy bruising are part of the picture, and tolerance for pressure work is genuinely lower. Start softer than feels necessary and stay there for a few sessions before deciding what you can take. Guarding around a lax joint may be doing stabilising work — the answer is not less release, it is release always followed by loading, which is why every item here has a load partner. Orthostatic: floor work means getting down and up; do it slowly and have a hand available.
items.dose: Sustained holds in the trial literature commonly run around 60–90 seconds per site [derived — self-myofascial release trial protocols, e.g. a 2025 latent-trigger-point study using 90 s per muscle]. Number of sites per session, sessions per week: [undetermined].

levels.name: Soft ball, short holds
levels.note: A soft or inflatable ball, and a lighter contact than you think you need. Learning what 'tender out of proportion' feels like is the whole job at this rung.

levels.name: Firmer ball, longer holds
levels.note: Same technique, more depth. Move up only when rung 1 stopped producing bruises or next-day soreness.

levels.name: Pressure plus movement
levels.note: Hold the contact and move the joint the muscle crosses. This is the pin-and-move family — see that guide.

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Sweat session
items.why: Skin = detox organ — sauna, hot bath, or intense exercise

items.name: Teep (Front Kick)
items.why: Chamber knee, push ball of foot forward, snap back quick

fields.release: From your fighting stance, lift your knee toward your chest (chamber), then push the ball of your foot straight forward like you are pushing a door open. Snap your foot back quickly to the chambered position before returning to stance. This is a push kick used to create distance. Keep your guard up and core tight throughout.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: hip flexors, quads, core.

items.name: The abdominal wall — gliding, not pressing
items.why: The abdominal wall is where a great deal of protective bracing lives and where almost nobody looks, because deep abdominal pressure is a bad idea and so the whole region gets skipped. Gliding the surface layer sidesteps the problem entirely — nothing is pressed in.

fields.tool: Flat hands.
fields.release: Lying on your back with knees bent so the abdominal wall is slack. Place a flat hand on your belly and move the skin and the loose layer beneath it over what lies underneath — side to side, up and down — without sliding across the skin or pressing inward. Work across the whole area, including out to the sides and up under the rib margin. Where it does not want to move, stay there with a gentle sustained shift in that direction and breathe.
fields.notice: Where it moves easily and where it feels tethered, and whether that map is symmetrical. Whether your belly is braced — a lot of people hold their abdomen in continuously and have done for years without knowing.
fields.careful: Surface only. No deep pressure into the abdomen, and nothing that presses on a pulse you can feel — a strong pulsing sensation in the middle of the abdomen is a reason to leave the area alone and mention it to a doctor, not to explore it. Skip this item entirely if you are pregnant, have a hernia, have had recent abdominal surgery, or have active abdominal or bowel symptoms; and if you have a diagnosed abdominal condition, this is a question for your clinician rather than an app.
fields.load: The deep abdominal connection item — finding the layer underneath and learning to produce it on purpose.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: skin that stretches more than average changes what 'normal glide' feels like — compare your own sides, not a standard. PEM/pacing: near-zero exertion.

levels.name: Map it
levels.note: Explore and notice. No treatment goal.

levels.name: Stay where it resists
levels.note: Gentle sustained shift into the restricted direction, with breathing.

loadAfter.name: Finding the deep abdominal layer

evidence.grade: Undetermined. Grouped with manual myofascial approaches in reviews; no separate trial base for the self-administered version.
evidence.basis: Reviews of fascia-targeted manual work include superficial-layer techniques within the broader category but do not test them separately, and nothing I found evaluates self-applied skin gliding. So there is no grade, and none is invented. It earns a place on gentleness and information value, not on evidence.

items.name: The arch of the foot
items.why: The foot is dense with findable spots and gives faster feedback than almost anywhere else — many people feel a change in how they stand within a minute.
items.equipment: A ball — tennis, lacrosse, or a golf ball for more bite

fields.tool: A ball on the floor. Softer for more surface, harder for more depth.
fields.release: Seated, roll the ball slowly from the heel toward the ball of the foot along the inside arch. When you meet a spot that bites, stop and rest your weight there rather than rolling through it.
fields.notice: Tenderness that spreads toward the heel or forward into the toes. Afterward, stand up and compare how the two feet meet the floor — that difference is usually the most convincing thing in this whole section.
fields.careful: Seated first, standing later. If you have had heel pain that is worst on the first steps of the morning, keep the pressure moderate and stop if it aggravates.
fields.load: Stand and press the ball of the big toe into the floor without curling it. Then rise onto the toes slowly, five times.

levels.name: Standing
levels.note: Bodyweight through the ball, near a counter for balance.

items.name: The back of the shoulder blade
items.why: The muscles covering the back of the shoulder blade below its ridge are the ones that stop your arm bone rolling forward. They are easy to reach, reliably tender, and often the reason for a deep ache that feels like it is inside the shoulder joint.

fields.tool: A ball against a wall — better than the floor here, because you can control pressure precisely and the angle is easier to find.
fields.release: Stand with your back to a wall and the ball on the flat area of your shoulder blade below its bony ridge — the plate of muscle between the ridge and the lower tip of the blade. Lean back and hunt for tender spots; there are usually two or three, and they are often nearer the outer edge than you expect. Once you find one, hold.
fields.notice: Sensation spreading down the outside of the arm or deep into the front of the shoulder is what is traditionally described here, and it is often why people think their problem is at the front. Whether the pattern matches an ache you already knew about.
fields.careful: On the flat muscle plate, not on the bony ridge or the edge of the blade. Come off for tingling into the arm.
fields.load: External rotation, and setting the shoulder blade.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: standing against a wall lets you control pressure far better than lying on the floor, which matters when tissue bruises easily.

levels.name: Add the arm reach
levels.note: Hold the ball and slowly reach the arm across your body and back. The tissue moves under the ball.

levels.name: On the floor
levels.note: More pressure available, less control. Only if the wall version has stopped producing.

loadAfter.name: Turning the arm out, under control

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: The back of the upper arm
items.why: One head of the muscle at the back of the upper arm crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow, which means a tight arm can limit reaching overhead — and almost nobody looks there when overhead range is the complaint.
items.equipment: A ball against a wall, or your opposite hand

fields.tool: A ball against a wall with the arm raised, or squeeze the muscle in your opposite hand.
fields.release: Raise the arm and place a ball against a wall on the back of the upper arm, working from the elbow up toward the armpit. The part nearest the armpit is the one that crosses the shoulder and is usually the most useful. Hold where it bites. Hand version: squeeze the back of the arm between fingers and thumb, working up its length.
fields.notice: Whether the top end, near the armpit, is much more tender than the middle. Whether overhead reach changes afterward.
fields.careful: Muscle only. There is a groove on the inside of the upper arm where a nerve runs close to the surface — tingling into the ring and little fingers means come off and move outward.
fields.load: Overhead reach and hold, and pushing work at whatever range you own.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: overhead positions take a lax shoulder a long way. Keep the arm raise modest for the wall version, and use the hand-squeeze version if overhead is uncomfortable.

levels.name: Hand squeeze
levels.note: No equipment, arm at your side.

levels.name: Ball against a wall
levels.note: Arm raised, more pressure, better access to the top end.

levels.name: Add the elbow bending
levels.note: Hold pressure and slowly bend and straighten the elbow.

loadAfter.name: Overhead reach and hold
loadAfter.note: Match against existing overhead/pressing content at S5.

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. items.name: The ball of the foot and between the toes
items.why: Shoes hold the forefoot still all day. The small muscles between the long bones stop being asked to do anything, and they get tender.

fields.tool: Thumb and finger, one on top and one underneath.
fields.release: Find the grooves between the long bones on the top of the foot, behind the toes. Press gently into a groove and hold. Work each one. Then squeeze the ball of the foot from top and bottom.
fields.notice: Sensation spreading into the toes. Often one groove is far worse than the others.
fields.careful: Gentle here — this is a thin area with nerves running between the bones. Burning or electric sensation into the toes means come off.
fields.load: Spread the toes apart without curling them, hold, release. Ten times. Harder than it sounds and the point of the whole thing.

items.name: The canister — why the floor, the diaphragm and the deep belly are one system
items.why: The single idea that makes this whole section make sense. These are not three muscles that happen to be near each other — they are the top, bottom and sides of one pressurised container, and they only work as a set.

fields.tool: Nothing.
fields.release:
Picture a container in your trunk. The diaphragm is the lid. The pelvic floor is the base. The deep abdominal layer wraps the front and sides, and small deep muscles line the back. Pressure inside that container is what lets your spine be stable without your back muscles gripping.

Breathe in: the lid drops, the base drops, the sides widen. Breathe out: everything comes back up. That is what it looks like when it works.

What it looks like when it doesn't: the lid barely moves, so the neck lifts the ribs instead. The base holds constantly instead of moving, or never produces at all. The sides are braced permanently so nothing widens. The back muscles take over the stabilising and are tight all day as a result.

So — a tight low back may be a breathing problem. A pelvic floor that will not let go may be a diaphragm problem. A neck that is always tight may be either. This is what counterforce means in one region: pressing on any one of these while the others keep shoving does not hold.
fields.notice: Put one hand on your lower ribs and one on your belly and just breathe. Which moves? Then notice whether anything at the base of the pelvis responds. Three parts, one system — find out how many of them are actually participating.
fields.careful: Nothing to be careful of. This is a reading item.
fields.load: Everything else in this section is the load for this idea.

levels.name: Read it and test yourself
levels.note: Two hands, one minute of breathing. Which parts move?

evidence.grade: Established anatomy and coordinated function; the extent to which restoring the coordination fixes downstream symptoms is less settled.
evidence.basis: That the diaphragm, pelvic floor, deep abdominal wall and deep spinal muscles act together in managing intra-abdominal pressure, and that they move in coordination with breathing, is well described. The stronger clinical claim — that retraining this coordination resolves a given person's back or pelvic symptoms — is a treatment claim this card does not make.

items.authoringNote: Candidate for the connection-card series rather than the item catalogue — Kevin's call on placement.

items.name: The columns beside the back of your neck
items.why: The two ropes of muscle either side of the bumps down the back of your neck do the actual work of holding your head up against gravity all day. If your head sits forward of your shoulders, they never get a break.
items.equipment: Two balls in a sock, or your fingertips

fields.tool: Two balls tied into a sock so they sit either side of the spine with a gap in the middle — the gap is the point, because it keeps pressure off the bones. Or your own fingertips.
fields.release: Lying down, place the pair of balls so the bony bumps sit in the gap between them and the balls press the muscle either side. Let the weight of your head settle onto them. Work slowly down the neck, a spot at a time. Seated, use fingertips instead, pressing forward and slightly inward from behind.
fields.notice: How much of your head's weight these muscles were holding. Whether one side is thicker or tenderer. Whether the sensation changes when you tuck your chin slightly.
fields.careful: Either side of the bumps, never directly on them. The lower part of the neck near the base is thinner tissue — lighter there. Come off for any dizziness, visual change, or nausea.
fields.load: Chin nods. These muscles are overworked because the front of the neck is not sharing the load, and pressing them does not change that on its own.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is close to the region where cervical instability shows up. Gentle, short, and if head-supported work leaves your neck feeling worse or less stable rather than easier, that is a clinician's question, not a reason to press harder or longer. Orthostatic: lying down for this is fine; get up in stages.

levels.name: Fingertips, seated
levels.note: Fully under your control, no floor, no equipment.

levels.name: Balls in a sock, lying
levels.note: Head weight does the pressing. Deeper, and easier on your hands.

levels.name: Add a slow chin tuck
levels.note: With the pressure on, tuck the chin gently and release. Pin-and-move for the neck.

loadAfter.name: Chin nods — the front of the neck

items.name: The corner stretch — nose to armpit
items.why: The position that targets this particular muscle rather than the whole side of the neck. The direction is oddly specific, and that specificity is why it works when a general neck stretch does nothing.
items.equipment: None; optionally something to hold the shoulder down

fields.tool: Nothing. Sitting on your own hand, or holding the edge of the chair, keeps the shoulder down so the stretch reaches the muscle instead of just lifting the shoulder.
fields.release: Sit tall, anchor the shoulder on the working side down. Turn your head about forty-five degrees away from that side, then look down toward your armpit — nose toward the opposite armpit. You should feel it in the back corner where neck meets shoulder, not down the front of the neck. Settle and wait.
fields.notice: Where you feel it. If it is at the front or side of the neck, the rotation is wrong — adjust the turn until it lands in the back corner. That hunting is the skill.
fields.careful: No hand pulling your head down. Should be a stretch, never a pull, and never anything sharp. Stop for dizziness, visual change or tingling into the arm.
fields.load: Follow with lower trapezius work and chin nods.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: a neck that already moves further than most does not need to be taken further. Use a smaller position and hold it with the shoulder anchor rather than the head angle. If holding this position leaves your neck feeling less supported afterward rather than easier, stop and raise it clinically.

levels.name: Small, shoulder anchored
levels.note: Anchor first, position second. The anchor is what makes it work.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back

evidence.grade: Established for range of motion; the change is mostly in stretch tolerance, not tissue length.
evidence.basis: A 2025 systematic review with meta-regression covering 65 studies and over 1,500 adults found that range-of-motion improvements after static stretching track changes in tolerance to passive stretch, with much weaker association to measured stiffness or fascicle length. The practical reading: you are training your nervous system's willingness to go there, which is real and useful — and is a different claim from lengthening tissue.

items.name: The corner where neck meets shoulder blade
items.why: A muscle running from the side of the neck down to the top inside corner of the shoulder blade. It is the classic 'knot' spot people reach for and rarely find, because they press the wrong end.

fields.tool: A ball against a wall, or lying on it on the floor if you tolerate that.
fields.release: Find the top inner corner of your shoulder blade — reach across your back, or feel for the bony corner about a hand's width out from your spine at the level of the top of your shoulder. The muscle attaches there. Put the ball just above and on that corner, lean back, and hunt for the tender point. Once you have it, reach the arm on that side across your body to slide the shoulder blade away from the ball, and hold.
fields.notice: Whether it refers up the side of the neck toward the ear. Whether looking down over that shoulder changes the sensation — that movement is what this muscle resists.
fields.careful: Muscle, not the bony edge of the shoulder blade or the spine. If the ball sits on bone you will feel it as a hard, flat ache rather than the tender-out-of-proportion feeling you want.
fields.load: Pair with lower trapezius work — this muscle overworks when the shoulder blade has nothing holding its lower half down.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: reaching across to move the shoulder blade puts your own shoulder at the far end of its range. Keep it small and supported.

levels.name: Add the reach
levels.note: Hold the pressure and reach the arm across to slide the shoulder blade under it.

levels.name: Add a head turn
levels.note: Hold the pressure and turn to look down over the opposite shoulder, slowly.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back

items.name: The deep corner between the last rib and the pelvis
items.why: A thick muscle spanning from the top of the pelvis up to the last rib, deep and toward the back. It hikes the hip and side-bends the trunk, and it is a frequent source of one-sided low back ache — including the kind that comes on from standing rather than from bending.
items.equipment: A ball, and a wall or the floor

fields.tool: A ball against a wall, or lying on it with knees bent.
fields.release: Find the top ridge of your pelvis at the back and the bottom rib above it. The muscle fills the corner between them, close in toward the spine. Standing with your back near-side-on to a wall, place a ball in that corner just outside the thick rope of muscle beside the spine, and lean in. Hunt. Then side-bend gently away from the ball while holding the contact.
fields.notice: Whether one side is much shorter — measure by feel, not by looking: side-bend each way and see which is more restricted. Whether the ache you already had is on the same side.
fields.careful: This region has no rib and no bone protecting the deeper structures — lighter than you would go on a thigh, and never a hard ball driven hard. Stop for any deep ache that does not feel muscular. Not right after eating.
fields.load: Side-of-hip strength and trunk side-bending under control. This muscle overworks when the hip beneath it will not hold the pelvis level, which makes the side-of-hip item the real partner.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: side-bending against the ball can go a long way without much sensation. Keep it small, and treat the side-of-hip loading as the main event. Orthostatic: the standing wall version avoids floor transfers.

levels.name: Add the side-bend
levels.note: Slow, small, tissue moving under the ball.

levels.name: Lying, knees dropped away
levels.note: Deeper access, less control. Knees falling to the opposite side opens the corner.

loadAfter.name: Side-lying leg raises — the side of the hip working
