items.name: The deep muscle behind the shin bone
items.why: Deep in the calf, behind the big superficial muscles, sits one that runs down behind the inner ankle and fans into the underside of the foot. It is the main active support for the arch. Roll the calf and you miss it entirely, because it lies underneath.

fields.tool: Thumbs are better than a ball here, because the target is narrow and specific.
fields.release:
Sit with the ankle across the opposite knee. Find the inner edge of your shin bone in the lower half of the calf, then press just behind that edge, angling in toward the back of the bone rather than into the calf bulk. That is where the muscle runs. Hold, and then slowly turn the sole of your foot inward and downward — the movement this muscle produces — a few times while keeping the contact.

Also follow it around: behind and just below the bony bump on the inside of the ankle, its tendon runs in a groove. Light contact only there.
fields.notice: Whether the arch of the foot on that side is lower. Whether turning the sole inward is weak. Whether the tenderness runs the whole length or sits near the ankle.
fields.careful: Behind the inner edge of the bone, and gently. A bundle of nerve and vessels runs behind the inner ankle — light contact there, and any pins and needles into the sole means come off. Pain along this line with activity, especially with a flattening arch, is a clinician's question rather than a release target.
fields.load: Calf raises done with the weight toward the big-toe side, and arch work — lifting the arch without curling the toes.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: flat or collapsing arches are common, and this muscle is often working hard against a foot that gives way. Loading it and the foot's own small muscles matters more than releasing it. Orthostatic: seated throughout.

levels.name: Find it with thumbs
levels.note: Locating the line behind the bone. Finding it is the rung.

levels.name: Add the foot turning
levels.note: Slow inward turn of the sole under sustained contact.

loadAfter.name: Lifting the arch, and calf raises that use it

evidence.grade: Undetermined for the self-administered form; clinician-delivered versions have small trials against comparators.
evidence.basis: Clinician-applied pin-and-stretch approaches have been compared against other manual techniques in small trials with mixed results. Nothing I found tests the self-administered version specifically. The rationale — that tissue moving under a fixed contact restores glide between layers — is a mechanism story, not a demonstrated finding, and is written here as such.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Authored as its own item rather than folded into the calf card, which is a vote for keeping tibialis posterior as a separate census entry (D40 provisional flag).

items.name: The deeper calf muscle — the one a straight-leg stretch misses
items.why: There are two calf muscles and they need different positions. The outer one crosses the knee, so a straight-leg stretch reaches it. The deeper one does not cross the knee — which means if your knee is straight you are not reaching it, and if your ankle is stiff it is very often the culprit.

fields.tool: A wall or a step, and a bent knee. The bent knee is the entire point.
fields.release:
Stand facing a wall in a short split stance with the back foot flat. Now bend the back knee while keeping that heel down. The stretch should drop from the middle of the calf down toward the ankle — that lower location is how you know you are on the right muscle.

From there: press the ball of the back foot gently into the floor as if pushing the heel up, without letting it lift. Hold lightly, then release completely and let the knee bend a little further. Repeat.
fields.notice: How much less range you have with the knee bent than straight. Whether one ankle is stiffer. This is one of the most testable items in the library — the knee-to-wall self-test measures exactly this.
fields.careful: Heel stays down; the moment it lifts the position stops working. Gentle contraction. If you have had an Achilles problem, keep it gentle and progress slowly.
fields.load: Bent-knee calf raises — the same position, working. Almost nobody does calf raises with a bent knee, which is why this muscle stays weak.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: the ankle may already have plenty of range, in which case the useful half of this item is the loading half, not the stretching half. Orthostatic: there is a seated version — sit with the foot flat and press the knee forward over the toes with the heel down.

levels.name: Seated, knee forward over the toes
Contract and release
levels.note: Add the gentle press-and-let-go, taking up slack each round.

loadAfter.name: Bent-knee calf raises, slow lowering
loadAfter.note: The imported 'Eccentric heel drops' card is the straight-knee version. The bent-knee variant may need authoring. Check at S5.

evidence.grade: Established for acute range of motion; no better than other stretching methods; mechanism is largely increased tolerance to stretch.
evidence.basis: Meta-analysis across stretching types finds contract-relax, static and dynamic stretching all improve range of motion acutely and over training periods, with no significant difference between them. A 2025 meta-analysis of static stretching mechanisms across 65 studies found range gains track increased tolerance to the stretch far more than any change in muscle length or stiffness. So: it works, and it works by changing what you will allow, not by lengthening tissue.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Pairs directly with the knee-to-wall self-test already in the library (D36).

items.name: The diamond of fascia across the low back
items.why: Across the low back sits a broad diamond of dense fibrous sheeting where several large muscles from above, below and both sides all attach. It is one of the three fascia-only targets in the vocabulary, and it is a place where pressing muscle misses the point — the tissue is the junction, not the muscle.

fields.tool: Flat hands.
fields.release: Lying on your side or your front, or seated leaning forward onto a table so the low back is slack. Place a flat hand over the low back to one side of the spine and move the skin and the layer beneath it over what lies underneath — side to side, up and down, diagonally — without sliding across the skin. Cover the whole diamond from the bottom ribs down to the top of the pelvis and out to the sides. Where it will not move, stay with a gentle sustained shift in that direction and breathe.
fields.notice: Where it glides and where it feels tethered, and whether that map is symmetrical. Whether the tethered areas correspond to anything you already knew about. This item is at least as much assessment as treatment.
fields.careful: Surface only, comfortable throughout. No dragging on dry skin.
fields.load: Movement that uses the junction — reaching diagonally across the body, rotating the trunk — and the deep abdominal connection, which tensions this sheet from the inside.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: skin and superficial tissue that move further than average change what normal glide feels like. Compare your own sides rather than any standard, and do not lift or shift to the limit. PEM/pacing: near-zero exertion.

levels.name: Map it
levels.note: Explore and notice. No treatment goal.

levels.name: Stay where it resists
levels.note: Gentle sustained shift into the restricted direction.

loadAfter.name: Finding the deep abdominal layer
loadAfter.note: Cross-file reference.

evidence.grade: Undetermined. Grouped with manual myofascial approaches in reviews; no separate trial base for the self-administered version.
evidence.basis: Reviews of fascia-targeted manual work include superficial-layer techniques within the broader category but do not test them separately, and nothing I found evaluates self-applied skin gliding. So there is no grade, and none is invented. It earns a place on gentleness and information value, not on evidence.

items.name: The exhale you never finish
items.why: Most people who breathe badly are not failing to breathe in — they are failing to breathe out. A diaphragm that never returns to its resting dome position never gets a rest, and everything above and below it compensates. This is release by breathing, not by pressing.

fields.tool: Breath. Hands on the lower ribs to feel what is happening.
fields.release:
Lie on your back with knees bent, hands on the sides of your lower ribs. Breathe out — and then keep going, gently, past where you would normally stop, letting the ribs draw down and in. Not forcing, not squeezing hard: just continuing. Pause for a moment at the bottom without gasping. Then let the in-breath come by itself, and let it widen the ribs sideways under your hands rather than lifting your chest.

The long out-breath is the release. The in-breath just has to be allowed.
fields.notice: Whether your ribs actually come down at the end of the out-breath or stay lifted. Whether the in-breath comes in sideways or upwards. Whether your shoulders rise — if they do, the neck is doing the breathing, which is what the scalene item elsewhere in this library is about.
fields.careful: Do not force the exhale hard or hold your breath at the bottom. Lightheadedness means it is too much — smaller and slower. If you have a respiratory condition, keep this comfortable and take breathing work to your clinician.
fields.load: The deep abdominal connection item — the muscles that manage the pressure inside the container the diaphragm sits on top of.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: some people find slow deep breathing provokes lightheadedness. Lying down, smaller breaths, stop if it builds. PEM/pacing: very low cost.

levels.name: Hands on ribs, just notice
levels.note: Where does the breath go? No changing anything yet.

levels.name: Extend the exhale
levels.note: Gently continue past the usual stopping point.

levels.name: Side-lying and seated
levels.note: Same thing in positions where gravity loads the ribs differently. Seated is the one that transfers to your day.

loadAfter.name: Finding the deep abdominal layer

evidence.grade: Expert consensus and small clinical series for down-training overactive muscle; not established as a strengthening method.
evidence.basis: For the high-tone pelvic floor specifically, expert consensus and treatment algorithms place relaxation-focused work — diaphragmatic breathing, paced exhale, graded desensitisation — as a first-line element, supported by pilot studies and clinical series rather than large trials. A separate and important finding: breathing-based approaches used alone are not effective for pelvic floor strengthening. Down-training and strengthening are different jobs and this family does the first one.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Distinct from the imported 'Under the rib margin' card, which is manual work on the rib margin; this is the breath-side approach to the same structure.

items.name: The fingers of muscle along your side ribs
items.why: A muscle that runs from the inner edge of the shoulder blade, around the ribs, and attaches to the side of the ribcage in a row of finger-like slips. It holds the shoulder blade against your back — and it is also a breathing muscle, which is why it turns up in this library twice over.

fields.tool: A ball, side-lying, or just your opposite hand while seated.
fields.release:
Lie on your side with the arm overhead, and place a ball on the side of your ribcage a few inches below the armpit, in the row where you can feel the slips of muscle running forward between the ribs. Roll slowly along the row and hold where it bites. Seated version: reach across with the opposite hand and press flat fingertips into the same area.

Then breathe into the side under the pressure, so the ribs widen against it.
fields.notice: Whether the ribs move at all under your hand when you breathe. Whether one side is stiffer. Whether pushing your arm forward — reaching, not shrugging — is something you can produce cleanly.
fields.careful: On the ribs, not into the soft area below them. Light pressure — the ribs are close to the surface here. Not directly on the side of the breast tissue.
fields.load: Reaching — pushing the arm forward while keeping the blade wrapped around the ribs — and breathing wide into that side.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: a shoulder blade that wings away from the ribs is common with hypermobility, and this muscle is often part of the story. Release plus reaching work, not release alone.

levels.name: Side-lying with a ball
levels.note: More pressure, with breathing into the side.

loadAfter.name: Reaching — the shoulder blade wrapping the ribs

items.name: The front corner of the hip — and why rolling the IT band doesn't do what you were told
items.why: The thick band down the outside of the thigh is famously rolled and famously painful to roll. It is also a sheet of dense fibrous tissue anchored to bone at both ends. This item goes after the muscle that tensions it instead, which is a small one at the front corner of the hip that almost nobody has heard of.
items.equipment: A ball and a wall, or a roller

fields.tool: A ball against a wall for the muscle; a roller if you want to work the band itself, understanding what that does and doesn't do.
fields.release:
The muscle: find the front corner of your pelvis — the bony point at the front of the hip bone. Move a couple of inches down and slightly outward and you are on a small muscle that runs into the top of the band. Standing side-on to a wall, put a ball there, lean in, and hold. It is often surprisingly tender for its size.

The band itself: you can roll it, and it will hurt, and it will feel different afterward. What it will not do is get longer — the band is dense fibrous tissue anchored to bone at both ends, and the forces needed to deform it meaningfully are not available to a foam roller. If rolling it makes the outside of your thigh feel better, that is a real effect and a nervous-system one. Just do not expect it to change the band's length, and do not conclude that more pain means more result.
fields.notice: How much more tender the small muscle at the corner of the hip is than the band below it. Whether the outside of the thigh feels tight on the side you stand on, or the side with the dropped hip.
fields.careful: Do not roll over the bony knob at the side of the hip. If the outside of your knee is the painful part, that is a different problem and grinding the band above it is not the answer.
fields.load: Side-of-hip strength, which is the actual fix: this small muscle overworks when the bigger stabilisers beside it are not doing their share.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this small muscle overworking is a classic pattern when a hip lacks passive support — it grips because something has to. Loading the side of the hip matters much more than releasing the band.

levels.name: Ball on the front corner of the hip
levels.note: The muscle, standing, controlled. This is the useful rung.

levels.name: Add hip movement
levels.note: Hold the ball and slowly swing the leg back and across.

levels.name: Roll the band, knowing what it does
levels.note: Optional, and honestly optional. Comfort and sensation change; length does not.

loadAfter.name: Side-lying leg raises — the side of the hip working

evidence.grade: Inherits the sustained-pressure grade for short-term effect. The specific claim that rolling lengthens the IT band is not supported.
evidence.basis: Rolling produces short-term comfort and range changes like any other self-myofascial work. The additional point this card makes — that the band is dense fibrous tissue anchored at both ends and is not meaningfully lengthened by rolling — is a mechanical argument that has been made in the biomechanics literature and is stated here because the opposite story is repeated everywhere. What rolling changes is how the area feels, which is worth having and is a different claim.

items.name: The front of the upper arm, and its tendon at the shoulder
items.why: The muscle at the front of the upper arm has a tendon that runs up into the shoulder joint through a groove in the bone. Front-of-shoulder ache is often attributed to the joint when the muscle below it is what has been working.

fields.tool: Fingers and thumb. This is a squeeze, not a press.
fields.release: Rest the arm so it is completely relaxed — on a table, or hanging. Take the muscle at the front of the upper arm in your opposite hand and squeeze it gently between fingers and thumb, working from just above the elbow up toward the shoulder. Near the top, the muscle narrows into a tendon that runs in a groove at the front of the upper arm bone; that area is often tender, and there it wants light contact only.
fields.notice: How much the muscle can be lifted away from the bone when the arm is genuinely relaxed — and how little when it isn't. Whether the top end is tender.
fields.careful: Light near the tendon at the top. Do not dig into the inner crease of the elbow, where vessels and nerves run close to the surface. If the front of your shoulder is painful with activity rather than just tender to touch, that is a clinician's question.
fields.load: Elbow and shoulder work through a controlled range, and — because this muscle also turns the forearm — slow palm-up and palm-down turning against light resistance.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: front-of-shoulder pain in a hypermobile shoulder can come from the joint rather than the muscle, and pressing the muscle harder will not tell you which. If the shoulder slips or catches, get it assessed rather than treating it as a tight muscle.

loadAfter.name: Elbow and forearm rotation under light load
loadAfter.note: Match at S5.

items.name: The inner thigh where it meets the pelvis
items.why: The inner thigh muscles attach to the front of the pelvis right beside the pelvic floor's own front attachments. They are frequently tight in people who grip through the pelvis, and they are reachable, which the floor is not.
items.equipment: A ball, or a rolled towel; a bolster or cushions

fields.tool: A ball under the inner thigh while lying face-down with that leg out to the side on a bolster, or seated with the ball between your inner thigh and the chair.
fields.release: Lying face down with one leg out to the side, knee bent, thigh supported on a cushion, place the ball under the inner thigh. Work slowly from just above the knee up toward the pelvis, stopping where it bites. Stop well short of the very top — the last stretch toward the groin has vessels and nerves in it and is not a self-treatment area. The seated version: ball between the inner thigh and the chair seat, pressing gently inward.
fields.notice: How far up the tenderness runs. Whether both sides match. Whether the inner thigh is one of the places you grip when you are stressed — for a lot of people it is, and they have never noticed.
fields.careful: Stay on the muscle of the thigh and stop before the crease of the groin. Pins and needles or shooting sensation down the leg means come off. Not over visible veins.
fields.load: Something that asks the inner thigh to work at length — a squeeze against a cushion, or a wide-stance movement — and the hip work that stops the adductors substituting for glutes.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: the face-down position takes the hip toward the end of its range; support the thigh well and keep the angle modest. Orthostatic: use the seated version.

levels.name: Seated, gentle
levels.note: Ball between inner thigh and chair. Fully under your control.

levels.name: Add the knee bending
levels.note: Hold the ball in place and slowly bend and straighten the knee. Pin-and-move.

items.name: The inside of the forearm, near the elbow
items.why: The gripping muscles. Anything you hold — a bag, a bar, a phone — loads these, and they rarely get anything back.
items.equipment: Thumb, or a ball against a desk

fields.tool: Your other thumb, or a ball on a table.
fields.release: Turn your forearm palm-up. Find the muscle mass just below the elbow crease on the little-finger side of centre. Press and hold, then work down the muscle.
fields.notice: Sensation can spread toward the wrist or into the palm. Make a fist while you press and you'll feel the muscle bunch under your finger.
fields.careful: Stay off the elbow crease itself, and off anything that pulses. Pins and needles into the fingers means move.
fields.load: Open the hand wide and hold; then wrist circles both directions.

levels.name: Press while gripping
levels.note: Hold pressure and slowly open and close your fist.

items.name: The jaw muscle in the cheek
items.why: One of the most consistently tender spots on people who hold tension, and one almost nobody has ever touched deliberately.

fields.tool: Two or three fingertips. Outside the mouth only.
fields.release: Clench your teeth lightly and feel the muscle bulge in your cheek, above the jaw angle. Unclench, then press into it with fingertips and hold. Work up and down its length.
fields.notice: Tenderness that spreads toward the teeth, the ear, or up the side of the head is the traditionally described pattern here. Notice too where your teeth sit when you are not thinking about it — they are meant to be slightly apart.
fields.careful: Outside the mouth only. Inside-the-mouth jaw work belongs to a dentist or a trained clinician, not to a self-care app. If your jaw clicks, locks, or has slipped out of place, keep pressure light and raise it with a clinician.
fields.load: Rest the tongue on the roof of the mouth with teeth slightly apart and lips closed — the resting position — then open and close the jaw slowly a few times, keeping it tracking straight.

levels.name: Press while opening
levels.note: Hold pressure and open the jaw slowly. More finding, same pressure.

evidence.grade: traditional claim, widely described
evidence.basis: Spread toward the teeth and ear is the pattern traditionally described for this muscle. Recorded as a claim.

items.name: The long ropes either side of the spine
items.why: The long muscles running the length of your back hold you upright against gravity all day. In anyone whose deep core is not participating, they do that job alone — which is why they are tight in the evening and why pressing them has never solved it.
items.equipment: A foam roller, or two balls in a sock

fields.tool: A roller across the back, or two balls in a sock so the spine sits in the gap between them.
fields.release: With a roller, work the upper and middle back only — lie with the roller across your back, hands supporting your head, and move slowly with pauses, keeping your ribs down rather than arching over it. For the low back, do not use a roller across the spine; use the two-ball setup instead, with the balls either side of the bony bumps, and let your weight settle without rolling.
fields.notice: Whether these muscles are working right now, sitting still. They should be quiet when you are supported. Whether your low back arches as soon as you are on the roller — a sign the front is not sharing.
fields.careful: Not on the bony bumps, and no rolling the low back across a roller — the low back has less bony protection and the roller forces it into extension. Support your head with your hands so the neck is not hanging back. Stop for anything sharp or shooting.
fields.load: The deep abdominal connection item. These muscles are tight because they are doing two jobs; the fix is the other job getting an owner.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: arching over a roller takes a mobile spine well past where the pressure is doing anything. Ribs down, small range, and treat it as pressure rather than as an extension stretch. Orthostatic: floor item; get up in stages, and the standing ball-against-a-wall version is a full substitute.

levels.name: Two balls, lying, no movement
levels.note: Weight settling, spine in the gap.

levels.name: Roller, upper and mid back
levels.note: Slow passes with pauses, ribs down.

levels.name: Roller with arms overhead
levels.note: Adds a stretch through the front. Only if the ribs stay down.

loadAfter.name: Finding the deep abdominal layer
loadAfter.note: Cross-file reference to release-pelvic-floor-deep-core.json.

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and recovery; no evidence of lasting tissue change.
evidence.basis: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis find rolling produces acute range-of-motion improvement without impairing strength, and shows some benefit for post-exercise soreness. Effects on measured tissue stiffness are small and short-lived, which again points at a nervous-system effect rather than a structural one.

items.name: The mound below the thumb
items.why: This muscle group works every time you grip, pinch, type, or hold a phone — which is most of the day.
items.equipment: Thumb, or a small ball against a desk

fields.tool: Your other thumb, or roll the mound on a small ball against a table.
fields.release: Press into the fleshy pad at the base of your thumb, on the palm side. Work it in strips from the wrist toward the thumb, pausing wherever it bites.
fields.notice: Tenderness here often shows up on the side you hold your phone with. Sensation can spread into the thumb itself or into the wrist.
fields.careful: Stay on the muscle pad, off the wrist crease — the nerve and vessels run there.
fields.load: Grip and release something soft ten times, then spread the fingers wide and hold.

levels.name: Ball on a desk
levels.note: More pressure, less thumb fatigue — and it frees the other hand.

items.name: The muscle down the front of the shin
items.why: The muscle just outside the shin bone lifts your foot with every step so your toes clear the ground. It is loaded every time you walk downhill or wear a stiff shoe, and it is almost never released — people work the calf and stop.

fields.tool: Knuckles or a ball while seated. Or kneeling with a ball under the shin, if that is comfortable.
fields.release: Sit and find the sharp front edge of your shin bone. The muscle sits just outside that edge — press there and lift your foot; you will feel it firm up under your fingers. Work down its length from just below the knee toward the ankle with knuckles or a ball, stopping where it bites.
fields.notice: How tender it is given how rarely it gets attention. Whether the top third near the knee is the worst part, which it usually is. Whether your foot lands quietly when you walk afterward.
fields.careful: Just outside the bone, not on it. If the shin bone itself is tender to press over a length of it, that is a different problem and it is not a release problem.
fields.load: Toe raises — lifting the front of the foot with the heel down — and slow controlled lowering of the foot when you walk, which is what this muscle actually does.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: seated item throughout, no floor transfer. Hypermobile: knuckles give you a finer pressure dial than kneeling on a ball.

levels.name: Add the foot movement
levels.note: Hold the contact and slowly point and lift the foot. Pin-and-move.

loadAfter.name: Toe raises — lifting the front of the foot
loadAfter.note: The imported 'Toe control' card may cover this. Match at S5.

items.name: The neck — what's in there, and where not to press
items.why: Read this before any neck item. The neck is the one region in this library where pressing in the wrong place is not just unproductive — it is the reason the app teaches the map before the technique.

fields.tool: Nothing. This one is reading and feeling.
fields.release:
Three zones, and they behave completely differently.

**The back — safe.** The column of muscle either side of the bony bumps down the middle of the back of your neck, and the ridge at the base of the skull. Firm muscle over bone. This is where nearly all safe neck release happens.

**The top of the shoulder and the inner edge of the shoulder blade — safe.** Thick muscle, easy to reach, no vulnerable structures near the surface.

**The front and the sides — largely off limits.** Find your windpipe at the front of your throat. Move your fingers a little to the side and you will feel a pulse: that is the carotid artery, and you never press it. Behind that runs the rope-like muscle from behind your ear to your collarbone. Behind that again, in the hollow above the collarbone, sit the nerves and vessels heading into your arm. Pressure in this whole area is a clinician's business, not an app's, with the two carefully described exceptions in this module.
fields.notice: Where your pulse is on each side, so you know exactly what you are avoiding. And what the back of your neck feels like compared with the front — most people have never deliberately touched either.
fields.careful: Never both sides of the front of the neck at once. Never press on a pulse. Never press the soft hollow above the collarbone hard. Stop immediately for dizziness, visual change, ringing in the ears, a taste change, numbness into the arm, or nausea — those are not release sensations, they are signals to come off and, if they persist, to be seen.
fields.load: Nothing to load — this is a map, not a technique.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: cervical instability is more common in hypermobile people and it changes this whole module. Symptoms during or after neck work — headache at the base of the skull, visual disturbance, a feeling of the head being heavy or unsupported, symptoms brought on by looking up — belong in a clinician's hands before you do more neck work, not in an app. Orthostatic: several of these positions involve head movement and getting up and down; symptoms provoked by head position rather than by standing are a different problem than orthostatic dizziness — see the vestibular module's first card.

levels.name: Read it and find the landmarks on yourself
levels.note: Locate your own pulse, your own windpipe, your own bony ridge at the base of the skull. Then the rest of this module has somewhere to stand.

evidence.grade: Anatomy, not an intervention.
evidence.basis: The structures and their positions are standard anatomy, described here in the app's own words. Nothing here is a treatment claim.

items.name: The observation — was it the nerve or the muscle?
items.why: The most useful thing this module gives you is not looser hamstrings. It is an answer to a question nothing else in the library can answer: when something will not let go, is it the muscle or the nerve?

fields.tool: Nothing but attention, before and after.
fields.release:
Pick something you can repeat exactly — how far you can reach down your shin with a straight knee, or how far the arm goes before the pull starts. Note where it is. Do the glide for that limb, small. Note where it is again.

Then ask two questions.

**Did the sensation travel while you were doing it?** A moving pull is neural. A pull that stayed in one spot is muscular.

**Did the range change more than stretching has been changing it?** If months of stretching a hamstring has moved nothing and one careful set of glides moves something, the restriction was probably never in the muscle.
fields.notice: Also notice the next day, which matters more than the moment. Nerve tissue that was pushed too hard tends to be louder the following morning; a muscle that was worked tends not to be.
fields.careful: There is no number here and no pass mark, deliberately. This is one person, testing themselves, unblinded, on something that varies with time of day, temperature and how the week has gone — that setup cannot support a threshold, and any threshold this card offered you would be invented. It is a comparison with yourself, worth repeating a few times before you believe it, and worth mentioning to a clinician either way.
fields.load: n/a

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: range measures are unreliable in hypermobile bodies from day to day, which makes a single before-and-after even weaker than usual. Look for a pattern across several attempts, never a single result.

evidence.grade: Exploratory. A self-administered observation, not a validated test.
evidence.basis: Clinicians do distinguish neural from musculoskeletal restriction using structured neurodynamic examination, which involves a trained examiner controlling the limb and interpreting the response. This card is not that, and does not claim to be. It is a structured way to notice something and take it to someone who can examine it. No threshold is offered because none would be defensible.

items.name: The outer edge of the palm
items.why: The pinky-side pad takes the load every time you rest your hand on a desk, a mouse, or a steering wheel.

fields.tool: Your other thumb, or a ball against a table.
fields.release: Press into the pad running along the little-finger side of your palm, from the wrist out toward the base of the pinky. Slow strips, pausing where it bites.
fields.notice: Often tender on the hand you lean on. Compare to the other side.
fields.careful: Ease off if you get pins and needles into the ring or little finger — a nerve runs near the wrist on this side.
fields.load: Spread all five fingers wide, hold, then make a fist. Three or four times.

items.name: The outside of the forearm, near the elbow
items.why: These muscles hold your wrist steady all day while your fingers do the work. They are a common source of elbow and hand complaints that have nothing wrong with the elbow itself.
items.equipment: Thumb, knuckles, or a ball against a desk

fields.tool: The thumb of your other hand, your knuckles, or a ball on a table.
fields.release: Rest your forearm palm-down. Find the muscle mass on the thumb side, just below the elbow crease — it bulges when you lift your hand at the wrist. Press into it and hold. Work down the muscle a few centimetres at a time.
fields.notice: Sensation often spreads toward the outside of the elbow or into the back of the hand. Lifting your wrist while you press makes the muscle move under your finger, which helps you tell muscle from bone.
fields.careful: Off the bony point of the elbow. Sharp pain right on that bone is a different problem and not a pressure target.
fields.load: Afterward, make slow wrist circles both directions, then press your palm flat on a table and lean gently to open the front of the forearm.

levels.name: Press while moving
levels.note: Hold pressure and slowly lift and lower your wrist. The moving version usually finds more than the still one.

evidence.grade: traditional claim, widely described
evidence.basis: Spread toward the outer elbow and back of the hand is the traditionally described pattern for this muscle group.

items.name: The outside of the lower leg
items.why: The muscles running down the outside of the lower leg stop your ankle rolling outward. Anyone who has sprained an ankle, walks on uneven ground, or has unstable ankles has been leaning on them heavily — and they are on nobody's list.

fields.tool: A ball while seated, or side-lying on a roller.
fields.release: Find the thin bone running down the outside of your lower leg — you can feel its head just below and behind the outside of the knee, and its bottom end as the bump on the outside of the ankle. The muscles sit on and just behind that bone through the middle of the leg. Work down that line with a ball, stopping where it bites. Their tendons run behind the outer ankle bump — light contact there only.
fields.notice: Whether this side is much more tender than the calf. Whether you have a history of rolling that ankle. Whether the outer edge of your shoe wears faster.
fields.careful: Just below the head of that outer bone near the knee, a nerve runs close to the surface and around it — do not press hard there, and numbness or a foot that feels weak afterward means you were on it. Stay lower down the leg.
fields.load: Turning the sole of the foot outward against resistance, and single-leg balance — this pair of muscles is a major ankle stabiliser and it responds better to being asked to work than to being pressed.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: unstable ankles are common, and these muscles are the active defence against rolling one. Release plus loading, and if your ankle gives way, earn the balance rungs rather than skipping to unstable surfaces. Orthostatic: seated version needs no floor.

levels.name: Add the foot turning
levels.note: Hold contact and slowly turn the sole out and in.

loadAfter.name: Turning the foot outward against a band, and single-leg balance

items.name: The pelvic floor — and why 'just do kegels' is often the wrong advice
items.why: Read this before anything else in this section. There are two opposite problems here and the same advice makes one of them worse.

fields.tool: Nothing. Reading and noticing.
fields.release:
A hammock of muscle slung across the base of your pelvis, front to back and side to side. It closes what needs closing, supports what sits above it, and — the part almost nobody is told — it moves with every breath. Breathe in, the diaphragm drops and the floor drops with it. Breathe out, both come back up. It is not a static shelf; it is the bottom of a moving container.

**Two opposite problems.** A floor can be *underactive* — not producing enough, not holding when you cough or lift. Or it can be *overactive* — holding constantly, never fully releasing, tired from never being off. Both can cause leaking. Both can cause a heavy or aching feeling. The symptoms overlap enough that you cannot reliably tell them apart from the outside, and the standard advice — squeeze more — helps the first and makes the second worse.

This is why the release section comes before any strengthening in this library, and why the honest recommendation for anyone with actual symptoms is a pelvic floor physiotherapist, who can assess which one you have instead of guessing.
fields.notice: Whether you can feel anything move down there when you breathe. Lie down, breathe slowly into your belly, and see whether anything at the base of the pelvis responds. Many people feel nothing at first — that is information, not failure. Notice too whether you are clenching right now, reading this. A lot of people are.
fields.careful: If you have leaking, pelvic pain, pain with sex, a feeling of heaviness or bulging, difficulty emptying, or symptoms after childbirth or surgery — those are reasons to see a pelvic floor physiotherapist, not reasons to work harder from an app. This section is not a substitute for that assessment and does not claim to be.
fields.load: Nothing to load yet. Read first.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: pelvic floor symptoms are more common with hypermobility, and both directions occur — connective tissue that gives more easily can mean less passive support, and muscles that compensate by gripping constantly. That combination is exactly the one where guessing goes wrong, so the case for an assessment rather than self-direction is stronger for you, not weaker.

levels.name: Read it, and notice whether anything moves with your breath
levels.note: That single observation is the whole first rung.

evidence.grade: The anatomy and the breath relationship are established. The two-problems framing reflects current clinical practice.
evidence.basis: Coordinated movement between the diaphragm and pelvic floor with breathing is well described. That overactive and underactive pelvic floors both exist, present with overlapping symptoms, and call for different management is standard clinical understanding, with treatment algorithms placing relaxation-focused work first for the high-tone presentation. Nothing here is a claim about any individual's floor.

items.name: The rope down the front of the neck
items.why: The muscle from behind the ear to the collarbone turns your head and, in a forward-head posture, works constantly to keep your eyes level. It is a common source of headache-like sensation, dizziness and ear symptoms — and it is one of the few front-of-neck structures that can be worked safely, because you can lift it away from everything else.

fields.tool: Thumb and index finger, pinching. Never a flat press.
fields.release: Turn your head away from the side you are working and the rope stands up clearly. Take it between finger and thumb and lift it away from the neck — it will come, and that lifting is what makes this safe, because everything you must avoid stays behind. Turn your head back to neutral so the muscle goes slack in your fingers. Then squeeze gently and hold, working slowly along its length from behind the ear down toward the collarbone.
fields.notice: Sensation into the forehead, behind the eye, into the ear or across the temple is what is traditionally described here — written as a claim. Whether one side is much thicker or tighter. Whether it is already standing out when your head is neutral, which it should not be.
fields.careful: One side only, ever, and only the muscle you have picked up between your fingers. If you cannot lift it clear, do not press. Never press flat into the front of the neck. Come off immediately for dizziness, nausea, visual change, ringing in the ears, or a racing heart. If you have carotid disease, a history of stroke or TIA, or have been told to avoid pressure on your neck, this item is not for you.
fields.load: Chin nods, and — more to the point — getting your head back over your shoulders during the day, which is what this muscle is compensating for.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: neck instability changes the picture here; if you have upper-neck symptoms, take this to a clinician instead. Orthostatic: pressure anywhere near the front of the neck deserves extra caution if your blood pressure is already unstable, and the sensory receptors that read blood pressure sit in this region. Sit or lie, keep it brief, stop for any lightheadedness. If you are unsure, this is a reasonable item to simply skip — the library has other doors.

levels.name: Find it and lift it
levels.note: Locating and lifting the muscle, no squeeze. Learning the anatomy on yourself is a legitimate whole session here.

items.name: The shoulder cap — all three parts of it
items.why: The muscle capping your shoulder has a front, a middle and a back, and they do opposite jobs. People roll the outside of the shoulder and miss two thirds of it — usually including the part that is actually complaining.
items.equipment: A ball, or your opposite hand

fields.tool: A ball against a wall, or squeeze it in your opposite hand.
fields.release:
Three passes. **Front:** the part in front of the shoulder joint, below the outer collarbone. **Middle:** the outside cap, straight out from the joint. **Back:** the part behind the joint, easiest to reach by squeezing between fingers and thumb, or with a ball against a wall while you face away.

On each, find tenderness and hold. The back is the one most people have never touched and the one most likely to be tender in anyone who works at a desk.
fields.notice: Which of the three is loudest. Whether it matches the direction your arm struggles with — the front for reaching back, the back for reaching across.
fields.careful: Muscle, not the point of the shoulder joint itself. Come off for anything sharp or catching in the joint.
fields.load: Arm work in the direction the released part resists, at a range you control.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: if your shoulder slips or feels unstable, the shoulder cap may be doing stabilising work that the cuff underneath is not — release it and give the job back, or it will simply grip again.

levels.name: Hand squeeze, all three parts
levels.note: No equipment, anywhere. Learn the three parts on yourself.

levels.name: Pressure while the arm moves
levels.note: Hold and move the arm through the range that part controls.

items.name: The side of the hip
items.why: The muscles on the side of the hip stop your pelvis dropping every time you stand on one leg — which is every step you take. They are a different target from the big muscle at the back of the hip, and they are reached from a different angle.
items.equipment: A ball and a wall, or a foam roller

fields.tool: A ball against a wall standing, or side-lying on a roller.
fields.release: Find the bony point on the side of your hip — the wide knob you can feel through the flesh. The muscles you want sit above and behind it, in the fan between that knob and the rim of the pelvis. Standing side-on to a wall, place a ball there and lean in. Hunt slowly through the fan; there are usually two or three distinct spots.
fields.notice: Sensation spreading down the outside of the thigh or into the low back is the pattern traditionally described here — worth noting because it means side-of-hip tenderness can present as a low back complaint. Whether it is worse on the side you stand on, or the side you sleep on.
fields.careful: On the muscle above and behind the bony knob, not on the knob itself — pressing directly on that point is uncomfortable and unproductive, and there is a fluid sac there that does not appreciate it. If pressing the point itself is sharply painful, that is worth mentioning to a clinician.
fields.load: Side-lying leg work and single-leg standing. This region is nearly always weak as well as tender, and releasing it without loading it just makes it a weaker tender region.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: standing against a wall gives you a pressure dial that side-lying on a roller does not, and this area bruises. Also, this muscle group is a major stabiliser of a hip that has less passive support than average — the load partner is doing more work for you than the release is.

levels.name: Add the leg movement
levels.note: Hold the ball and slowly swing the leg forward and back, letting the tissue move underneath.

items.name: The side of the neck — the careful one
items.why: The muscles running down the side of the neck to the first ribs lift the ribs with every breath. In anyone who breathes into their chest rather than their belly, they have been doing a job meant for the diaphragm — for years. Included because they matter, written carefully because of what runs between them.

fields.tool: Flat fingertips. No ball, no tool, no thumb driving in. Nothing that concentrates force.
fields.release: First find the rope-like muscle that runs from behind your ear down to your collarbone — turn your head hard to one side and it stands out. The muscles this item targets sit just behind it. Place flat fingertips there, behind that rope and above the collarbone, with the lightest contact that lets you feel muscle. Then simply breathe: slow breaths in through the nose, letting the belly move, and on each out-breath let the area under your fingers soften. You are monitoring and inviting, not pressing.
fields.notice: Whether this area tightens when you breathe in. It should barely move during quiet breathing — if it lifts noticeably with every breath, your ribs are being pulled up by your neck, and the real fix is the diaphragm, not this muscle.
fields.careful: This is the most restricted item in the library. Flat fingertips only, one side at a time, feather pressure, short. Never press into the hollow above the collarbone. Any tingling, numbness, heaviness or coldness into the arm or hand means come off immediately — the nerves and vessels for the whole arm pass right here. Dizziness or visual change is also a stop. If you have symptoms into your arm or hand at all, this item is a clinician's territory and not yours.
fields.load: The pairing here is not strength — it is diaphragmatic breathing. This muscle stops overworking when something else does the breathing.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: a lax shoulder girdle that hangs low can crowd this space, and symptoms into the arm are more likely rather than less. If you get them, this item is out for you until a clinician has looked. Orthostatic: sit or lie for this one.

levels.name: Contact and breathe
levels.note: Monitoring only, no pressure worth the name. This may be the only rung you ever need.

levels.note: Slightly more, still flat fingertips, still short.
