items.name: The side of the trunk, between ribs and hip
items.why: The gap between the bottom rib and the top of the pelvis is spanned entirely by muscle. It gets short in anyone who sits leaning to one side, carries on one hip, or has been guarding a painful area — and it pulls the ribcage down toward the pelvis on that side, which is a breathing problem as much as a movement one.
items.equipment: A foam roller or ball; a cushion

fields.tool: A foam roller or a ball, lying on your side.
fields.release: Lie on your side with the roller under the gap between your bottom rib and the top of your pelvis, propped on your forearm. Move slowly and cover the area rather than rolling back and forth. This is soft tissue over no bone — go lighter than you would on a thigh. Then take the pressure and breathe into the side under it: the ribs widening against the roller is the release.
fields.notice: How big the gap is on each side. Whether one side is shorter. Whether you can breathe into the side that is under pressure, or whether the breath refuses to go there.
fields.careful: This region has no bony protection over the kidney area, so lighter than elsewhere and never a hard ball driven in. Stop for any deep ache that is not muscular in character. Not immediately after eating.
fields.load: Side-lying work that asks these muscles to hold — and, more importantly, breathing into the side you just opened.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: light pressure, and be aware that side-lying propped on a forearm loads a shoulder that may not enjoy it — use a cushion under the ribs and less prop. Orthostatic: floor position, get up slowly.

levels.name: Roller with breathing
levels.note: Broader contact, breathing into the side under pressure.

levels.name: Add the reach
levels.note: Hold the pressure and reach the top arm overhead, lengthening the side. Pin-and-move.

loadAfter.name: Finding the deep abdominal layer

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: The skin over the back of the neck
items.why: The gentlest neck item there is. Nothing is pressed at all. For a neck that will not tolerate contact, or for a day when nothing else is available.

fields.tool: Your fingers.
fields.release: Reach behind your neck and pick up a fold of skin between fingers and thumb — just the skin and the loose layer under it, not the muscle. Lift it slightly and roll it slowly between your fingers, or place a flat hand and move the skin over what lies beneath without sliding across it. Work across the back of the neck and out over the top of the shoulders, noticing where it lifts easily and where it feels thick or stuck.
fields.notice: Where it moves and where it doesn't, and whether the two sides differ. Places that feel stuck are often nowhere near where you would have pressed. This is as much a map as a treatment.
fields.careful: No pinching hard, no dragging across dry skin. Back and sides only; not the front of the throat. Comfortable throughout.
fields.load: Move the neck normally afterward — a few slow turns and tips through your comfortable range.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: skin that stretches further than average is part of the picture, so compare one side of your own neck to the other rather than to any standard. Do not lift to the limit of what the skin will do. PEM/pacing: about as close to free as an item in this library gets.

levels.name: Map it
levels.note: Explore and notice. No treatment goal at this rung.

levels.name: Stay where it resists
levels.note: Gentle sustained shift into the direction that does not give.

loadAfter.name: Chin nods — the front of the neck

evidence.grade: Undetermined. Grouped with manual myofascial approaches in reviews; no separate trial base for the self-administered version.
evidence.basis: Reviews of fascia-targeted manual work include superficial-layer techniques within the broader category but do not test them separately, and nothing I found evaluates self-applied skin gliding. So there is no grade, and none is invented. It earns a place on gentleness and information value, not on evidence.

items.name: The small muscles right beside the spine
items.why: Deep to the long back muscles sit short ones spanning only a segment or two. They stabilise individual joints rather than moving the trunk, and they are a different target from the big ropes a foam roller reaches.
items.equipment: A ball, or two balls in a sock

fields.tool: One ball, or two in a sock so the spine sits in the gap between them.
fields.release: Lying on your back, place the ball just beside the spine in the low back — in the groove between the bony bumps and the thick rope of muscle, not on the bumps and not out on the rope. Let your weight settle. Then, keeping the contact, do a very small pelvic tilt — flattening and arching the low back a fraction. The tissue moves under the ball. Work a few spots up and down.
fields.notice: That the tenderness is often at one specific level rather than spread out. Whether the small tilt is easy or whether your whole trunk has to move to produce it — a low back that can only move in one piece is the finding.
fields.careful: Beside the spine, never on the bony bumps. Light pressure — this is deep tissue and pressing hard reaches it no better. Numbness or shooting sensation into the leg means come off. Not over an area of unexplained pain or after a recent back injury without a clinician's word.
fields.load: Small, controlled back movements under your own power — segmental tilts and cat-cow-style movement, and the deep abdominal connection so front and back share the job.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: small movements only, and stop short of end range in either direction. A hypermobile low back does not need more range; it needs control of the range it has, which is what the load partner is for. Orthostatic: floor item; get up in stages.

levels.name: Static ball
levels.note: Find it and hold, no movement.

levels.name: Standing against a wall
levels.note: Same targets, upright, pressure under your control. Easier on the neck and easier to get out of.

loadAfter.name: Finding the deep abdominal layer

evidence.grade: Undetermined for the self-administered form; clinician-delivered versions have small trials against comparators.
evidence.basis: Clinician-applied pin-and-stretch approaches have been compared against other manual techniques in small trials with mixed results. Nothing I found tests the self-administered version specifically. The rationale — that tissue moving under a fixed contact restores glide between layers — is a mechanism story, not a demonstrated finding, and is written here as such.

items.name: The temple
items.why: A closing muscle for the jaw that most people have never thought of as a muscle at all.

fields.tool: Fingertips.
fields.release: Put your fingers flat on your temple and clench lightly — you will feel it move. Unclench, then press with small circles or steady holds across the whole fan-shaped area above and in front of the ear.
fields.notice: Sensation spreading toward the temple, behind the eye, or into the upper teeth is traditionally described here.
fields.careful: Moderate pressure. If you get headaches, work lighter and shorter and see whether it settles or provokes.
fields.load: Same as the cheek: resting jaw position, then slow open and close.

items.name: The temple and the side of the head — light gliding
items.why: A gentler alternative to pressing the temple, for people who get headaches and find that direct pressure there provokes rather than relieves. Same target, different family.

fields.tool: Flat fingers or a flat palm.
fields.release: Place a flat hand on the side of your head above and in front of the ear. Rather than pressing in, move the scalp itself over the bone underneath — small slow shifts forward and back, up and down. Then work outward across the whole fan-shaped area. Clench lightly once to feel where the muscle is, then unclench and continue.
fields.notice: Whether the scalp moves freely over the bone or feels tethered, and whether the two sides differ. Whether this is more or less provoking than direct pressure — that comparison is worth making deliberately once.
fields.careful: Light. If you get headaches, keep it short the first few times and notice what happens over the following hours rather than deciding immediately.
fields.load: Jaw resting position and slow tracking.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: nothing specific to this item beyond the general jaw cautions.

levels.name: Gliding only
levels.note: No pressure into the tissue at all.

levels.name: Gliding plus gentle sustained contact
levels.note: Add a light hold where the scalp feels tethered.

loadAfter.name: Jaw resting position and straight tracking

evidence.grade: Undetermined. Grouped with manual myofascial approaches in reviews; no separate trial base for the self-administered version.
evidence.basis: Reviews of fascia-targeted manual work include superficial-layer techniques within the broader category but do not test them separately, and nothing I found evaluates self-applied skin gliding. So there is no grade, and none is invented. It earns a place on gentleness and information value, not on evidence.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Sibling to the fingertip-pressure temple item in the tender-point entry set, for people who don't tolerate that one.

items.name: The web of the thumb
items.why: The most reliable find on most people. If you have never located a tender point before, start here — it usually takes under a minute.

fields.tool: The thumb and index finger of your other hand.
fields.release: Pinch the fleshy web between your thumb and index finger, squeezing from both sides rather than pressing straight down. Work slowly toward the bone of the index finger — the tender spot usually sits closer to that side than to the middle. Hold what you find.
fields.notice: Most people are surprised by how tender this is. Sensation often spreads into the thumb or up the back of the hand. Compare sides — one is usually worse, and that difference is your first real finding.
fields.careful: Firm squeeze, not a crush. Coming off with a bruise means it was too hard.
fields.load: Afterward, open and close your hand fully several times, spread the fingers wide, and make a real fist. Use what you opened.

levels.name: Find it
levels.note: Just locate it and hold. 30–60 seconds a side.

levels.name: Work the area
levels.note: Once you know where it is, work slowly across the whole web rather than parking on one spot.

evidence.grade: traditional claim, widely described
evidence.basis: Spread into the thumb and hand is the pattern traditionally described for this area. Recorded as a claim; your own experience is the better evidence here.

items.name: Thoracic Spine Extension (Roller)
items.why: Roller under upper back, extend over it, open chest

fields.release: Place the foam roller under your upper back, perpendicular to your spine. Support your head with your hands and keep your hips on the floor. Extend your upper back over the roller, letting your chest open up toward the ceiling. Move the roller to different positions along your upper back to target different segments. This counteracts the hunched posture from sitting.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: thoracic spine.

items.name: Thoracic Spine Rotation
items.why: Lock hips, rotate through upper back only, reach and open

fields.release: Lie on your side with knees bent and stacked. Keeping your hips locked in place, rotate your upper back to open your top arm toward the floor on the other side. Return to the starting position. The key is isolating the rotation to your thoracic spine while your hips stay still. This is especially beneficial if you sit for long periods.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: thoracic spine, obliques.

levels.name: Open Book
levels.note: Lying on side, open top arm

items.name: Thread the Needle
items.why: On all fours, reach one arm under body and rotate, then open up

fields.release: Start on all fours. Reach one arm under your body and across to the other side, letting your shoulder and head rest on the floor as you rotate. Then reverse the motion and open that arm up toward the ceiling, rotating your thoracic spine in the opposite direction. Move slowly and breathe into the stretch. Alternate sides.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: thoracic spine, shoulders.

items.name: Tibialis Raise
items.why: Lean back against wall, lift toes toward shins

fields.release: Lean your back against a wall with your feet about a foot away from the wall. Lift your toes and the balls of your feet off the ground toward your shins, keeping your heels on the floor. Lower with control. This strengthens the tibialis anterior muscle on the front of the shin, which is important for ankle stability and preventing shin splints.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: tibialis anterior.

levels.name: Single-Leg
levels.note: One foot at a time for ankle strength

items.name: Toe control
items.dose: Daily. It takes two minutes and you can do it sitting down.
items.why: Proprioception training — the direct route to knowing where your body is and what it is doing.

fields.tool: Bare feet, a towel
fields.release: TOE SPREAD — spread all your toes apart without curling them. Hold 5 seconds. ×10. BIG TOE LIFT — press the other four toes down and lift only the big toe. Then reverse: big toe down, lift the other four. TOWEL SCRUNCH — towel flat on the floor, use your toes to drag it toward you. ×10 each foot. The lifts will be close to impossible at first. That is the point — it is a connection you do not have yet.
fields.notice: Individual toe control is a direct readout of the nerve pathway you are trying to rebuild. Watching it go from impossible to easy is the clearest progress marker in this entire document.
fields.careful: Cramping is common at first. Stop, stretch the foot out, come back tomorrow.

items.name: Toes-to-Bar
items.why: Controlled raise, touch toes to bar, no excessive swing

fields.release: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms fully extended. Engage your core and raise your legs, keeping them as straight as possible, until your toes touch the bar. Lower with control, minimizing any swing. This is an advanced core exercise; begin with knee raises or straight-leg raises to build the necessary strength and control.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: abs, hip flexors.

items.name: Tongue posture
items.dose: All day, as a default you keep returning to.
items.why: Myofunctional therapy. Real evidence for mild apnea and upper-airway resistance, and rarely offered.

fields.tool: None
fields.release: The whole tongue — not just the tip — suctioned flat against the roof of the mouth. Tip rests on the ridge just BEHIND your top front teeth, not on the teeth themselves. Lips sealed, teeth slightly apart, breathing through the nose. That is the resting position. Everything else in this section is training you toward holding it without thinking about it.
fields.notice: You already use this deliberately as an airway compensation. The goal is making it automatic, including while asleep, which is where it would actually help the collapse.
fields.careful: Jaw tension means you are pressing with the jaw instead of the tongue. Teeth stay apart.

items.name: Tongue press & suction
items.dose: 5–10 minutes daily, split however suits you. Give it 2–3 months before judging whether it works.
items.why: Myofunctional therapy. Real evidence for mild apnea and upper-airway resistance, and rarely offered.

fields.tool: None
fields.release: PRESS — whole tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, push up hard. Hold 10 seconds. ×10. SUCTION HOLD — suction the whole tongue flat to the palate so it makes a vacuum. Keeping that seal, slowly open your jaw as wide as you can WITHOUT the tongue peeling off. Hold 5 seconds, then close. ×10. SLIDE — tip of the tongue on the ridge behind the top front teeth, then slide it backwards along the roof of the mouth as far as it will go. ×10. STRONG SWALLOW — anchor the tongue tip on that ridge and swallow, pressing the tongue up hard through the whole swallow. ×10.
fields.notice: Waking less dry-mouthed. Tongue posture starting to hold without attention. Effects on sleep take months, not days — this is the slowest-acting thing in this document and also one of the highest-value. Your tongue gets tired, which tells you it was weak.
fields.careful: Jaw fatigue is expected; jaw pain is not. If your jaw clicks, locks, or has a history of trouble, go easy on the wide-open suction hold and cut the range right back if the joint complains.

items.name: Top of the shoulder — ball against a wall
items.why: The muscle that runs from the base of your skull out to the tip of your shoulder is the one that lifts when you are braced, cold, concentrating, or on a phone call. On most people it has been quietly on for years.
items.equipment: A ball, and a wall or a doorframe

fields.tool: A ball trapped between your body and a wall. Standing means you control the pressure by how much you lean, which is a finer dial than lying on it.
fields.release: Put the ball on the slope between your neck and the point of your shoulder, and lean back into the wall. Turn slightly so the ball is on the thick part of the muscle, not on the bony ridge of your shoulder blade. Lean in until you find something tender, then stop moving and let your shoulder drop. Letting the shoulder drop is most of the work — pressing into a muscle that is still holding itself up achieves very little.
fields.notice: Whether your shoulder was already up before you started. Whether the tenderness runs the whole length of the slope or sits in one or two spots. Compare sides — the side you carry a bag on is usually the loud one.
fields.careful: Stay on the muscle slope. Do not let the ball creep forward onto the hollow above the collarbone, where the nerves to the arm run — tingling or electricity into the arm means come off immediately and move the ball backwards.
fields.load: This muscle is usually not weak so much as always on. The pairing is not to load it harder — it is to teach the muscles underneath the shoulder blade to take the job back.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: a shoulder that hangs from a lax joint gives this muscle a genuine holding job, and switching it off without giving the job to something else just makes it hold harder next time. The load partner matters more here than almost anywhere in this library.

levels.name: Light lean
levels.note: Barely leaning. Find where the muscle is before deciding how much pressure it wants.

levels.name: More lean, shoulder actively dropping
levels.note: Deeper pressure, and deliberately letting the shoulder fall away from the ear while you hold.

levels.name: Pressure while the arm moves
levels.note: Hold the lean and slowly raise and lower the arm on that side. See the pin-and-move guide.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Top of the shoulder — contract and let go
items.why: No hands, no ball, and it builds a small amount of control on the way through — which is the version to reach for if your neck does not like being pressed.

fields.tool: Your own muscle. Optionally a hand on your head, used as a rest, not a lever.
fields.release: Sit tall and let the shoulder on the working side drop. Tip your ear toward the opposite shoulder until you feel the first stretch down the side of your neck — the first stretch, not the biggest. Now gently shrug that shoulder up toward the ear against nothing but your own control, hold it lightly, then let it go completely on an out-breath and let the shoulder sink. Usually the tip goes a little further afterward. Repeat.
fields.notice: Whether the shoulder actually drops when you let go, or whether it stays up. A shoulder that will not come down when told to is the finding.
fields.careful: Do not pull your head down with your hand. This is a hypermobile-friendly item precisely because there is no external force on the neck, and adding one removes the reason it is here. Stop for any dizziness or visual change.
fields.load: Follow with the deep neck flexor nod — the front of the neck taking back the job of holding the head up.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is the neck release family with the best safety profile for you, because you never pull on the joint. Keep the head tip small; the goal is the release of the shrug, not the depth of the side bend.

levels.name: Shrug and release
levels.note: Head barely tipped. Learn what dropping the shoulder actually feels like.

levels.name: Several rounds
levels.note: Take up whatever slack appears after each release.

levels.name: Add the opposite side
levels.note: After releasing, actively hold the head in the new position without any hand help.

loadAfter.name: Chin nods — the front of the neck

evidence.grade: Established for acute range of motion; no better than other stretching methods; mechanism is largely increased tolerance to stretch.
evidence.basis: Meta-analysis across stretching types finds contract-relax, static and dynamic stretching all improve range of motion acutely and over training periods, with no significant difference between them. A 2025 meta-analysis of static stretching mechanisms across 65 studies found range gains track increased tolerance to the stretch far more than any change in muscle length or stiffness. So: it works, and it works by changing what you will allow, not by lengthening tissue.

items.name: Top of the shoulder — squeezing it in your hand
items.why: The no-equipment, anywhere version. You can do it at a desk, in a car park, in a waiting room, without anyone noticing.

fields.tool: Your opposite hand, reaching across.
fields.release: Reach across and take the slope of muscle between your neck and shoulder in your whole hand — thumb behind, fingers in front, and squeeze the muscle between them rather than digging fingertips down into it. The muscle is a sheet you can pick up; grabbing the sheet is safer and more effective than poking through it. Squeeze and hold, then move along its length.
fields.notice: That it lifts away from what is underneath — which tells you where the muscle actually is. Where along the length it is thickest and most tender.
fields.careful: Squeeze the muscle you have lifted; do not drive fingertips down into the hollow above the collarbone. Your reaching arm gets tired — swap or rest rather than pressing harder to make up for it.
fields.load: As above: give the job to the muscles under and around the shoulder blade.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: a gentle squeeze does not need to become a pinch, and this area bruises. Also worth noticing — reaching across holds your own shoulder in an end-range position while you work, so keep the reaching arm supported if it is a joint that complains.

levels.name: Whole-hand squeeze
levels.note: Broad, gentle, moving along the length.

levels.name: Squeeze and turn the head
levels.note: Hold the squeeze and slowly turn or tip your head away. Pin-and-move applied to a muscle you can hold in your hand.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Tracing a path with a laser
items.why: Trains steady, accurate control of where you are pointing — first with your hand, later with your head, which is where it becomes a neck position-sense drill.
items.equipment: Laser pointer (the head-mountable kind) and a winding line drawn on a wall

fields.tool: A laser pointer and a winding line on the wall — more a road than a maze.
fields.release: Stand facing the line and trace it end to end with the laser beam, keeping the dot on the line.
fields.notice: How far the dot strays, and whether you drift smoothly back or jerk back.
fields.careful: Rung 3 stacks a balance demand on a drill that can already make you dizzy. Do it near a counter. If your ankles are unstable, earn rung 2 first.

levels.name: Hand-held
levels.note: Hold the laser in your hand. This is where the clinic started — deliberately, to keep it light.

levels.name: Head-mounted
levels.note: Wear the laser. Now your neck aims the beam, not your hand. This is the version the tool is built for.

levels.name: On an unstable surface
levels.note: Head-mounted, standing on a wobble board or similar. Clinic-mentioned as the way to make it harder. No purchase needed — the boards are already on hand.

items.name: Turning the arm out, under control
items.why: The load partner for every rotator cuff and shoulder item here. The muscles that turn the arm outward are the ones that keep the head of the arm bone centred, and they are almost universally the weaker side of the pair — because nothing in a normal day asks for them.
items.equipment: None, or a light band; a rolled towel

fields.tool: A rolled towel tucked between your elbow and your side, and optionally a light band.
fields.release:
Elbow bent to a right angle and tucked against your side with the towel keeping it there. Keeping the elbow in contact, turn the forearm outward, away from your belly, as far as you can without the elbow drifting away from your body or your shoulder shrugging. Then slowly back. The towel is the honesty check — if it drops, something else took over.

With a band, the same movement against light resistance.
fields.notice: How small the range is when the elbow stays put. Whether the shoulder shrugs, which means the top of the shoulder has taken the job. Whether one side is much weaker.
fields.careful: Light resistance. This is a control exercise and heavy load defeats it. Any catching or pinching in the shoulder means reduce the range.
fields.load: This is the load.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this is one of the highest-value items in the shoulder module for you. Active support is what a lax shoulder needs. Light, controlled, frequent, and progress by adding hold time and steadiness rather than resistance.
items.dose: [undetermined] — reps, sets and resistance are a clinician's numbers. Worth asking for.

levels.name: No resistance, towel at the elbow
levels.note: Just the movement, clean. Finding it without the shrug is the rung.

levels.name: Light band
levels.note: Same movement, light resistance, elbow still pinned.

levels.name: Arm away from the side
levels.note: Elbow raised out to the side, same rotation. Harder and closer to how you use the shoulder.

evidence.grade: Established as standard shoulder rehabilitation content.
evidence.basis: Rotator cuff strengthening including external rotation is core content in shoulder rehabilitation with a large trial literature behind the general approach. Specific protocols vary and none is reproduced here.

items.authoringNote: Authored here as a load partner; may belong in the strength and activation file.

items.name: Two kinds of dizziness — which one is yours?
items.why: Read this before any drill in this section. Two very different things both get called dizziness, and the drills here are aimed at one of them.

fields.release:
Notice what brings yours on and what settles it.

The **standing** pattern: it arrives when you stand up, get worse the longer you stay upright, and eases when you sit or lie down. It often comes with a racing heart, greying vision, or heat. This is a blood-flow and blood-pressure pattern.

The **motion** pattern: it arrives when you turn your head, roll over in bed, look up, or walk down a busy aisle. Sitting still doesn't necessarily fix it, and standing up isn't what set it off. This is a balance-and-orientation pattern.
fields.notice: Which one describes yours — and be open to both. Having one does not protect you from the other; in people with orthostatic problems, motion-provoked dizziness turns out to be common too. The useful question is not which label fits but which of the two is happening in any given episode.
fields.careful: The drills in this section train the motion pattern. **They do not treat the standing pattern, and doing them standing can make it worse.** If yours is mostly the standing kind, do them seated, and take the standing pattern to a clinician — it has its own management and this isn't it.
fields.load: Whichever you have, tell your clinician which one it is and what provokes it. That sentence is worth more in a visit than a general report of dizziness.

levels.name: Read it
levels.note: Once. Come back if the pattern changes.

evidence.grade: established as a clinical distinction; the overlap between the two is well documented
evidence.basis: Orthostatic and vestibular causes of dizziness are separated routinely in clinical assessment. In people with orthostatic intolerance, vestibular symptoms are common rather than rare — in one clinic series nearly all reported unsteadiness and roughly half reported vertigo, and a majority were offered vestibular rehabilitation. Which is why this card teaches both/and rather than either/or.

items.name: Typewriter Pull-Up
items.why: Pull up, shift weight side to side at top

fields.release: Perform a pull-up with a wide grip. At the top, shift your body weight toward one hand while keeping the other arm extended along the bar, then slide across to the other side before lowering. This is an advanced exercise that builds unilateral pulling strength. Master standard wide-grip pull-ups before attempting.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: lats, biceps.

levels.name: Archer Pull-Up
levels.note: Pull to one hand, other arm straight

items.name: Ulnar glide — forearm on the desk
items.why: The same nerve with the elbow range taken out of it. This is the version for someone whose little finger goes numb at a keyboard and who cannot afford to provoke it during a working day.

fields.tool: The desk, taking the whole weight of the forearm.
fields.release:
Forearm flat on the desk, elbow bent, palm down.

Together: lift the hand at the wrist so the fingers come up and the little-finger edge of the hand leads, AND tilt your head away from that arm. Then reverse: let the hand settle, head back to centre.

The elbow angle does not change at all. That is the point of this version — the elbow is where this nerve gets provoked, and here it is parked.
fields.notice: Whether keeping the elbow still changes what you feel. If the desk version says nothing and the full version says a lot, the elbow is where your problem lives, and that is worth telling a clinician.
fields.careful: Small movements. If the little finger tingles, stop for the day. Do not compensate for the small range by doing more repetitions — that is the mistake this whole module warns about.
fields.load: Grip something for a few seconds, or press the fingertips into the desk one at a time.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: fingers that bend backward a long way will reach the end of the wrist movement without the nerve having moved much — lead with the edge of the hand rather than with the fingers.

loadAfter.name: Grip and hand work — legacy card, name to be resolved at S5

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.name: Ulnar glide — the little-finger side
items.why: The nerve behind the funny bone, which serves the little finger and half the ring finger. It is the one that complains after a long phone call, a night asleep with the arm curled, or a drive with the elbow on the door.

fields.tool: Nothing. Sitting or standing, whichever you can keep still in.
fields.release:
Start with the arm down by your side, palm forward, wrist relaxed.

Together: bend the elbow and bring the hand up toward the side of your face, palm turning to face you, wrist bending so the fingers point back over your shoulder — AND tilt your head away from that hand. Then reverse together: lower the hand back down to your side, straighten the elbow, relax the wrist, AND bring your head back to centre or a little toward the arm.

The hand does not have to reach your face. Most people should stop well short of it.
fields.notice: A sensation along the inside of the forearm and into the little finger, moving as the elbow bends. This is the drill that most often reproduces something in people who have not thought about this nerve before, which is exactly why the first attempt should be a quarter of the range.
fields.careful: This is the most provocative arm item in the module, because bending the elbow loads this nerve more than any other single movement. Quarter range on the first attempt, one side, one short set — then judge by the next day. Any tingling into the little finger means stop, not ease off.
fields.load: Open and close the hand a few times, then grip something — a rail, a mug — for a few seconds. The nerve serves the small muscles of the hand, and using them is the point.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: elbows that hyperextend give this drill a much bigger range at the bottom of the movement than it is meant to have; stop short of straight rather than resting at your end range. Orthostatic: do it seated the first few times.

levels.name: Elbow bending a quarter of the way, head still
levels.note: The starting version, and for many people the only one needed for a while.

levels.name: Elbow to halfway, small head tilt
levels.note: Add the neck once a day has passed with no increase in symptoms.

levels.name: Hand toward the face, head tilting away
levels.note: The full version. Still stops where symptoms would start.

loadAfter.name: Grip and hand work — legacy card, name to be resolved at S5

evidence.grade: Low to moderate, short-term, on limited-quality evidence — and the evidence is better for a clinician moving your limb than for you doing it at home. Strongest where symptoms travel down an arm from an irritated nerve in the neck; weakest, and in one good trial absent, as an add-on for mild carpal tunnel.
evidence.basis: An umbrella review pooling earlier meta-analyses reported a moderate effect on pain and a large one on disability, while rating the underlying quality as limited; a published re-analysis in the same journal showed the disability finding did not survive removing primary studies that had been counted more than once across the pooled reviews. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nerve-related neck and arm pain covering 20 randomised trials and 953 people found the clinician-applied cervical lateral glide reduced pain against no treatment, and by a smaller margin against other physiotherapy. Carpal tunnel is the weak spot: a randomised trial in 80 people with mild carpal tunnel found gliding exercises added nothing to a wrist splint alone, and a review of four trials found benefit only where gliding was combined with conventional treatment rather than used on its own. Slider-versus-tensioner comparisons contradict each other on which is better. The mechanism usually offered — freeing a nerve that has become stuck, or dispersing fluid inside it — has support for the movement itself on ultrasound imaging, but remains a hypothesis about why symptoms change rather than a demonstrated explanation. In the library because the drills are cheap, self-administrable, and diagnostically informative in a way few things are; graded honestly because most of the trial base is not the situation the app is in.

items.name: Under the chin — the floor of the mouth
items.why: The soft area between your chin and the front of your throat holds a set of small muscles that work every time you swallow, speak, or hold your jaw shut against gravity. Nobody thinks of it as a muscle group, and in people with a forward head or a clenching habit it is often quietly rigid.

fields.tool: One or two fingertips, flat, from underneath.
fields.release: Tip your head back very slightly so the area is accessible. Place flat fingertips in the soft triangle between the point of your chin and the top of your throat, close under the jawbone rather than down toward the throat. Gentle upward-and-inward contact against the underside of the jaw. Hold, and let the tongue go heavy. Then swallow once and feel everything move under your fingers.
fields.notice: Whether it is soft or firm at rest. Whether the tongue is pressing down rather than resting up. How much movement a single swallow produces.
fields.careful: Stay tucked up under the jawbone. Do not press down or back into the throat itself, and never press hard enough to affect swallowing or breathing. Under the jaw are salivary glands and lymph nodes; if you find a firm lump that is tender and new, that is something to have looked at rather than something to release. One side at a time if you prefer.
fields.load: Tongue to the roof of the mouth and hold — the direct opposite action, and the one that most people cannot do for long.

items.populationCareful: Orthostatic: tipping the head back can be provocative; do this seated with support, and only a slight tip. Hypermobile: keep the head tip minimal — this area is accessible without extending the neck much at all.

levels.name: Contact and notice
levels.note: Just feeling what is there at rest and during a swallow.

levels.name: Gentle sustained contact
levels.note: Light hold with the tongue deliberately heavy.

loadAfter.name: Jaw resting position and straight tracking

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.name: Under the collarbone — the small chest muscle
items.why: Underneath the big chest muscle sits a small one running from the ribs up to a hook of bone on the front of the shoulder blade. When it is short it pulls the whole shoulder blade forward and down over the ribs — which is most of what a rounded shoulder actually is, and it is a different muscle from the one a chest stretch reaches.
items.equipment: Fingertips, or a ball against a wall

fields.tool: Flat fingertips, or a ball against a doorframe.
fields.release: Find the bony point at the front of your shoulder, just below the outer end of the collarbone and slightly toward the armpit — a hard knob you can press. The muscle runs from there down and inward toward the ribs. Place flat fingertips just below and inside that knob, angled toward the ribs, and press gently while letting the shoulder drop back. Hold.
fields.notice: Whether your shoulder can drop back at all, or whether it sits forward and stays there. Whether it is tender on the side you sleep on or drive on.
fields.careful: Below and inside the bony point, angled toward the ribs, not up into the hollow above the collarbone where the nerves and vessels for the arm run. Tingling or numbness into the arm means come off immediately and reposition lower. Gentle.
fields.load: The muscles that pull the blade back and down — setting the blade — and time spent with the chest open rather than closed.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: this area is close to the space where nerves and vessels pass into the arm, and a low-hanging shoulder girdle crowds it further. Light and short, and any arm symptoms mean stop and ask a clinician.

levels.name: Fingertips, shoulder dropping back
levels.note: Gentle contact, and the shoulder letting go is most of the effect.

levels.name: Add slow arm movement
levels.note: Hold contact and slowly raise the arm out to the side and back down.

levels.name: Ball against a doorframe
levels.note: More pressure, hands free. Same careful field.

loadAfter.name: Setting the shoulder blade down and back
loadAfter.note: Cross-file reference to release-neck-jaw.json.

evidence.grade: Moderate for short-term range of motion and tenderness; mechanism uncertain; durable structural change unsupported.
evidence.basis: Self-myofascial release with balls and rollers reliably produces short-term range-of-motion gains without loss of muscle performance across several systematic reviews and an umbrella review. What it is doing is much less settled: current reading favours a neural effect — mechanoreceptor input raising stretch tolerance and lowering perceived tightness — rather than the tissue being physically remodelled by a ball. The popular 'breaking up adhesions' story is not what the evidence supports, and this library does not tell it.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Distinct target from the imported 'Chest & front of shoulder' card, which addresses the large chest muscle.

items.name: Under the rib margin
items.equipment: Your fingers. There is no tool for this
items.dose: 3 breaths per spot, 4–5 spots per side. Every other day.
items.why: This works what pulls on the rib cage, not the cage itself.

fields.tool: Your fingers. There is no tool for this
fields.release: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Let your belly go completely soft. Find the bottom edge of your rib cage at the front, starting near the centre just below the breastbone. Hook your fingertips gently just UNDER the rib margin, pointing up and in, toward your head. Exhale slowly. As you exhale, let your fingers sink slightly further under the edge. Hold there as you inhale. Do not dig and do not push against the breath. 3 breaths. Move about an inch outward along the rib arch and repeat. Work from the centre out to the side, then do the other side.
fields.notice: Belly breath comes without effort afterwards. This is the most direct access you have to the muscle itself, and the psoas attaches into the same lumbar fascia — your best release and your main symptom are literally continuous tissue. Deep and uncomfortable, occasionally oddly emotional. It should never be sharp.
fields.careful: Not on a full stomach. Gentle — you are reaching under the ribs near organs, and patience works far better than pressure. Sharp pain means stop.

items.name: Uppercut
items.why: Drop slightly, drive fist upward with legs and hips

fields.release: From your boxing stance, bend your knees slightly to dip, then drive your fist upward in a compact vertical arc, rotating your hips and driving up through your legs. Keep the punching arm close to your body and your other hand up guarding your chin. The power comes from your legs and hip rotation, not just your arm.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: shoulders, biceps, core.

items.name: Vertical Jump Practice
items.why: Dip and drive arms, jump as high as possible, reach at peak

fields.release: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Quickly dip into a quarter squat while swinging your arms back, then explosively jump as high as possible, swinging your arms upward and reaching at the peak. Land softly with bent knees. Focus on maximum effort each rep, resting fully between jumps. Mark a spot on the wall to track your progress.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads, glutes, calves.

levels.name: Approach
levels.note: Add a step into the jump

items.name: Waking dry mouth
items.why: Re-test: Weekly, first thing. Lower is better.

fields.release: 0 = none. 1 = slight. 2 = clearly dry. 3 = unpleasant. Crude, but it is one of the few home readouts on whether the tongue work is reaching sleep — and that takes months, so the record matters more than any single morning.
fields.notice: Recorded in 0–3.

items.name: Waking up the soles of the feet
items.why: Your feet are one of the three things balance runs on, alongside the inner ear and vision. Shoes hold them still and flat all day, and the information they send gets quieter.
items.equipment: Different surfaces — carpet, tile, a towel, a ball; bare feet

fields.tool: Bare feet and a few different textures. Nothing to buy.
fields.release: Seated. Roll a ball slowly under the foot with light pressure — enough to feel it, not enough to be release work. Then stand and walk slowly across two or three different surfaces, paying attention to what each one feels like under the arch, the heel, the ball of the foot. A minute or two per foot.
fields.notice: Whether the two feet report differently. Whether parts of the sole feel vague or numb compared to others. That vagueness is what this is aimed at.
fields.careful: Light. This is about sensation, not pressure — the arch release card is where pressure belongs. If you have reduced feeling in your feet from any cause, that belongs to a clinician before it belongs to a drill.
fields.load: Follow with a rung of the balance ladder while still barefoot. The information is freshest right afterward, which is the whole reason to pair them.

levels.name: Paired with balance
levels.note: Sensory work, then straight into your balance rung, barefoot.

evidence.grade: single small trial, promising and directly on-population
evidence.basis: A 2025 randomised trial in 65 young adults with generalized joint hypermobility tested a two-week home plantar sensory training programme against information alone, measuring touch, vibration, two-point discrimination, proprioception, strength and balance. One trial in an asymptomatic group is a starting point, not a settled finding — but it is unusually close to the population this module serves.

items.authoringNote: worth asking where he'd place it relative to the balance ladder.

items.name: Walking knee-to-chest
items.why: Opens the back of the hip on the moving leg while the standing leg quietly practises balance.

fields.release: Each step, lift the knee and draw it in toward your chest with both hands, then release it and step through onto that foot. Alternate down the room.
fields.load: Pair with glute and hip-flexor strengthening.
fields.notice: The standing leg. Balance on one side is often noticeably worse — that is information, not a failure.
fields.careful: Pull the knee in; don't wrench it. If the standing leg's balance is poor, do this near a wall.

levels.name: As demonstrated
levels.note: A handful of passes across the room.

items.name: Walking side lunge
items.why: Opens the inner thigh in the sideways direction that almost nothing else in a day asks for.

fields.release: Step wide to the side and sink into that hip, keeping the trailing leg straight and both feet flat. Come up, step through, repeat down the room.
fields.load: Pair with adductor and glute-medius strengthening so the range you open has something holding it.
fields.notice: Whether one side sinks further than the other, and whether the trailing foot wants to roll.
fields.careful: Controlled descent. Do not drop into the bottom of the range and bounce.

levels.name: As demonstrated
levels.note: A handful of passes across the room.

items.name: Walking straight-leg scoop
items.why: Opens the whole back line of the leg with each step, while you are already moving — a stretch that doesn't require standing still.

fields.release: Step the lead leg out with the heel down and the toe pulled up, knee straight. Hinge forward over that leg and scoop your hands upward through the air as you go. Alternate legs, walking the length of the room.
fields.load: Pair with posterior-chain strengthening in the days after — bridges or hinges — so the new range gets used.
fields.notice: Where the stretch lands: behind the knee, mid-hamstring, or up into the low back. That tells you which part is actually tight.
fields.careful: Straight does not mean locked. If your knee snaps back past straight, stop short of that — the aim is a long hamstring, not a hyperextended joint.

levels.name: As demonstrated
levels.note: A handful of passes across the room. Rep count not stated — ask.

items.name: Wall angel
items.why: Re-test: Monthly. Higher is better.

fields.release: Back to the wall, low back flat and held flat. Slide the arms up. 0 = forearms nowhere near. 1 = wrists touch. 2 = forearms touch but the back arches. 3 = forearms stay on the wall with the back flat.
fields.notice: Recorded in 0–3.

items.name: Wall Calf Stretch
items.why: Step back, press heel into floor, lean into wall

fields.release: Stand facing a wall. Step one foot back, keeping it straight with heel pressed into floor. Lean into the wall, bending the front knee. Feel the stretch in the back calf. For soleus (deeper calf), slightly bend the back knee while keeping heel down.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: calves, achilles.

levels.name: Both Versions
levels.note: Both versions (straight + bent knee), 15 sec each

items.name: Wall Sit
items.why: Back flat on wall, thighs parallel to floor, hold

fields.release: Stand with your back flat against a wall and slide down until your thighs are parallel to the floor, knees bent at 90 degrees. Keep your back pressed firmly against the wall and your feet flat on the floor. Hold this position for as long as you can. You should feel a deep burn in your quads. Avoid placing your hands on your thighs for support.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: quads.

items.name: Wall Slide
items.why: Back and arms flat on wall, slide arms up and down

fields.release: Stand with your back flat against a wall, feet about six inches away. Place the back of your hands and forearms against the wall at shoulder height. Slowly slide your arms up overhead while keeping your back, hands, and forearms in contact with the wall, then slide back down. If anything loses wall contact, you have limited mobility in that range.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: upper back, shoulders, posture.

items.name: When this module is the wrong answer
items.why: Some nerve symptoms are a signal to be examined, and gliding them is at best a delay. This card is here so the module has somewhere to send you, and it sits second on purpose.

fields.tool: Nothing.
fields.release:
Stop and arrange to be seen, rather than working through this module, if any of these are true.

**Weakness you can see, not just feel.** A foot that slaps or catches when you walk. A hand that drops things or cannot hold a grip. Weakness that is getting worse week on week.

**Numbness through the saddle area, or any change in bladder or bowel control, alongside back or leg symptoms.** This one is not a wait-and-see. It is a same-day medical assessment.

**Symptoms in both arms or both legs at once**, or symptoms that came on after a fall, a crash, or a blow to the head or neck.

**Symptoms that wake you at night**, or that are steadily worse rather than varying with what you do.

**Numbness or burning that is patchy, symmetrical, or in a glove-and-stocking pattern** rather than following one nerve's territory. That pattern points somewhere other than a compressed nerve, and it deserves a diagnosis rather than a drill.
fields.notice: Whether your symptoms actually follow one nerve's territory — the map card is next door — or whether they are more scattered than that. That distinction is most of what a clinician wants to hear from you.
fields.careful: Nothing on this card is a diagnosis and none of it is a checklist you can pass. It is a list of reasons to hand the question to someone who can examine you.
fields.load: n/a

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: add one to the list. Symptoms brought on by looking up, by holding your head in one position, or by neck movement — particularly with headache at the base of the skull, visual change, or a feeling of the head being heavy — belong with a clinician before any neck-involving drill, and every item in this module involves the neck. Orthostatic: dizziness on standing is a different problem from nerve symptoms; if the two are getting tangled, see the vestibular module's first card, which exists to separate them.

evidence.grade: Standard referral practice, not an intervention.
evidence.basis: These are the presentations that conventionally prompt examination rather than self-management. Stated here as reasons to be seen, with no diagnostic claim attached to any of them.

items.name: Where the arch meets the heel
items.why: The anchor point of the whole arch. Tightness upstream in the calf tends to show up here.

fields.tool: A ball, or both thumbs.
fields.release: Find the front edge of the heel pad, where the softer arch tissue begins. Press there and hold. Pulling your toes back with your other hand puts the tissue on tension and often makes the spot easier to find.
fields.notice: Whether it spreads forward into the arch. Compare sides.
fields.careful: Moderate pressure. This area does not respond well to being attacked, and if morning first-step pain is part of your picture, less is more.
fields.load: Calf raises, slow down on the lowering — the calf is upstream of this and it is the more useful place to get stronger.

items.name: Which nerve is which — a map you can use on yourself
items.why: There is no point gliding the wrong nerve. Each of the five tracts in this module serves a different patch of skin, and where your symptoms sit is the cheapest clue available.

fields.tool: Your own hand, and your own leg.
fields.release:
**In the arm, three tracts share the job.**

The one running down the middle of the forearm and into the palm serves the thumb, the index and middle fingers, and half the ring finger. It passes through the tunnel at the front of the wrist. Symptoms here are the classic ones — thumb-side fingers going numb at night, dropping things, a hand that feels swollen when it is not.

The one running behind the bony point on the inside of the elbow — the funny bone — serves the little finger and the outer half of the ring finger. Symptoms tend to appear when the elbow has been bent for a long time: on a phone, on a steering wheel, asleep with the arm curled.

The one wrapping around the back of the upper arm serves the back of the hand and the web of the thumb. It is the one to think about with symptoms across the back of the hand, or a wrist that feels weak lifting.

**In the leg, two.**

The large tract down the back of the thigh serves the back of the leg, the calf, and most of the foot. Below the knee it divides — one branch running down the back of the calf into the sole, the other around the outside of the knee and down the front of the shin to the top of the foot.

The tract at the front of the hip serves the front of the thigh and, through a long branch, the inner side of the shin down toward the inner ankle.
fields.notice: Draw the edge of your own symptoms with a finger. Does the border follow one of these patches, or does it ignore them? A border that follows one patch points at one nerve. A border that ignores all of them points somewhere else, and the get-evaluated card covers that.
fields.careful: These territories overlap between people, and the textbook borders are tidier than real bodies. Use this to choose which item to try, never to conclude what is wrong with you.
fields.load: n/a

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: in hypermobile people symptoms often refuse to sit inside any one of these patches, and that is itself information — it makes a single compressed nerve less likely and a small-fibre problem more so, which is a clinician's question.

evidence.grade: Standard anatomy, described in the app's own words.
evidence.basis: Peripheral nerve sensory territories are textbook anatomy. Described here from anatomy rather than reproduced from any chart, with the overlap between people stated rather than hidden.

items.name: Woodchop
items.why: Rotate from hips, arms follow torso, control the motion

fields.release: Anchor a resistance band low or high to one side. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and grab the band with both hands. Rotate your torso to pull the band diagonally across your body in a chopping motion, pivoting at your hips. Control the return. The power comes from your hips and core, not your arms. Keep your arms relatively straight throughout.
fields.notice: Where the work should land: obliques, core.

items.name: World's Greatest Stretch
items.why: Lunge, plant hand, rotate and reach to sky, feel every part open

fields.release: Step into a deep lunge position and plant the hand on the same side as your front foot on the floor inside the foot. Rotate your torso and reach the other arm toward the sky, opening your chest. Hold briefly, then return your hand to the floor. This stretch hits the hips, hamstrings, thoracic spine, and groin all in one movement.
fields.notice: Where you should feel it: hip flexors, hamstrings, thoracic spine, groin.

levels.name: Add Hamstring Reach
levels.note: Straighten front leg to stretch hamstring

items.name: Wrapping the calf, then moving it
items.why: The compression flossing family's first appearance in this library, applied to the segment it has actually been studied on. Read the family guide before this item — the evidence has a twist that changes how you should read your own result.

fields.tool: A flat rubber floss band, several inches wide. Not a resistance band.
fields.release: Wrap the calf in a firm overlapping spiral working upward from just above the ankle, tight enough to be clearly compressive but not so tight that the foot goes white, cold or numb. Then move: ankle circles, pointing and lifting the foot, and squats or heel raises if you can. Keep moving the whole time it is on. Then unwrap immediately and move the ankle again straight away.
fields.notice: Range before and after — and then, once, do the same movements without the band and compare that too. The trial evidence says the movements are doing most of the work, and you can test that on yourself in one session.
fields.careful: Short applications only. Off immediately for numbness, pins and needles, colour change, or coldness in the foot. Never over a wound, a rash, a varicose vein, or a numb area. If you have circulation problems, blood clots in your history, or take blood thinners, do not use this family without asking a clinician first.
fields.load: The movements under the band are the load, and continue them afterward.

items.populationCareful: Hypermobile: bruising and skin fragility make firm circumferential compression a poor first choice, and extra ankle range is probably not what you need. Orthostatic: compression and abrupt changes in limb blood flow sit badly with unstable blood pressure — raise this one with a clinician rather than experimenting.
items.dose: Around two minutes is the typical application in trials [derived — flossing trial protocols and a perfusion study using a two-minute application]. This library does not recommend longer.

levels.name: Light wrap, short, ankle movement only
levels.note: Learn the sensation before doing anything more.

levels.name: Add loaded movement
levels.note: Heel raises or squats while the band is on.

loadAfter.name: Calf raises, slow lowering
loadAfter.note: The imported 'Eccentric heel drops' card. Match at S5.

evidence.grade: Grade B, and the finding cuts against the technique: range improves before-to-after, but not compared with doing the same movements without the band.
evidence.basis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of compression flossing for ankle dorsiflexion found moderate improvement from before to after, and no effect compared with a control of the same range-of-motion activities alone — the authors' reading was that the gains came from the exercises, not the band. A separate perfusion study measured a marked drop in tissue oxygen during a two-minute application and did not confirm the rebound-blood-flow story the technique is usually sold with. It is in the library for breadth and because people ask about it; it is exploratory tier and the card says plainly what the trials found.

items.sourceNote: App content, not clinician-prescribed. Worth raising with a clinician before use if you have orthostatic symptoms or any circulatory history.
